Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ING_Group:
Dutch multinational banking and financial services corporation

The **ING Group** ([Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language"): _ING Groep__[N.V.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naamloze_vennootschap "Naamloze vennootschap")_) is a [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands")[multinational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation")[banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank "Bank") and [financial services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_services "Financial services") corporation headquartered in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"). Its primary businesses are [retail banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_banking "Retail banking"), [direct banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_bank "Direct bank"), [commercial banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_bank "Commercial bank"), [investment banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_banking "Investment banking"), [wholesale banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wholesale_banking "Wholesale banking"), [private banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_banking "Private banking"), and [asset management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset_management "Asset management"). With [total assets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset "Asset") of €1,316 billion (as of March 2026),[\[19\]](about:blank#cite_note-:13-19) it consistently ranks among the [largest banks globally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_banks "List of largest banks").

The ING is the Dutch member of the [Inter-Alpha Group of Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-Alpha_Group_of_Banks "Inter-Alpha Group of Banks"), a co-operative [consortium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consortium "Consortium") of 11 prominent European banks.[\[20\]](about:blank#cite_note-20) ING Bank has been a member in the [list of global systemically important banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_systemically_important_banks "List of systemically important banks") since the list was created in 2011.[\[21\]](about:blank#cite_note-21) It has been designated as a Significant Institution since the entry into force of [European Banking Supervision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Banking_Supervision "European Banking Supervision") in late 2014, and as a consequence is directly supervised by the [European Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank "European Central Bank").[\[22\]](about:blank#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](about:blank#cite_note-23)

As of the first quarter of 2026, ING served 40.8 million customers across nine retail markets and a wider wholesale banking footprint.[\[24\]](about:blank#cite_note-:11-24) It is a component of the [EURO STOXX 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EURO_STOXX_50 "EURO STOXX 50")[stock market index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_market_index "Stock market index").[\[25\]](about:blank#cite_note-25) As of December 2019, the long-term debt for the company is €150 billion.[\[26\]](about:blank#cite_note-26)_ING_ is an abbreviation of __Internationale Nederlanden Groep__ (lit.'International Netherlands Group'). The ING's logo [alludes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_symbols_of_the_Netherlands "National symbols of the Netherlands") to the [Dutch symbolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_the_Netherlands "Coat of arms of the Netherlands") used by several of ING's corporate predecessors, including [_Postbank_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postbank_N.V. "Postbank N.V."). Its original blue [lion symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_depictions_of_lions "Cultural depictions of lions") was refreshed in 2000, and later replaced by the [orange variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_\(colour\) "Orange (colour)") between 2007 and 2009.[\[27\]](about:blank#cite_note-:26-27)[\[28\]](about:blank#cite_note-:27-28)[\[29\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_Engelen2009196,_240-29)

### Origins in insurance and banking

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins in insurance and banking")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Achtergevel_-_Koog_aan_de_Zaan_-_20126774_-_RCE.jpg/250px-Achtergevel_-_Koog_aan_de_Zaan_-_20126774_-_RCE.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Achtergevel_-_Koog_aan_de_Zaan_-_20126774_-_RCE.jpg)

[Reformed church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Churches_in_the_Netherlands "Reformed Churches in the Netherlands") with the cemetery in [Koog aan de Zaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koog_aan_de_Zaan "Koog aan de Zaan"), where the [burial fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_society "Burial society")_Kooger Doodenbos_ set up in 1743 made ING history

The ING Group traces its roots to two major insurance companies in the Netherlands and the banking services of the [Dutch government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_Netherlands "Politics of the Netherlands"). Its oldest predecessor was the [burial fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_society "Burial society")_Kooger Doodenbos_, founded in 1743 in [Koog aan de Zaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koog_aan_de_Zaan "Koog aan de Zaan") in [North Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Holland "North Holland"), by nine local men. They declared that they were entering into a contract with one another "for the collection and [deposit of funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deposit_account "Deposit account"), which are to be used for a proper burial of the partners of the said contract".[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-:28-2)

An initial sum of [fl.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_guilder "Dutch guilder") 300 was transferred to the [savings bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savings_bank "Savings bank") in 1820, and by 1835 the fund decided to stop distributing its [surplus cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surplus_sharing "Surplus sharing") and [invest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment "Investment") it in the bank or in [securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_\(finance\) "Security (finance)") instead. In 1949, the Kooger Doodenbos — contributing an insured capital of fl. 30,915 and 229 contracts — merged into Vesta, a birth-benefit life insurer that had relocated from Amsterdam to [Arnhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnhem "Arnhem"). Through a series of further mergers, it eventually became part of _[Nationale-Nederlanden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NN_Group "NN Group")_.[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-:28-2)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Stadsarchief_Amsterdam%2C_Afb_OSIM00005001166.jpg/250px-Stadsarchief_Amsterdam%2C_Afb_OSIM00005001166.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stadsarchief_Amsterdam,_Afb_OSIM00005001166.jpg)

Office of the _Fire Insurance Company of the Netherlands of 1845_, at the [Munplein square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muntplein,_Amsterdam "Muntplein, Amsterdam") in Amsterdam, ca. 1890

On 12 April 1845, the fire insurance company _Assurantie Maatschappij tegen Brandschade de Nederlanden van 1845_ ("Fire Insurance Company of the Netherlands of 1845") was founded, as approved by [King Willem II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_II_of_the_Netherlands "William II of the Netherlands"). The company grew to be the leading Dutch insurance company, opening its first foreign agency in Batavia (now [Jakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta "Jakarta")) in 1857 and reaching [branches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branch_\(banking\) "Branch (banking)") across 139 locations worldwide by 1900. It later changed its name to _De Nederlanden van 1845_.[\[30\]](about:blank#cite_note-:14-30)[\[31\]](about:blank#cite_note-:15-31)

Two decades later, in 1863, the [life insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_insurance "Life insurance") company _Nationale Levensverzekerings Bank_ ("National Life Insurance Bank") was founded in [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam").[\[30\]](about:blank#cite_note-:14-30)[\[31\]](about:blank#cite_note-:15-31) From 1932, the two companies cooperated on [group insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_insurance "Group insurance") and [pension insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pension_insurance_contract "Pension insurance contract"), and in 1938 De Nederlanden van 1845 acquired its first foreign insurer, De Vaderlandsche in [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"). During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the offices of both companies were bombed and 46 employees were killed.[\[30\]](about:blank#cite_note-:14-30)[\[31\]](about:blank#cite_note-:15-31) The two firms [merged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") on 3 April 1963, to form _Nationale-Nederlanden_, combining the country's largest insurer with its second-largest. The new group expanded significantly internationally during the 1970s and 1980s, introducing its iconic orange _N_ logo in 1970.[\[32\]](about:blank#cite_note-32) In 1986, Nationale-Nederlanden expanded its portfolio to include the banking sector, becoming the sole owner of the struggling [mortgage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage "Mortgage") bank Westland-Utrecht Hypotheekbank.[\[33\]](about:blank#cite_note-:29-33)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Mr%2C_SFA022810721.jpg/250px-Mr%2C_SFA022810721.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mr,_SFA022810721.jpg)

Johan Herman Carel Bussing, the newly-appointed director of the _Rijkspostspaarbank_, at his desk, in 1913

In April 1881, the _Rijkspostspaarbank_ was created with the [statutory task](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statutory_instrument "Statutory instrument") of providing [savings opportunities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savings_account "Savings account") to broad Dutch population by leveraging the existing post-office network into a [postal savings system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_savings_system "Postal savings system"), to encourage workers to start saving. Around 1916, the [municipally-run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipally_owned_corporation "Municipally owned corporation")_Gemeentegiro Amsterdam_ (GGA) was established to centralize Amsterdam's municipal cash transactions, opening its services to private individuals in 1918.[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_Engelen2009261%E2%80%93268-3) In 1961, the GGA became the first bank in the Netherlands to issue [plastic payment cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_card "Payment card") (_giropassen_), and in 1969 it introduced the country's first [automated teller machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATM "ATM"), installed in Amsterdam's newly built district [Bijlmermeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijlmermeer "Bijlmermeer").[\[34\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_Engelen200936,_47-34)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Roofoverval_op_bijkantoor_Nederlandse_Middenstands_Bank_Beethovenstraat%2C_Amsterd%2C_Bestanddeelnr_924-0492.jpg/250px-Roofoverval_op_bijkantoor_Nederlandse_Middenstands_Bank_Beethovenstraat%2C_Amsterd%2C_Bestanddeelnr_924-0492.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Roofoverval_op_bijkantoor_Nederlandse_Middenstands_Bank_Beethovenstraat,_Amsterd,_Bestanddeelnr_924-0492.jpg)

Branch of the _Nederlandse Middenstands Bank_ on Beethovenstraat in Amsterdam, pictured in 1970

In 1918, the _Postcheque- en Girodienst_ (PCGD) was established as part of the state telecommunication company [PTT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPN "KPN"), creating the Netherlands' first national [giro-based](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_\(banking\) "Giro (banking)")[payment services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_service_provider "Payment service provider") allowing working families and [SMEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_and_medium_enterprises "Small and medium enterprises") to manage their income and expenses through post offices.[\[4\]](about:blank#cite_note-:16-4)[\[35\]](about:blank#cite_note-35) In 1965, the PCGD became the first fully automated giro system in the world, and in 1979 it took over the GGA, bringing Amsterdam's municipal giro services under national administration.[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_Engelen2009261%E2%80%93268-3)[\[4\]](about:blank#cite_note-:16-4) These state-run postal financial services were brought under the [official prudential supervision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_regulation_and_supervision "Bank regulation and supervision") of the [Dutch central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Nederlandsche_Bank "De Nederlandsche Bank") from 1979.[\[36\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMooijPrast2003Section_5-36)

Separately, in 1927 the _Nederlandsche Middenstands Bank_ (NMB) was created through the merger of several institutions — to provide credit to middle-class and SME businesses in the Netherlands and abroad, following the Dutch banking crisis of the early 1920s.[\[37\]](about:blank#cite_note-:17-37)[\[38\]](about:blank#cite_note-38)[During World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_in_World_War_II "Netherlands in World War II"), the Dutch government took over 86% of NMB's capital, and its gradual privatization continued until the turn of the 1980s and 1990s.[\[33\]](about:blank#cite_note-:29-33) During the 1960s, NMB increasingly focused on the retail market and expanded internationally.[\[37\]](about:blank#cite_note-:17-37)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Prins_Bernhard_opent_nieuw_gebouw_NMB_in_Amsterdam_bij_maquette_rechts_de_voorz%2C_Bestanddeelnr_927-2640.jpg/250px-Prins_Bernhard_opent_nieuw_gebouw_NMB_in_Amsterdam_bij_maquette_rechts_de_voorz%2C_Bestanddeelnr_927-2640.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prins_Bernhard_opent_nieuw_gebouw_NMB_in_Amsterdam_bij_maquette_rechts_de_voorz,_Bestanddeelnr_927-2640.jpg)

[Prince Bernhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Bernhard_of_Lippe-Biesterfeld "Prince Bernhard of Lippe-Biesterfeld") opens the new NMB building in Amsterdam, June 1974

In 1986, the _Rijkspostspaarbank_ and the PCGD were combined to form the single banking entity [Postbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postbank_N.V. "Postbank N.V."),[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_Engelen2009261%E2%80%93268-3) and had more than 7.5 million private account holders.[\[30\]](about:blank#cite_note-:14-30)[\[37\]](about:blank#cite_note-:17-37) That year, Postbank introduced _Girotel_, the first [electronic home banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_banking "Online banking") system in the Netherlands (by 2006, it had evolved into the internet platform _MijnPostbank_, used by 2 million customers).[\[39\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_Engelen200979%E2%80%9390,_179%E2%80%93193-39) The Dutch government formally privatized Postbank in 1987, and it entered the free market subject to restrictions barring it from commercial lending, [corporate securities trading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_\(finance\) "Security (finance)") and selling insurance — limits that constrained its ability to compete as an independent commercial bank.[\[40\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEvan_Engelen2009196,_240,_254-40) In 1989, Postbank merged with the NMB to form NMB Postbank Groep, which became one of the five largest Dutch banks of the time.[\[37\]](about:blank#cite_note-:17-37)

### Merger and formation of ING Group

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Merger and formation of ING Group")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Geldautomaat_Potterstraat.jpg/250px-Geldautomaat_Potterstraat.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Geldautomaat_Potterstraat.jpg)

Postbank ATMs on Potterstraat, next to the [main post office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht_Post_Office "Utrecht Post Office") in [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht "Utrecht"), in 2008

In 1991, the banking business of NMB Postbank Groep and the insurance business of Nationale-Nederlanden were merged to create the _ING Group_.[\[41\]](about:blank#cite_note-41) The merger, completed on 4 March 1991, was made possible by the liberalization of [Dutch financial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_Netherlands "Law of the Netherlands") in 1990, which permitted [cross-ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_ownership "Cross ownership") between banking and insurance institutions. A decade prior, in 1981, Nationale-Nederlanden and [Aegon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegon "Aegon") rescued struggling regional mortgage banks, a move facilitated by the Minister of Finance and considered the first step toward lifting the ban on cross-sector mergers in the Netherlands.[\[36\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMooijPrast2003Section_5-36)

The newly formed group adopted a [bancassurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bancassurance "Bancassurance") model, distributing Nationale-Nederlanden's insurance products through Postbank's extensive retail deposit base. The 1990 liberalization made the Netherlands a pioneer in bancassurance, and the rapid emergence of conglomerates like ING prompted the 1990 Protocol, which mandated strict cooperation and information exchange between banking and insurance supervisors.[\[42\]](about:blank#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMooijPrast2003Section_6-42)[Aad Jacobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aad_Jacobs "Aad Jacobs") served as the group's first [chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chair_\(officer\) "Chair (officer

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Operational_Resilience_Act:
Financial regulation in the EU

The **Digital Operational Resilience Act** (**DORA**), officially Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 is a [European Union regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_\(European_Union\) "Regulation (European Union)").[\[1\]](about:blank#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-2) It requires financial entities to improve their digital operational resilience.

DORA aims to improve the digital operational resilience of financial entities in the EU and their [ICT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_and_communications_technology "Information and communications technology") suppliers and create a uniform regulatory framework across the EU, in order to reduce the susceptibility to cyber threats across the entire value chain of the financial sector. In addition, DORA intends to harmonize national regulations regarding the security of [IT systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_technology "Information technology") in the financial sector, thus strengthening the European financial market as a whole against cyber risks and information and communications technology incidents.

The regulation applies to financial entities and third-party suppliers of ICT services. Article 2 defines financial entities as:

The regulation explicitly does not apply to:

*   [Insurance intermediaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance_intermediaries "Insurance intermediaries"), reinsurance intermediaries and ancillary insurance intermediaries which are [microenterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-enterprise "Micro-enterprise") or small or medium-sized enterprises
*   Insurance and reinsurance undertakings as referred to in Article 4 of Directive 2009/138/EC
*   Institutions for occupational retirement provision which operate pension schemes which together do not have more than 15 members in total
*   Managers of alternative investment funds as referred to in Article 3(2) of [Directive 2011/61/EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directive_2011/61/EU "Directive 2011/61/EU")
*   Natural or legal persons exempted pursuant to Articles 2 and 3 of [Directive 2014/65/EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directive_2014/65/EU "Directive 2014/65/EU")
*   Post office [giro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_\(banking\) "Giro (banking)") institutions as referred to in Article 2(5), point (3), of [Directive 2013/36/EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directive_2013/36/EU "Directive 2013/36/EU")

## Proportionality principle

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Digital_Operational_Resilience_Act&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Proportionality principle")\]

Article 4 defines the [proportionality principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportionality_principle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Proportionality principle (page does not exist)"), resulting in some exceptions for smaller enterprises which fall within the scope of the regulation despite their size. This allows for a simplified implementation of certain requirements in accordance with the overall risk profile of the enterprise. An example for this is the simplified ICT risk management framework according to Article 16 in combination with a [regulatory technical standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_technical_standard?action=edit&redlink=1 "Regulatory technical standard (page does not exist)") (RTS).

The regulation comprises 64 articles divided into 9 chapters:

1.  General provisions (Art. 1–4)
2.  ICT risk management (Art. 5–16)
3.  ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting (Art. 17–23)
4.  Digital operational resilience testing (Art. 24–27)
5.  Managing of ICT third-party risk (Art. 28–44)
6.  Information-sharing arrangements (Art. 45)
7.  Competent authorities (Art. 46–56)
8.  Delegated acts (Art. 57)
9.  Transitional and final provisions (Art. 58–64)

In addition, the [European Supervisory Authorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Supervisory_Authorities "European Supervisory Authorities") develop regulatory and implementing technical standards (RTS and ITS), which, being published in the [Official Journal of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Journal_of_the_European_Union "Official Journal of the European Union"), also become legally binding:

| Type       | Subject                                                                                                                                         | DORA reference | Implemented                                    | Status                                                            |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| RTS        | ICT risk management framework                                                                                                                   | Art. 15        | Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 | In force                                                          |
| RTS        | Simplified ICT risk management framework                                                                                                        | Art. 16 (3)    | Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 | In force                                                          |
| RTS        | Classification of ICT-related incidents and cyber threats                                                                                       | Art. 18 (3)    | Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 | In force                                                          |
| RTS        | Content of the reports for major ICT-related incidents                                                                                          | Art. 20 (a)    |                                                | Adopted October 23, 2024; pending publication in Official Journal |
| ITS        | Standard forms, templates and procedures for financial entities to report a major ICT-related incident                                          | Art. 20 (b)    |                                                | Final draft published July 17, 2024                               |
| RTS        | Threat-led penetration testing                                                                                                                  | Art. 26 (11)   |                                                | Final draft published July 17, 2024                               |

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_Intelligence_Act:
2024 European Union regulation

The **Artificial Intelligence Act** (**AI Act**)[\[1\]](about:blank#cite_note-32024R1689-1) is a [European Union regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_\(European_Union\) "Regulation (European Union)") concerning [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") (AI). It establishes a common regulatory and [legal framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_framework "Legal framework") for AI within the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU).[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-2) The regulation entered into force on 1 August 2024,[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-ecpressrelease-3) with provisions that shall come into operation gradually over the following 6 to 36 months.[\[4\]](about:blank#cite_note-4)

It covers most AI systems across a wide range of sectors, with exemptions for AI used only for military, national security, research purposes, or for non-professional use.[\[5\]](about:blank#cite_note-5) As a form of product regulation, it does not create individual rights; instead, it places duties on AI providers and on organisations that use AI in a professional context.[\[6\]](about:blank#cite_note-:10-6)[\[7\]](about:blank#cite_note-:4-7)

The Act classifies non-exempt AI applications by their risk of causing harm. There are four levels – unacceptable, high, limited, minimal – plus an additional category for general-purpose AI.[\[8\]](about:blank#cite_note-8)

*   Applications with unacceptable risks are banned.
*   High-risk applications must comply with security, [transparency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_\(behavior\) "Transparency (behavior)") and quality obligations, and undergo [conformity assessments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformity_assessment "Conformity assessment").
*   Limited-risk applications only have transparency obligations.
*   Minimal-risk applications are not regulated.

For general-purpose AI, transparency requirements are imposed, with reduced requirements for [open source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_source "Open source") models, and additional evaluations for high-capability models.[\[9\]](about:blank#cite_note-:1-9)[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-:2-10)

The Act also creates a European Artificial Intelligence Board to promote national cooperation and ensure compliance with the regulation.[\[11\]](about:blank#cite_note-11) Like the EU's [General Data Protection Regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Data_Protection_Regulation "General Data Protection Regulation"), the Act can apply [extraterritorially](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraterritoriality "Extraterritoriality") to providers from outside the EU if they have users within the EU.[\[7\]](about:blank#cite_note-:4-7)

Proposed by the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") on 21 April 2021,[\[12\]](about:blank#cite_note-52021PC0206-12) it passed the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") on 13 March 2024,[\[13\]](about:blank#cite_note-CNBC-13) and was unanimously approved by the [EU Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_the_European_Union "Council of the European Union") on 21 May 2024.[\[14\]](about:blank#cite_note-auto-14) The draft Act was revised to address the rise in popularity of [generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_AI "Generative AI") systems, such as [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT"), whose general-purpose capabilities did not fit the main framework.[\[15\]](about:blank#cite_note-15)

There are different risk categories depending on the type of application, with a specific category dedicated to general-purpose generative AI:

*   Unacceptable risk – AI applications in this category are banned, except for [specific exemptions](about:blank#Exemptions).[\[16\]](about:blank#cite_note-LQDN_technosolutionist_goldrush-16) When no exemption applies, this includes AI applications that [manipulate human behaviour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manipulation_\(psychology\) "Manipulation (psychology)"), those that use real-time remote [biometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biometrics "Biometrics") identification (such as [facial recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_recognition_system "Facial recognition system")) in public spaces, and those used for [social scoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Credit_System "Social Credit System") (ranking individuals based on their personal characteristics, socio-economic status, or behaviour).[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-:2-10)[\[17\]](about:blank#cite_note-17)
*   High-risk – AI applications that are expected to pose significant threats to health, safety, or the [fundamental rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_rights "Fundamental rights") of persons. Notably, AI systems used in health, education, recruitment, critical infrastructure management, law enforcement or justice. They are subject to quality, transparency, human oversight and safety obligations, and in some cases require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before deployment.[\[18\]](about:blank#cite_note-:11-18)[\[19\]](about:blank#cite_note-19) A Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) is an ex ante review to identify and mitigate potential impacts on fundamental rights before an AI system is deployed.[\[18\]](about:blank#cite_note-:11-18)[\[20\]](about:blank#cite_note-20) Earlier work on algorithmic impact assessments has suggested that such tools should identify which individuals and communities are affected by an automated system, describe possible harms, and provide a basis for public and institutional scrutiny of its use.[\[21\]](about:blank#cite_note-:13-21) They must be evaluated both before they are placed on the market and throughout their life cycle. The list of high-risk applications can be expanded over time, without the need to modify the AI Act itself.[\[7\]](about:blank#cite_note-:4-7) Citizens also have a right to submit complaints about AI systems and to receive [explanations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_explanation "Right to explanation") of decisions made by high-risk AI that affect their rights.[\[22\]](about:blank#cite_note-EUParliamentPassage-22)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Content_containing_AI_label.svg/250px-Content_containing_AI_label.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Content_containing_AI_label.svg)

Unofficial example of label indicating AI content.

*   Limited risk – AI systems in this category have transparency obligations, ensuring users are informed that they are interacting with an AI system and allowing them to make informed choices. This category includes, for example, AI applications that make it possible to generate or manipulate images, sound, or videos (like [deepfakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake "Deepfake")).[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-:2-10)
*   Minimal risk – This category includes, for example, AI systems used for video games or [spam filters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spam_filters "Spam filters"). Most AI applications are expected to fall into this category.[\[23\]](about:blank#cite_note-23) These systems are not regulated, and Member States cannot impose additional regulations due to [maximum harmonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_harmonisation "Maximum harmonisation") rules. Existing national laws regarding the design or use of such systems are overridden. However, a voluntary code of conduct is suggested.[\[24\]](about:blank#cite_note-Veale-24)

The risk-based scheme follows a product-safety model in which regulatory duties are assigned to the providers and deployers of AI systems, and these duties become more demanding as the potential impact on health, safety, or fundamental rights increases. This structure is meant to ensure that oversight focuses on systems likely to create significant risks while allowing lighter approaches for uses considered less sensitive.[\[25\]](about:blank#cite_note-:14-25) Some legal scholars also argue that, in practice, the Act frames "trustworthy AI" as systems that can show compliance with these safety and risk thresholds.[\[26\]](about:blank#cite_note-:15-26) According to an initial appraisal by the European Parliamentary Research Service, the Commission's impact assessment drew on stakeholder consultations and a wide range of existing research when comparing policy options for this risk-based framework.[\[27\]](about:blank#cite_note-:16-27)

Added in 2023, the general-purpose AI category includes [foundation models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_model "Foundation model") (for example, ChatGPT) that can perform a wide range of tasks. If a model's weights and design are made open source, developers must publish a training data summary and a copyright policy; closed-source models must meet broader transparency requirements. High-impact models that pose systemic risks (require more than 1025[floating-point operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLOPS "FLOPS") to train)[\[28\]](about:blank#cite_note-:3-28) must undergo extra evaluation.[\[6\]](about:blank#cite_note-:10-6)[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-:2-10) A [General-Purpose AI Code of Practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-Purpose_AI_Code_of_Practice "General-Purpose AI Code of Practice"), published on 10 July 2025, outlines three main chapters on transparency, copyright, and safety and security to help providers demonstrate compliance with the AI Act. Participation in the code is voluntary.[\[29\]](about:blank#cite_note-29)

Beyond these basic transparency duties, the Act sets a common list of obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models. They must publish a summary of the training data, adopt a policy to comply with copyright law, and provide technical documentation to downstream providers and supervisory authorities. Models that are designated as posing systemic risk must also carry out model evaluations and adversarial testing, assess and mitigate risks such as bias and security failures, report serious incidents, and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity.[\[30\]](about:blank#cite_note-:17-30)

Articles 2.3 and 2.6 exempt AI systems used for [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence#Military "Artificial intelligence") or [national security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_in_government "Artificial intelligence in government") purposes or pure scientific research and development from the AI Act.[\[16\]](about:blank#cite_note-LQDN_technosolutionist_goldrush-16) In particular, the Regulation does not apply where AI systems are used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, or to systems developed and put into service solely for scientific research and development; if such systems are later used for other purposes (for example, civilian or law-enforcement uses), the Act applies.[\[1\]](about:blank#cite_note-32024R1689-1) These activities remain governed by separate EU and national rules on defence, security, and intelligence rather than by the AI Act itself.[\[31\]](about:blank#cite_note-:18-31)

Article 5.2 bans algorithmic video surveillance of people ("The use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces"[\[32\]](about:blank#cite_note-32)) only if it is conducted in real time. Exceptions allowing real-time algorithmic video surveillance include policing aims including "a real and present or real and foreseeable threat of terrorist attack".[\[16\]](about:blank#cite_note-LQDN_technosolutionist_goldrush-16)

Recital 31 of the Act states that it aims to prohibit "AI systems providing social scoring of natural persons by public or private actors", but allows for "lawful evaluation practices of natural persons that are carried out for a specific purpose in accordance with Union and national law."[\[33\]](about:blank#cite_note-33)[La Quadrature du Net](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Quadrature_du_Net "La Quadrature du Net") interprets this exemption as permitting sector-specific social scoring systems,[\[16\]](about:blank#cite_note-LQDN_technosolutionist_goldrush-16) such as the suspicion score used by the French family payments agency [Caisse d'allocations familiales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caisse_d'allocations_familiales "Caisse d'allocations familiales").[\[34\]](about:blank#cite_note-LQDN_notation_CAF-34)[\[16\]](about:blank#cite_note-LQDN_technosolutionist_goldrush-16)

The AI Act establishes various new bodies in Article 64 and the following articles. These bodies are tasked with implementing and enforcing the Act. The approach combines EU-level coordination with national implementation, involving both public authorities and private sector participation.

The following bodies have been established:[\[35\]](about:blank#cite_note-35)[\[36\]](about:blank#cite_note-36)[\[37\]](about:blank#cite_note-:7-37)

1.  AI Office: attached to the European Commission, this authority will coordinate the implementation of the AI Act in all Member States and oversee the compliance of general-purpose AI providers. It can also request information or open investigations when serious issues are suspected.[\[6\]](about:blank#cite_note-:10-6)
2.  European Artificial Intelligence Board: composed of one representative from each Member State, the Board will advise and assist the Commission and Member States to facilitate the consistent and effective application of the AI Act. Its tasks include gathering and sharing technical and regulatory expertise, providing recommendations, written opinions, and other advice.
3.  Advisory Forum: established to advise and provide technical expertise to the Board and the Commission, this forum will represent a balanced selection of stakeholders, including industry, start-ups, small and medium-sized enterprises, civil society, and academia, ensuring that a broad spectrum of opinions is represented during the implementation and application process.
4.  Scientific Panel of Independent Experts: this panel will provide technical advice and input to the AI Office and national authorities, enforce rules for general-purpose AI models (notably by launching qualified alerts of possible risks to the AI Office), and ensure that the rules and implementations of the AI Act correspond to the latest scientific findings.

While the establishment of new bodies is planned at the EU level, Member States will have to designate "national competent authorities".[\[note 1\]](about:blank#cite_note-38) These authorities will be responsible for ensuring the application and implementation of the AI Act, and for conducting "market surveillance".[\[38\]](about:blank#cite_note-39) They will verify that AI systems comply with the regulations, notably by checking the proper performance of conformity assessments and by appointing third-parties to carry out external conformity assessments.

Once harmonised standards for the AI Act are published in the Official Journal, compliant products are presumed to conform with the regulation; these standards are being drafted by CEN/CENELEC Joint Technical Committee 21 (JTC 21).[\[39\]](about:blank#cite_note-40)

The Act regulates entry to the [EU internal market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EU_internal_market "EU internal market") using the [New Legislative Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Legislative_Framework "New Legislative Framework"). It contains essential requirements that all AI systems must meet to access the EU market. These essential requirements are passed on to [European Standardisation Organisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Standardisation_Organisations "European Standardisation Organisations"), which develop technical standards that further detail these requirements.[\[40\]](about:blank#cite_note-41) These standards are developed by CEN/CENELEC JTC 21.[\[41\]](about:blank#cite_note-42)

The Act mandates that member states establish their own notifying bodies. Conformity assessments are conducted to verify whether AI systems comply with the standards set out in the AI Act.[\[42\]](about:blank#cite_note-43) This assessment can be done in two ways: either through self-assessment, where the AI system provider checks conformity, or through third-party conformity assessment, where the notifying body conducts the assessment.[\[24\]](about:blank#cite_note-Veale-24) Notifying bodies also have the authority to carry out audits to ensure proper conformity assessments.[\[43\]](about:blank#cite_note-44)

Each EU Member State must also designate a national supervisory authority to monitor compliance, handle complaints, and share information with the European AI Office, which coordinates enforcement across the Union.[\[6\]](about:blank#cite_note-:10-6)

Together, these actors form a multi-level supervision system. National market surveillance and supervisory authorities carry out checks and enforce the rules on high-risk AI systems and other regulated uses, while EU-level bodies such as the AI Office and the European Artificial Intelligence Board support implementation of the Act and help ensure consistent application, in particular for general-purpose AI models.[\[25\]](about:blank#cite_note-:14-25)

Criticism has arisen regarding the fact that many high-risk AI systems do not require third-party conformity assessments.[\[44\]](about:blank#cite_note-45)[\[45\]](about:blank#cite_note-46)[\[46\]](about:blank#cite_note-:12-47) Some commentators argue that independent third-party assessments are necessary for high-risk AI systems to ensure safety before deployment. Legal scholars have suggested that AI systems capable of generating deepfakes for political misinformation or creating non-consensual intimate imagery s

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Payments_Initiative:
The EPI system is based on the [SEPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_Euro_Payments_Area "Single Euro Payments Area") instant credit transfer (SCT Inst) scheme, allowing it to capitalise on existing infrastructures such as the Eurosystem's [TARGET Instant Payment Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TARGET_Instant_Payment_Settlement "TARGET Instant Payment Settlement") (TIPS).[\[9\]](about:blank#cite_note-9) Wero, with its payment network, digital wallet and international instant payments scheme, aims to replace European domestic solutions such as Swish, iDEAL, [Bizum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizum "Bizum") and [Blik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blik "Blik"). [QR code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_code "QR code") payments will be available for both money transfers and payments, with plans for more payment options in the future.  

Wero is available both through the [mobile apps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_app "Mobile app") of most member banks or, for some banks, via a standalone Wero app. It offers currency conversion throughout Europe.

The European Payments Initiative (EPI) announced its intention to launch Wero, its wallet-based payment method in Germany in mid-2024, followed by France and Belgium later in that year and the Netherlands in 2025. The rest of Europe will follow in subsequent years.

Wero initially allows person-to-person (P2P) and person-to-professional (P2Pro) payments, which will be followed by online and mobile shopping payments and then [point-of-sale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point-of-sale "Point-of-sale") payments. It will offer a range of transaction types, including one-off payments, subscriptions, installments, payments upon delivery and reservations. 

Value-added services will be incorporated into the solution over time, including responsible ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ (BNPL) financing, digital identity features (allowing the tracking of consumers in every EU country and the blocking of payments when needed) and the integration of merchant loyalty programmes.

In October 2024, seven French banks deployed Wero.[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-10) It replaces [Paylib](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paylib "fr:Paylib") for them.

EPI Company acquired the payment providers Currence iDEAL BV and Payconiq International SA in October 2023.[\[11\]](about:blank#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](about:blank#cite_note-12) The payment methods _iDEAL_ in the Netherlands, _Payconiq_ in Luxembourg and _Payconiq by Bancontact_ in Belgium are offerings in their local markets, but set to be fully integrated into Wero in 2026–2027.

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_Intelligence_Act:
 developed by the [AI Now Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_Now_Institute "AI Now Institute") for public agencies, argue that impact assessments should map affected communities, examine fairness, bias and due process, and allow ongoing public and researcher scrutiny of automated decision systems.[\[21\]](about:blank#cite_note-:13-21)

A broad civil society coalition coordinated by [European Digital Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Digital_Rights "European Digital Rights") (EDRi) published a joint analysis comparing the final AI Act with its earlier demands and concluded that the law falls short of what is needed to protect rights to privacy, equality, non-discrimination and the presumption of innocence. The coalition also called for stronger safeguards for people on the move and for people with disabilities, arguing that the final rules leave significant gaps in these areas.[\[61\]](about:blank#cite_note-62)

Organisations representing authors, performers, publishers and producers have also criticised the implementation of the Act, particularly its rules for general-purpose AI. A joint statement from 38 global creators' organisations, reported by _[Le Monde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Monde "Le Monde")_, argued that the Code of Practice, the guidelines for general-purpose AI and the template for training-data summaries under Article 53 do not adequately protect intellectual property rights or ensure sufficient transparency about the data used to train generative AI models, describing the outcome as a missed opportunity to deliver on the Act's stated goals. This criticism has been discussed as part of wider debates about how the AI Act and its general-purpose AI provisions may affect the position of cultural and creative industries in the EU.[\[62\]](about:blank#cite_note-63)

Building on these critiques, scholars have raised concerns in particular about the Act's approach to regulating the secondary uses of trained AI models, which may have significant societal impacts.[\[63\]](about:blank#cite_note-:8-64)[\[64\]](about:blank#cite_note-:9-65) They argue that the Act's narrow focus on deployment contexts and reliance on providers to self-declare intended purposes creates opportunities for misinterpretation and insufficient oversight.[\[64\]](about:blank#cite_note-:9-65) Additionally, the Act often exempts [open-source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-source_artificial_intelligence "Open-source artificial intelligence") models and neglects critical lifecycle phases, such as the reuse of trained models.[\[63\]](about:blank#cite_note-:8-64) Trained models store decision-mappings as parameters that approximate patterns from the [training data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Training_data "Training data"). This "model data" is distinct from the original training data and is typically classified as non-personal, as it often cannot be traced back to individual data subjects. Consequently, it falls outside the scope of other regulations like the [GDPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Data_Protection_Regulation "General Data Protection Regulation").[\[63\]](about:blank#cite_note-:8-64) Some scholars also criticize the AI Act for not sufficiently regulating the reuse of model data, warning of potentially harmful consequences for individual privacy, social equity, and democratic processes.[\[63\]](about:blank#cite_note-:8-64) Other commentators have also questioned the democratic legitimacy, transparency, and practical enforceability of the new rules for general-purpose AI, noting that their impact will depend on how oversight bodies apply them over time.[\[30\]](about:blank#cite_note-:17-30)

Legal scholars have argued that compliance-based frameworks such as the EU AI Act may be insufficient to prevent harm, as optimizing systems can satisfy formal requirements while producing prohibited outcomes — a phenomenon described as the 'Synthetic Outlaw' problem, in which the gap between nominal compliance and actual impact remains ungoverned.[\[65\]](about:blank#cite_note-66)

### International expansion and major acquisitions

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: International expansion and major acquisitions")\]

[![Chart showing the formation of the ING Group](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/ING_Group_structure.svg/500px-ING_Group_structure.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ING_Group_structure.svg)

Chart showing the formation of the ING Group

Since its founding, ING Group has grown through a sustained [program of acquisitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consolidation_\(business\) "Consolidation (business)"). Throughout the 1990s, ING broadened its asset management capabilities through the purchase of Parcom (1994) and Clarion (1998), and expanded in insurance through Wellington (1995), Equitable of Iowa (1997, for US$2.2 billion).[\[43\]](about:blank#cite_note-43) By then, ING operated in 58 countries and was the Netherlands' largest insurer and third-largest bank.[\[44\]](about:blank#cite_note-:32-44) In 1998, ING sold its U.S. [general insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_insurance "General insurance") subsidiary, the Netherlands Insurance Group of Cos., to British insurer [Guardian Royal Exchange Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardian_Royal_Exchange_Assurance "Guardian Royal Exchange Assurance") for $775 million, while acquiring Guardian's Canadian insurance unit for $375 million.[\[45\]](about:blank#cite_note-45)

Banking operations were also strengthened through the acquisitions of Furman Selz for US$600 million,[\[46\]](about:blank#cite_note-46) and the gradual purchase of Dutch cash-management specialist [Bank Mendes Gans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Mendes_Gans "Bank Mendes Gans"), whose remaining shares ING acquired by 2000, when the company was delisted from the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. Separately, ING acquired [Bank Brussels Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Brussels_Lambert "Bank Brussels Lambert") after launching a bid in 1997 valued at US$4.68 billion, with [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") clearance granted in January 1998, establishing ING's leading position in the [Belgian market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_banks_in_Belgium "List of banks in Belgium"). In 1999, ING took over the German [BHF-Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oddo_BHF "Oddo BHF") and Canadian Group Underwriters.[\[47\]](about:blank#cite_note-:19-47)

The early 2000s brought further geographic expansion: [Aetna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aetna "Aetna")'s financial services and international units (for US$7.7 billion),[\[48\]](about:blank#cite_note-48)[\[49\]](about:blank#cite_note-49)[\[50\]](about:blank#cite_note-50) and ReliaStar (for US$6.1 billion)[\[51\]](about:blank#cite_note-51)[\[52\]](about:blank#cite_note-52) (both 2000), Seguros Comercial América in Latin America (2001), and DiBa in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") (2002). In 2004, ING added Alliance of Canada to its insurance portfolio and [Rodamco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield "Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield") Asia to its asset management operations. In the same year, it agreed to sell most of ING BHF-Bank to the German bank [Sal. Oppenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sal._Oppenheim "Sal. Oppenheim") for €600 million, transferring €6 billion in risk-weighted assets and around 1,800 employees, while retaining certain assets under the name ING Bank Deutschland and selling the London branch to [Deutsche Postbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Postbank "Deutsche Postbank").[\[53\]](about:blank#cite_note-53)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Bruxelles_-_ING_Building_%281%29.jpg/250px-Bruxelles_-_ING_Building_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bruxelles_-_ING_Building_\(1\).jpg)

_The Marnix_ on Avenue Marnix in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), designed by [Gordon Bunshaft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Bunshaft "Gordon Bunshaft"), the 1965 headquarters of [Bank Brussels Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Brussels_Lambert "Bank Brussels Lambert"), acquired by ING in 1998

Expanding its retail banking business overseas, ING used the direct banking [business model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_model "Business model") it had developed with NMB Postbank to launch direct banking in other countries. The first of these was set up in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") in 1997 as _ING Bank of Canada_, and was soon followed in several other countries including the US, UK, Germany, [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"). In July 2007, ING paid $1.3 billion for the Latin American [pensions business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pension_fund "Pension fund") of [Banco Santander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Santander "Banco Santander"), becoming the region's second-largest behind [BBVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Bilbao_Vizcaya_Argentaria "Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria") and increasing Latin American funds under management to €35.5 billion.[\[54\]](about:blank#cite_note-54)

By early 2008, ING Direct had grown to 20 million customers in nine countries, with €210 billion in deposits and close to €90 billion in mortgages, contributing about 7% of group profits in 2006.[\[55\]](about:blank#cite_note-55) In 2008, ING acquired CitiStreet — an American [retirement-plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pension "Pension") and [benefit administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employee_benefits "Employee benefits") company, with more than 14 million participants — from [Citigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup "Citigroup") and [State Street Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_Corporation "State Street Corporation") for €578 million.[\[56\]](about:blank#cite_note-56)[\[57\]](about:blank#cite_note-57)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Sir_Francis_Baring%2C_Banker_and_Director_of_the_East_India_Company%2C_with_his_Associates.jpg/250px-Sir_Francis_Baring%2C_Banker_and_Director_of_the_East_India_Company%2C_with_his_Associates.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sir_Francis_Baring,_Banker_and_Director_of_the_East_India_Company,_with_his_Associates.jpg)

Portrait of merchant bankers [Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Francis_Baring,_1st_Baronet "Sir Francis Baring, 1st Baronet") and [John Barings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Baring_\(1730–1816\) "John Baring (1730–1816)"), and Charles Wall, by [Thomas Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Lawrence "Thomas Lawrence"), from the Barings art collection acquired by ING in 1995

The 1995 purchase of [Barings Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barings_Bank "Barings Bank") for a symbolic [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_sterling "Pound sterling")1 after its dramatic collapse led to a boost in ING's wholesale and [investment banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_banking "Investment banking") business. Barings was founded in 1762 by [Francis Baring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Francis_Baring,_1st_Baronet "Sir Francis Baring, 1st Baronet"), a British-born member of the German–British [Baring family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baring_family "Baring family") of merchants and bankers, and was, after [Berenberg Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berenberg_Bank "Berenberg Bank"), one of England's oldest [merchant banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_bank "Merchant bank").[\[58\]](about:blank#cite_note-:18-58)

In 1995, the 233-year-old bank collapsed after [Nick Leeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Leeson "Nick Leeson") — the 28-year-old head of Barings Futures Singapore — accumulated £830 million in catastrophic unauthorized losses on [Nikkei 225](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikkei_225 "Nikkei 225")[futures contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futures_contract "Futures contract"), [concealed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraudulent_concealment "Fraudulent concealment") in an [error account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_account "Error account"). His positions were destroyed by the [plunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_market_crash "Stock market crash") in the Nikkei following the [Kobe earthquake of 17 January 1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Hanshin_earthquake "1995 Hanshin earthquake"). Barings was declared [insolvent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insolvency "Insolvency") on 26 February 1995 and Leeson was subsequently sentenced to six and a half years in a [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") prison.[\[58\]](about:blank#cite_note-:18-58) ING acquired Barings for £1, assuming its liabilities and establishing ING Barings — gaining an investment-banking platform, international [brand recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_awareness "Brand awareness") and the historic Barings Archive. In 2001, ING sold the US operations of ING Barings to [ABN AMRO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABN_AMRO "ABN AMRO") for US$275 million.[\[58\]](about:blank#cite_note-:18-58) The Barings art collection and the [charitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_\(nonprofit\) "Foundation (nonprofit)") Baring Foundation remain based at ING's London office.[\[59\]](about:blank#cite_note-59)[\[60\]](about:blank#cite_note-60)

### Acquisition of Oyak Bank

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Acquisition of Oyak Bank")\]

In June 2007, ING announced the acquisition of the Turkish bank Oyak Bank for US$2.673 billion, marking its entry into the Turkish market. Oyak Bank, founded in 1984, was among the ten largest banks in [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") with a [market share](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_share "Market share") of around 3%. The bank had a total of 360 branches, 1.2 million active retail customers and 10,000 SME customers. In 2006, the bank reported a pre-tax profit of 165 million Turkish lira (€94.6 million), with total assets of 11.8 billion Turkish lira (€6.77 billion) and a [book value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_value "Book value") of [TRY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_lira "Turkish lira") 988 million (€566 million).[\[61\]](about:blank#cite_note-61)[\[62\]](about:blank#cite_note-62)

### Capital injection and divestiture

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Capital injection and divestiture")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Regus_%28373123266%29.jpg/250px-Regus_%28373123266%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Regus_\(373123266\).jpg)

ING offices over the Utrechtsebaan in [The Hague Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague_Center "The Hague Center"), pictured in 2007

In 2008, as part of the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), ING Group, together with many other major banks in the Netherlands, accepted a capital injection from the Dutch government (see § _[Government capital injection and state aid](about:blank#Government_capital_injection_and_state_aid)_ below). Following reports of alleged capital shortfalls, on Friday, 17 October 2008, ING's share price fell by more than 27%.[\[63\]](about:blank#cite_note-:1-63) ING also recorded a loss of €500 million in the third quarter of 2008, its first quarterly loss ever,[\[64\]](about:blank#cite_note-64) and a reported net loss of €729 million for the full year.[\[65\]](about:blank#cite_note-65) As a condition of Dutch state aid, the EU demanded changes to the company structure, including the sale of insurance businesses in Latin America, Asia, Canada, Australia and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), and ING Direct units in the US, Canada, and the UK.[\[66\]](about:blank#cite_note-66) This included the sale of the ING Direct US operations to [Capital One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_One "Capital One"), ING Direct Canada to [Scotiabank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotiabank "Scotiabank") (doing business as [_Tangerine_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangerine_Bank "Tangerine Bank")), and the ING Direct UK operations to [Barclays Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclays_Bank "Barclays Bank") in 2012.[\[67\]](about:blank#cite_note-67)[\[68\]](about:blank#cite_note-Barclays_to_acquire_ING_Direct_UK-68) The spun-off insurance businesses in North America were renamed _[Voya Financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voya_Financial "Voya Financial")_ in 2014.[\[69\]](about:blank#cite_note-69)[\[70\]](about:blank#cite_note-70)

In 2009, Postbank and ING Bank were merged into a single [brand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand "Brand"), _ING_. The merger was completed in January 2009 under CEO Nick Jue.[\[71\]](about:blank#cite_note-71) The [rebranding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebranding "Rebranding") officially launched on 10 February 2009, costing €890 million and 2,500 jobs, largely driven by Postbank's historical inability to sell complex, higher-margin financial products.[\[72\]](about:blank#cite_note-:30-72) In October 2009, ING announced that its insurance arm would again be separated from ING Group. In April 2016, ING sold the last shares in NN Group, making it exclusively a bank again.[\[73\]](about:blank#cite_note-73)[\[74\]](about:blank#cite_note-74)

## Government capital injection and state aid

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Government capital injection and state aid")\]

In October 2008, in a move to increase its core [Tier 1 capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tier_1_capital "Tier 1 capital") ratio above 8%, ING Group accepted a capital injection plan from the Dutch Government.[\[75\]](about:blank#cite_note-75) The plan supplied €10billion (US$13.5billion) to the operation, in exchange for securities and veto rights on major operational changes and investments. As a further condition of the state aid, the European Commission required ING to divest itself of its insurance and investment management operations (see § _[Corporate restructuring](about:blank#Corporate_restructuring_\(2009%E2%80%932016\))_ below).[\[76\]](about:blank#cite_note-:24-76)

### Repayment of the capital injection

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Repayment of the capital injection")\]

In December 2009, ING Group repaid half of the state aid (€5 billion, plus interest and an agreed early-repayment [premium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_of_options "Valuation of options")) through a [rights issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rights_issue "Rights issue") that raised €7.5 billion.[\[77\]](about:blank#cite_note-77) A dispute between ING and the Dutch government on one side and the European Commission on the other, concerning the partial withholding of approval, was referred to the [Court of Justice of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Justice_of_the_European_Union "Court of Justice of the European Union").[\[78\]](about:blank#cite_note-:2-78)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/20080906-07_Den_Haag_%280283%29.jpg/250px-20080906-07_Den_Haag_%280283%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20080906-07_Den_Haag_\(0283\).jpg)

_The [Binnenhof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binnenhof "Binnenhof")_, the parliament complex on the [Hofvijver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hofvijver "Hofvijver") lake in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague")

In May 2011, ING Group repaid a further €2 billion in a second [tranche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tranche "Tranche"), plus a 50% premium, bringing the total payment to €3 billion; by then a total of €8.6 billion had flowed back to the State.[\[78\]](about:blank#cite_note-:2-78) The bank stated its intention to repay the remaining €3 billion of the [state loan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government-backed_loan "Government-backed loan") by May 2012 at the latest. On 26 November 2012, ING Group repaid a further €1.125 billion,[\[79\]](about:blank#cite_note-79) and on 6 November 2013 another €1.125 billion was transferred to the State.[\[80\]](about:blank#cite_note-80) On 25 March 2014, it was announced that ING would repay a penultimate tranche of €1.225 billion – €100 million more than planned – with a final payment of €1.025 billion to follow by May 2015 at the latest.[\[81\]](about:blank#cite_note-81)

On 7 November 2014, ING repaid the final tranche of state aid; with this payment, ING had repaid a total of €13.5 billion to the Dutch State, representing an average annual return of 12.7% for the State.[\[82\]](about:blank#cite_note-82)[\[83\]](about:blank#cite_note-:41-83)

In early 2011, public debate arose over ING's intention to once again award its [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") a substantial bonus, which many considered particularly inappropriate given that ING was still dependent on state aid at the time. In response, the [Dutch House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_\(Netherlands\) "House of Representatives (Netherlands)") adopted a motion to fully and retroactively tax away bonuses at banks receiving state aid, and the [Minister of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_\(Netherlands\) "Ministry of Finance (Netherlands)") announced a statutory ban on bonuses for directors of banks receiving state support.[\[84\]](about:blank#cite_note-84)[\[85\]](about:blank#cite_note-85)

Under the original terms, ING was permitted to fully or partially repurchase the core capital securities issued to the Dutch State for €15 per unit. The Dutch State classified these securities as Tier 1 capital. The State ranked equally with holders of ordinary shares, but dilution for existing [shareholders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shareholder "Shareholder") was limited. On the trading day following the announcement of the capital injection, ING's share price rose 29.24%.[\[86\]](about:blank#cite_note-86)

### Alt-A mortgage guarantees

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ING_Group&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Alt-A mortgage guarantees")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Ministerie_van_Financien_Korte_Voorhout_7_The_Hague_2020.jpg/250px-Ministerie_van_Financien_Korte_Voorhout_7_The_Hague_2020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ministerie_van_Financien_Korte_Voorhout_7_The_Hague_2020.jpg)

Headquarters of the Dutch Ministry of Finance in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague")

On 26 January 2009, ING Group and the Ministry of Finance announced that the Dutch State would provide an 80% guarantee on the value of a €27.7 billion portfolio of U.S. [Alt-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-A "Alt-A") mortgages held in the portfolios of subsidiaries ING Direct and ING Insurance Americas. Contents of https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/high-level-summary/:
f independent experts, that a model presents a systemic risk, despite not reaching the compute threshold.

In addition to the four obligations above, providers of GPAI models with systemic risk must also:

*   Perform **model evaluations**, including conducting and documenting **adversarial testing** to identify and mitigate systemic risk.
*   **Assess and mitigate possible systemic risks**, including their sources.
*   **Track, document and report serious incidents** and possible corrective measures to the [AI Office](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-office) and relevant national competent authorities without undue delay.
*   Ensure an adequate level of **cybersecurity protection**.

All GPAI model providers may demonstrate compliance with their obligations if they voluntarily adhere to the General-Purpose Code of Practice until European harmonised standards are published. Providers that don’t adhere to the Code of Practice must demonstrate **alternative adequate means of compliance**.

**The General-Purpose Code of Practice**

*   Voluntary tool developed in a multi-stakeholder process which GPAI model providers may use to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act’s relevant obligations. 
*   Published on 10 July 2025 and declared adequate by the European Commission and the AI Board on 1 August 2025. 
*   The [Code of Practice](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai) contains three chapters, namely on Transparency, Copyright and Safety and Security, covering the obligations of all GPAI model providers, as well as the obligations solely applicable to the providers of GPAI models with systemic risk.
*   More than 20 providers have signed up to the Code of Practice as of August 2026. 
*   Alongside the Code of Practice, providers are also guided by the Commission [Guidelines](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/guidelines-scope-obligations-providers-general-purpose-ai-models-under-ai-act) on on the scope of obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models under the AI Act.

### Governance

How will the AI Act be implemented?

*   The [AI Office](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-office), sitting within the Commission, monitors the effective implementation and compliance of GPAI model providers, as well as providers of AI systems built on a GPAI model developed by the same provider (unless an exception applies), and AI systems that constitute or that are integrated into a very large online platform or very large online search engine under the Digital Services Act (DSA).
*   Downstream providers can lodge a complaint regarding the upstream (GPAI model) providers’ infringement of the AI Act to the AI Office.
*   The AI Office may conduct evaluations of the GPAI model to:
    *   assess compliance where the information gathered under its powers to request information is insufficient
    *   investigate systemic risks, particularly following a qualified alert from the scientific panel of independent experts.

### Timelines

*   After the AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, the application of the Act’s provisions has been and is continued to be rolled out gradually.
*   Most prohibitions of AI systems have been applicable since 2 February 2025, with prohibitions on AI systems generating non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material (CSAM) coming into play on 2 December 2026. 
*   GPAI model obligations kicked in on 2 August 2025. The General-Purpose Code of Practice was declared adequate on 1 August 2025. 
*   AI Office’s supervision and enforcement powers can be exercised from 2 August 2026.
*   The transparency obligations under Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026. There is a grace period for AI systems placed on the market before this date, which have time to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026. 
*   The obligations for AI systems that are high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III AI Act will become applicable on 2 December 2027.
*   The obligations for AI systems that are high-risk under Article 6(1) and Annex I AI Act will come into play on 2 August 2028.

_See our [full implementation timeline](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/implementation-timeline/)_for all key milestones relating to the implementation of the AI Act.__
