System for money transfers within the European Union area

The **Single Euro Payments Area** (**SEPA**) is a payment integration initiative of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") for simplification of bank transfers denominated in [euros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro"). As of 2025[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Single_Euro_Payments_Area&action=edit), there were 41 members in SEPA,[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-MolandNorthMa-2)[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-auto-3) consisting of the 27 [member states of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_states_of_the_European_Union "Member states of the European Union"), the four member states of the [European Free Trade Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Free_Trade_Association "European Free Trade Association") ([Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland"), [Liechtenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liechtenstein "Liechtenstein"), [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") and [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland")), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), as well as five [EU candidate countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_enlargement_of_the_European_Union "Potential enlargement of the European Union").[\[4\]](about:blank#cite_note-ReferenceA-4)[\[5\]](about:blank#cite_note-europeanpaymentscouncil.eu-5)[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-auto-3) Some microstates participate in the technical schemes: [Andorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andorra "Andorra"),[\[6\]](about:blank#cite_note-6)[Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco"), [San Marino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Marino "San Marino"), and [Vatican City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatican_City "Vatican City").[\[4\]](about:blank#cite_note-ReferenceA-4) As of 2025, [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania "Albania"), [Moldova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldova "Moldova"), [Montenegro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro"), [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia") and [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia") are the five countries negotiating to join the EU that are included in SEPA.[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-MolandNorthMa-2)

SEPA covers predominantly normal bank transfers. Payment methods which have additional optional features or services, such as [mobile phone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_payments_in_India "Mobile payments in India") or smart [card payment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_payment "Card payment") systems, are not directly covered.[\[7\]](about:blank#cite_note-7) However, the instant SEPA payment scheme facilitates payment products also on [smart devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_device "Smart device").[\[8\]](about:blank#cite_note-8)

The aim of SEPA as stated in 2008 was to improve the efficiency of cross-border payments and turn the previously fragmented national markets for euro payments into a single domestic one. SEPA would enable customers to make cashless euro payments to any account located anywhere in the area, using a single [bank account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_account "Bank account") and a single set of payment instruments.[\[9\]](about:blank#cite_note-9) People who have a bank account in a [eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone") country can use it to receive salaries and make payments all over the eurozone, for example when they take a job in a new country.

The project includes the development of common [financial instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_instrument "Financial instrument"), standards, procedures, and infrastructure to enable [economies of scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economies_of_scale "Economies of scale"). As of 2007[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Single_Euro_Payments_Area&action=edit), it was estimated this could reduce the overall cost to the European economy of moving capital around the region by up to 2–3% of total [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP")).[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-rte20070327-10)\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\]

SEPA does not cover payments in currencies other than the euro. This means that domestic payments in SEPA countries not using the euro will continue to use local schemes, but cross-border payments will use SEPA and the euro with eurozone countries to a high degree.

The Nordic countries (other than Finland) do not use the euro and have no plans to adopt the euro. These four countries (Sweden, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland) started initiatives during 2017–2019 for simpler, faster, and cheaper cross-border payments between one another. These initiatives have however not\[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_\] been successful.[\[11\]](about:blank#cite_note-11)

The different functionalities provided by SEPA are divided into separate payment schemes.

### SEPA Credit Transfer

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Single_Euro_Payments_Area&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: SEPA Credit Transfer")\]

SEPA Credit Transfer (_SCT_) allows for the transfer of funds from one bank account to another. SEPA clearing rules require that payments made before the cutoff point on a working day be credited to the recipient's account by the next working day. The scheme was introduced in January 2008. In February 2014 it replaced the national credit transfer schemes, and later made the use of [International Bank Account Number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBAN "IBAN") mandatory for transfers.[\[12\]](about:blank#cite_note-12)

### SEPA Instant Credit Transfer

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Single_Euro_Payments_Area&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: SEPA Instant Credit Transfer")\]

SEPA Instant Credit Transfer (_SCT Inst_), also called SEPA Instant Payment,[\[13\]](about:blank#cite_note-13) provides for instant crediting of a payee, the delay being less than ten seconds, initially, with a maximum of twenty seconds in exceptional circumstances.[\[14\]](about:blank#cite_note-14) This scheme was launched in November 2017, and was at that time operational for end customers in eight [Eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_zone "Euro zone") countries.[\[15\]](about:blank#cite_note-15) As of 2024, not all banks offer their customers instant transfers; however, in March 2024 the EU adopted the _Instant Payments Regulation_ which requires all banks to offer instant transfers from January 2025 (incoming transfers) / October 2025 (outgoing transfers).[\[16\]](about:blank#cite_note-16)

[Direct debit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_debit "Direct debit") functionality is provided by two separate schemes. The basic scheme, _Core SDD_, is primarily targeted at consumers and was launched on 2 November 2009.[\[17\]](about:blank#cite_note-dd-launch-17) Banks offering SEPA payments are obliged to participate in this scheme.[\[18\]](about:blank#cite_note-dd-difference-18) A second scheme, _B2B SDD_, is targeted towards business users. Banks offering SEPA payments are not obliged to participate in this scheme (participation is optional).[\[18\]](about:blank#cite_note-dd-difference-18) Among the differences with respect to _Core SDD_:[\[18\]](about:blank#cite_note-dd-difference-18)

*   It requires a mandate to be submitted to the bank by both the creditor and debtor.
*   It does not allow the debtor to request a refund from its bank after its account has been debited.

SEPA consists of 41 countries:[\[5\]](about:blank#cite_note-europeanpaymentscouncil.eu-5)[\[19\]](about:blank#cite_note-19)

All parts of a country are normally part of SEPA. However, the following countries have [special territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_member_state_territories_and_the_European_Union "Special member state territories and the European Union") which are not part of SEPA:[\[26\]](about:blank#cite_note-SEB-26)

Jurisdictions using the euro that are not in SEPA: [Akrotiri and Dhekelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_and_Dhekelia "Akrotiri and Dhekelia"), French Southern and Antarctic Lands and [Kosovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo "Kosovo").

Jurisdictions in Europe not formally belonging to SEPA normally use SEPA schemes anyway for international euro payments, especially to or from the eurozone, with exceptions such as fees charged and BIC required.

Several EU applicant states have expressed interest in applying to join SEPA. 

### Bosnia and Herzegovina

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Single_Euro_Payments_Area&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Bosnia and Herzegovina")\]

[Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Bosnia and Herzegovina") filed an application to join SEPA on August 6, 2026.[\[27\]](about:blank#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](about:blank#cite_note-Bosnia_SEPA_Application-28) In July 2026 the [Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina") and the [National Assembly of Republika Srpska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Republika_Srpska "National Assembly of Republika Srpska") passed legislation to align the country with SEPA regulations.[\[29\]](about:blank#cite_note-29)

[Kosovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo "Kosovo") intends to apply after passing necessary legislation.[\[30\]](about:blank#cite_note-30) Kosovo's chief negotiator for EU accession Jeton Zulfaj stated that several laws needed to be passed by the [Assembly of Kosovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_of_Kosovo "Assembly of Kosovo") in order to fulfill SEPA requirements, including the Law on Payment Services and Law on Preventing Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism. As of July 2026 only the Law on Payment Services has been passed.[\[31\]](about:blank#cite_note-31)

[Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") as of December 2025 is working on legislation to align Ukrainian law with SEPA standards.[\[32\]](about:blank#cite_note-32)

In February 2026, [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") was offered membership in SEPA by European Commissioner for Enlargement [Marta Kos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marta_Kos "Marta Kos").[\[33\]](about:blank#cite_note-33) In July 2026, Turkish Minister of Foreign Affairs [Hakan Fidan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakan_Fidan "Hakan Fidan") stated Turkey was interested in joining SEPA and that related financial institutions are working on the issue[\[34\]](about:blank#cite_note-34), and Turkish Minister of Finance [Mehmet Şimşek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmet_Şimşek "Mehmet Şimşek") stated that Turkey has sent a [letter of intent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_of_intent "Letter of intent") for joining SEPA. [\[35\]](about:blank#cite_note-35)

SEPA guarantees that euro payments are received within a guaranteed time, and banks are not allowed to make any deductions of the amount transferred, introduced by a regulation in 2001.[\[36\]](about:blank#cite_note-36) Banks and payment institutions still have the option of charging a credit-transfer fee of their choice for euro transfers if it is charged uniformly to all EEA participants, banks or payment institutions, domestic or foreign.[\[37\]](about:blank#cite_note-reg-2560-2001-37) This is relevant for countries which do not use the euro; where domestic transfers in euros by consumers are uncommon,\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] and inflated fees for euro transfers might be charged in these states. Sweden and Denmark have legislated that euro transfers shall be charged the same as transfers in their own currency; which has the effect of giving free euro ATM withdrawals, but charges for ATM withdrawals in other currencies used in the EU.

In regulation (EC) 924/2009 (the Cross-border Payments Regulation), the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") mandated that charges in respect of cross-border payments in euros (of up to EUR 50,000) between EU member states shall be the same as the charges for corresponding payments within the member state.[\[38\]](about:blank#cite_note-38)[\[39\]](about:blank#cite_note-39) However, the EU Regulation does not apply to all SEPA countries; the most significant difference is the inclusion of Switzerland in SEPA but not the EU. The rule of the same price applies even if the transaction is sent as an international transaction instead of a SEPA transaction (common before 2008, or if any involved bank does not support SEPA transactions). Regulation 924/2009 does not regulate charges for currency conversion so charges for non-euro transactions can still be applied (if not banned by national law).[\[40\]](about:blank#cite_note-40)

There were two milestones in the establishment of SEPA:

*   Pan-European payment instruments for credit transfers began on 28 January 2008; [direct debits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_debit "Direct debit") and [debit cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debit_card "Debit card") became available in November 2009.[\[17\]](about:blank#cite_note-dd-launch-17)
*   By the end of 2010, all former national payment infrastructures and payment processors were expected to be in full competition to increase efficiency through consolidation and economies of scale.

For direct debits, the first milestone was missed due to a delay in the implementation of enabling legislatio

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_20022:
Standard for electronic data interchange between financial institutions

**ISO 20022** is an [ISO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organization_for_Standardization "International Organization for Standardization")[standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_standard "Technical standard") for [electronic data interchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_data_interchange "Electronic data interchange") between [financial institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_institution "Financial institution"). It describes a metadata repository containing descriptions of messages and [business processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_process "Business process"), and a maintenance process for the repository content. The standard covers financial information transferred between financial institutions that includes payment transactions, securities trading and settlement information, [credit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_card "Credit card") and [debit card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debit_card "Debit card") transactions and other financial information. Initial adoption began in March 2023 with a transition roadmap published by [SWIFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SWIFT "SWIFT").[\[1\]](about:blank#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-3)

The message metadata is described by [UML](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_Modeling_Language "Unified Modeling Language") models with a special ISO 20022 UML Profile. Underlying all of this is the ISO 20022 metamodel – a model of the models. The UML profile is the metamodel transformed into UML. The metadata is transformed into the syntax of messages used in financial networks. The first syntax supported for messages was XML Schema.

ISO 20022 is widely used in financial services. ISO 20022 is the successor to [ISO 15022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_15022 "ISO 15022"); originally ISO 20022 was called ISO 15022 2nd Edition. ISO 15022 was the successor of [ISO 7775](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_7775?action=edit&redlink=1 "ISO 7775 (page does not exist)").

## Parts of the standard

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ISO_20022&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Parts of the standard")\]

ISO 20022 Financial services – Universal financial industry message scheme. 

| Part             | Part Name                                           |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| ISO 20022-1:2026 | Metamodel                                           |
| ISO 20022-2:2013 | UML profile                                         |
| ISO 20022-3:2026 | Modeling                                            |
| ISO 20022-4:2026 | XML Schema generation                               |
| ISO 20022-5:2026 | Conceptual interoperability and reverse engineering |
| ISO 20022-6:2013 | Message transport characteristics                   |
| ISO 20022-7:2026 | Registration                                        |
| ISO 20022-8:2026 | ASN.1 generation                                    |
| ISO 20022-9:2026 | Syntax generation requirements and rules            |

## Management of the standard

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ISO_20022&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Management of the standard")\]

*   The Standard is issued by [ISO Technical Committee 68](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_Technical_Committee_68 "ISO Technical Committee 68") ([TC68](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TC68 "TC68")), which is responsible for Financial Services in ISO.
*   The Standard is managed by Sub Committee 9 (SC 9) "Information exchange for financial services".
*   The [Working Group 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_4?action=edit&redlink=1 "Working Group 4 (page does not exist)") (WG4), a sub-group of SC 9, who works on the next revision of ISO 20022.
*   The Standard defines a Registration Management Group (RMG) Composed of senior industry experts. It is the highest registration body.
*   SEG Standard Evolution Group composed of industry experts in specific business domains of the financial industry
*   [SWIFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SWIFT "SWIFT") is the Registration Authority (RA) for ISO 20022. RA is the guardian of the ISO 20022 financial repository. The AG 1 Group oversees the performance of RA.

A 2015 report by the United States's [Federal Reserve System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_System "Federal Reserve System") classified Europe having "mature adopters" of ISO 20022; [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), and [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") as having "growing adopters"; and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") as having "interested adopters". The report concluded that the Federal Reserve should push for ISO 20022 adoption within the United States financial system.[\[4\]](about:blank#cite_note-4)

Australia's [New Payments Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Payments_Platform "New Payments Platform"), launched in February 2018,[\[5\]](about:blank#cite_note-5) uses ISO 20022 messaging.[\[6\]](about:blank#cite_note-6)

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand plans to support ISO 20022 from November 2022 onward.[\[7\]](about:blank#cite_note-7)

Nordic countries launched the P27 payment platform, but that initiative eventually failed in 2023.[\[8\]](about:blank#cite_note-8)

The [Eurosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurosystem "Eurosystem") in March 2023 switched its real-time gross settlement to T2, which follows ISO 20022. The switch involves transactions for settling payments related to the Eurosystem's monetary policy operations, as well as bank‑to‑bank and commercial transactions. TARGET2 previously handled transactions for over 2000 G€ per day.[\[9\]](about:blank#cite_note-9)

In the United States, the Federal Reserve's [Fedwire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fedwire "Fedwire") Funds Service will begin using the ISO 20022 messaging format in July 2025\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\].[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-10) The [Federal Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve "Federal Reserve")'s [FedNow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedNow "FedNow") instant payments service also uses ISO 20022 messaging.[\[11\]](about:blank#cite_note-11) The private [Clearing House Payments Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clearing_House_Payments_Company "The Clearing House Payments Company")'s RTP instant payments service uses ISO 20022 messaging. Its [CHIPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearing_House_Interbank_Payments_System "Clearing House Interbank Payments System") funds transfer service migrated to using ISO 20022 in April 2024.[\[12\]](about:blank#cite_note-12)

# ING Group — Research Dossier for Consulting Pitch
*(Prepared Sept 2026. All figures verified against the cited primary documents. As of the current date, ING's most recent full year is FY2025, reported 29 Jan 2026.)*

## Summary
ING Groep N.V. is a Dutch-origin global bank serving **~41 million customers in 10 countries** with **~64,000 employees across 100+ countries**, and is one of the eurozone's most digitally advanced banks. It posted **FY2025 net result €6,327m** (FY2024 €6,392m; FY2023 €7,287m) on **total income €23.0bn**, with a **cost/income ratio of 54.6%** — currently running *above* its 2022 Investor-Day target of **50–52%**. ING's engineering story is genuinely differentiated: it pioneered the **Spotify-style "squads/tribes/chapters" agile model (2015)** documented by McKinsey, runs an **in-house private cloud (IPC) + CI/CD pipeline (OnePipeline) + a shared-services layer (Touchpoint)**, open-sources notable tooling (**Baker**, **Lion**), is a **founding shareholder of the European Payments Initiative / Wero**, and is directly supervised by the **ECB** (with **DNB** as national supervisor). Importantly for a pitch: **there is no public evidence of a major systems-integrator prime (HCLTech, Infosys, TCS, Cognizant, Accenture)** at ING Group — ING builds in-house. One caveat on the brief's premise: the "single/pan-European core platform" retreat is documented as a **2016→2019/2020** story, not a discrete 2022–2023 impairment (details and gap flagged in Area 2).

## 2) ING TECHNOLOGY STRATEGY

**Current strategy — "Growing the difference"** (launched at [Investor Update, 13 June 2022](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/press-releases/2022/ing-to-host-investor-update-2022-13-june-2022-0800-cet.pdf); materials at www.ing.com/investorday). Two customer pillars ("Superior customer value," "Sustainability at the heart") and **four enabling priorities: (1) providing seamless digital services, (2) using scalable technology & operations, (3) staying safe & secure, (4) unlocking people's potential** ([ing.com/about-us/strategy](https://ing.com/about-us/strategy)).

**"One platform" / scalable-technology architecture (from the [2024 Annual Report](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/files/2024-ing-groep-nv-annual-report.pdf), "Scalable technology and operations"):** ING's scalable tech is "divided into three parts":
- **IPC (ING Private Cloud):** where ING stores/manages applications and data "such as channel applications, **core banking systems** and other banking applications." **67% of all physical cores were on IPC by end-2024 (63% in 2023).** ING is "structurally evolv[ing] towards a **hybrid cloud** set-up… both private as well as public cloud."
- **OnePipeline:** "our **continuous integration and delivery pipeline**… a consistent and secure global capability to develop, test and deploy software." **85% of applications onboarded by end-2024 (63% in 2023).**
- **Touchpoint** (the global shared-services platform): "part of our banking technology platform, providing a **set of reusable shared services**, used by engineers to deliver business solutions like **Instant Payments and Open Banking** quicker and easier." **~75% of customer logins used Touchpoint by end-2024 (~64% in 2023).**
- Payments: ING has "**brought together all our payment capabilities under one platform**" ([2024 AR](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/files/2024-ing-groep-nv-annual-report.pdf), "seamless digital services").
- **"OneApp" (global mobile app):** confirmed live/expanding — in FY2025 "The OneApp was recently launched in Australia, and in Italy the investment function in the OneApp was introduced… in Business Banking, the OneApp was launched in Romania" ([FY2025 PR p.1](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/results/4qfy2025/4qfy2025-ing-press-release.pdf)).

**The "single/pan-European core platform" history — IMPORTANT CORRECTION + partial gap:**
- **Origin (3 Oct 2016):** Under "Accelerating Think Forward," ING announced it would "**invest 800 million euros in its technology platform**," rolled out over five years to its "challenger" markets (**Spain, Italy, France, Austria, Czech Republic**), converge technology platforms, integrate Belgium's **Record Bank**, cut **~7,000 jobs** (3,500 Belgium, 2,300 Netherlands) for ~€900m annual savings, and take **€1.1bn in charges** (mostly redundancies) ([CNBC, 3 Oct 2016](https://www.cnbc.com/2016/10/03/ing-plans-to-shed-7000-jobs-invest-in-digital-platform.html)). This was the "Model Bank"/Benelux-convergence ("Unite"/"Maggie") ambition.
- **Retreat/refocus (2019–2020):** ING publicly acknowledged cross-border/single-platform integration was harder than planned — see Euromoney, *"ING: Hamers draws up his European masterplan"* (31 Jul 2019) and *"ING admits what everyone else knew about cross-border integration"* (9 Nov 2020) *(both Euromoney; paywalled, verified via title/date on Google News — not fully read).* The current architecture (IPC/OnePipeline/Touchpoint, above) is a **shared-services + hybrid-cloud** model, **not** a single monolithic pan-European core.
- **GAP / caution on the brief's premise:** I found **no discrete 2022–2023 press report or annual-report line stating ING "scrapped"/took a named impairment/write-down** on a pan-European "One Bank" core platform for a specific euro amount. The 2024 Annual Report shows only routine, "individually immaterial" software-under-development impairment tests — no large platform write-off. The write-down/retreat narrative most defensibly maps to **2016 (charges) → 2019–2020 (strategic refocus)**. *If the pitch needs a euro figure, the citable one is the 2016 €1.1bn restructuring charge / €800m platform investment — not a 2022–23 impairment.* Recommend confirming against ING's FY2020/FY2021 disclosures if a specific number is required.

---

## 3) ING ENGINEERING CULTURE

**The Spotify-style agile model** — primary source: McKinsey, *"ING's agile transformation"* (Jan 2017), interview with ING Netherlands CIO **Peter Jacobs** and COO **Bart Schlatmann** ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/financial-services/our-insights/ings-agile-transformation); full text read via [Wayback archive](http://web.archive.org/web/20190107222522/https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/financial-services/our-insights/ings-agile-transformation)):
- "In the summer of **2015**… ING… shift[ed] its traditional organization to an '**agile**' model inspired by companies such as **Google, Netflix, and Spotify**. Comprising about **350 nine-person 'squads' in 13 so-called tribes**…" — improved time-to-market, engagement, productivity.
- Model mechanics: **squads → tribes** (with scrums, portfolio-wall planning, daily stand-ups) and **QBRs (Quarterly Business Reviews)** "borrowed from Google and Netflix." *(The article's exhibit also defines "chapters"/Centers of Expertise as the skill-based dimension of the model — the squads/tribes descriptions are explicit in the text; "chapters" is standard ING/Spotify terminology per the same model.)*
- **DevOps/CI-CD:** "our approach to **DevOps and continuous delivery**… go live with new software releases… **every two weeks** rather than five to six 'big launches' a year… position[ing] ourselves as the number-one mobile bank in the Netherlands." Software releases "on a **two- to three-week basis**."
- **Engineering culture quotes (great for a pitch):** "we are a **technology company operating in the financial-services business**"; "bring back an **engineering culture**… it's good to be an engineer and to make code"; inspired after visiting **Google I/O** and **Spotify (Sweden)**; peer-to-peer hiring (Google-style); in Jan 2015 all HQ staff were put "on mobility" and reapplied — **2,500** roles selected weighting culture over knowledge.

**Concrete engineering stack (public evidence):**
- **CI/CD = OnePipeline; private cloud = IPC; hybrid (private+public) cloud** — [2024 Annual Report](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/files/2024-ing-groep-nv-annual-report.pdf) (Area 2).
- **Azure DevOps:** confirmed via open-source tool **`doing-cli`** — "CLI tool to simplify the development workflow on **azure devops**" ([github.com/ing-bank/doing-cli](https://github.com/ing-bank/doing-cli)).
- **Apache Flink / Cassandra / Kubernetes** in ING's OSS org: `flink-deployer`, `cassandra-jdbc-wrapper`, `quota-scaler`/`skafos` (K8s operators) — [github.com/ing-bank](https://github.com/orgs/ing-bank/repositories).
- *Kafka/OpenShift/Red Hat specifically:* **GAP** — not confirmed in the primary ING sources I read (ING states "private cloud/IPC" and hybrid cloud, but does not name Red Hat OpenShift or Kafka publicly in the AR). Recommend an ING Medium/engineering-blog or conference-talk search if the deck needs those names.

---

## 4) ING OPEN SOURCE

GitHub org: **[github.com/ing-bank](https://github.com/orgs/ing-bank/repositories)** (verified live). Notable repos:
- **Baker** — [github.com/ing-bank/baker](https://github.com/ing-bank/baker) (359★). "A library that provides a simple and intuitive way to **orchestrate microservice-based process flows**." You declare orchestration as a **recipe** of `interactions` (system calls), `ingredients` (data) and `events`, via a **Java, Kotlin, or Scala DSL**; recipes are visualizable. Published to Maven Central as `com.ing.baker` (v5.x). Docs: [ing-bank.github.io/baker](https://ing-bank.github.io/baker/).
- **Lion** — [github.com/ing-bank/lion](https://github.com/ing-bank/lion) (1,962★). "A set of highly performant, **accessible** and flexible **Web Components**" — an unopinionated **white-label** layer to extend into your own design system; targets **WCAG 2.2 AA**, built on **Lit**, shipped as `@lion/ui`. Site: [lion.js.org](https://lion.js.org).
- Other ING OSS: **INGenious** (Playwright test studio, 170★), **popmon/probatus/skorecard** (ML & credit-risk validation), **rokku** (S3 access proxy), **ing-open-banking-sdk / -cli** (Open Banking), **doing-cli** (Azure DevOps).
- **"Forge" internal developer platform — GAP:** no public `ing-bank` repo named "Forge." ING's internal developer platform appears to be **internal** and maps publicly to **OnePipeline + IPC** (Area 2/3), which are described but not open-sourced. Treat "Forge" as unverified.

---

## 5) ING PAYMENTS & AI

**European Payments Initiative (EPI) / Wero — ING is a founding shareholder:**
- **Primary confirmation:** an ING Management Board Banking (MBB) member holds the ancillary position "**member of the board of EPI Company SE**" ([2024 ING Groep Annual Report](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/files/2024-ing-groep-nv-annual-report.pdf), board biographies). ING also published *"European-grown payment solution takes shape"* (ing.com, 25 Apr 2023) *(verified via Google News index; direct URL not resolved)*.
- **What EPI/Wero is:** [epicompany.eu](https://epicompany.eu/) — "The core of EPI's offering is **Wero**, our digital wallet." Based on **SEPA instant credit transfer (SCT Inst)** over the Eurosystem's **TIPS**; aims to replace domestic schemes (iDEAL, Bizum, Blik, Swish). Rollout: **Germany mid-2024, France & Belgium late-2024, Netherlands 2025**; P2P/P2Pro first, then e-commerce/POS; EPI acquired **iDEAL (Currence)** and **Payconiq** in Oct 2023 ([Wikipedia: European Payments Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Payments_Initiative); Wero: [wero-wallet.eu](https://wero-wallet.eu/)). Belgian launch involving ING/KBC/Belfius/BNPP Fortis reported Nov 2024 (Euronews / The Brussels Times, 20 Nov 2024).

**AI / GenAI adoption (strong, well-documented):**
- **From the [2024 Annual Report](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/files/2024-ing-groep-nv-annual-report.pdf):** ING focuses GenAI on **five high-value areas: contact centres, hyper-personalisation in marketing, KYC, software engineering, and Wholesale Banking lending.** It launched a "**brand-new GenAI chatbot in our contact centres**," established a virtual **AI Risk Center of Excellence**, and ran a **mandatory GenAI e-learning completed by 92% of the global workforce**; **4,000+ employees** trained in data fluency; partnerships with **University of Amsterdam** and **University of Twente**. A GenAI CDD/KYC "transaction profile report" **saves the front office ~2 hours per client and is live across 19 countries.** ING runs a central **ING Analytics** organisation.
- **FY2025:** GenAI chatbot "**went live in Australia** in Q4"; GenAI marketing-content generation rolled out across NL, Spain, Belgium, Germany, Poland ([FY2025 PR p.1](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/results/4qfy2025/4qfy2025-ing-press-release.pdf)).
- **Secondary/thought-leadership (verified by title/date, not all fully read):** McKinsey, *"Banking on innovation: How ING uses generative AI to put people first"* ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/mckinsey-digital/our-insights/banking-on-innovation-how-ing-uses-generative-ai-to-put-people-first), 11 Jan 2024) — *McKinsey partnership on GenAI is evidenced by this joint article*; McKinsey, *"Deploying AI at speed and scale: Talking with ING's Marnix van Stiphout"* (1 Jul 2025); Computer Weekly, *"How ING reaps benefits of centralising AI"* (13 Jan 2026); FStech, *"All of ING's product fulfilment is likely to be impacted by agentic AI, says COO"* (4 Dec 2025).
- **Chatbot name "Marie" — GAP/unverified:** ING's customer-facing GenAI **contact-centre chatbot is confirmed**, but I could **not** verify the specific brand name "Marie"/"ING Assistant" in ING's own sources. Do not assert the name without a market-specific source.
- **Microsoft (cloud/security) link:** *"ING uses Microsoft Security solutions to reimagine banking…"* (Microsoft, 18 Oct 2022) — consistent with ING's hybrid public-cloud strategy. No public **OpenAI** direct-partnership evidence found.

---

## 6) ING + HCLTech / OTHER SYSTEM INTEGRATORS

**Key finding (high value for a pitch): NO public evidence of a major ING Group ↔ SI prime relationship.** Targeted news searches for ING with **HCLTech, Infosys, TCS, Cognizant, Accenture, Capgemini, Wipro** returned **no ING Group engagement**.
- The apparent "ING + Infosys/HCL/TCS" hits all concern the unrelated former **ING Vysya Bank (India)** — divested and merged into **Kotak Mahindra Bank in 2014–15** — not ING Groep. (e.g., Livemint, *"Kotak Mahindra Bank–ING Vysya Bank deal…"* Nov 2014.)
- ING is fundamentally an **in-house engineering organisation** (Areas 2–3), which is itself the pitch angle (SI whitespace).
- **The public third-party tech/ops relationships that DO exist** (verified by title/date via news indexes; not SIs): **Worldline** — *"Worldline signs a multi-year deal with ING"* (Worldline, 30 Jan 2023, payments processing); **Temenos** — *"ING Belgium"* case reference (Temenos, core-banking, dated May 2025); **Microsoft** (security/cloud, Oct 2022). Historical: ING signed an **€800m outsourcing deal** back in 2006 (Finextra, 4 Jul 2006).
- **GAP:** I could not fully open the Worldline/Temenos/Microsoft pages (search-engine/Cloudflare/JS blocks); recommend confirming scope directly on worldline.com and temenos.com before citing in the deck.

---

## 7) ING REGULATORY HOME

**Confirmed: ING is directly supervised by the ECB, with DNB as national/home supervisor.**
- **Primary (ING's own 2024 Annual Report):** "We are subject to the regulatory supervision of the **ECB** and other regulators… **In its capacity as the principal prudential supervisor in the EU, the ECB has extensive supervisory and investigatory powers**… under the **Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM)**…" ([2024 ING Groep Annual Report](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/files/2024-ing-groep-nv-annual-report.pdf), risk-factors section).
- **DNB as national supervisor:** the AR states the **2.0% O-SII buffer** "is set separately for Dutch systemic banks by the **Dutch Central Bank (De Nederlandsche Bank)**," and references DNB methodology on multiple risk items — confirming DNB as ING's national competent authority within the SSM ([2024 ING Groep Annual Report](https://ing.com/binaries/content/assets/documents/files/2024-ing-groep-nv-annual-report.pdf)).
- **ECB "Significant Institution" list:** ING Groep N.V. is a directly-supervised significant institution — [ECB list of supervised entities](https://www.bankingsupervision.europa.eu/framework/supervised-banks/html/index.en.html) *(the ECB page is JS-rendered; ING's presence on the SI list is well-established and corroborated by ING's own SSM statements above).* ING is also a **Global Systemically Important Bank (G-SIB)** — see ING's [2025 G-SIB indicators disclosure](https://ing.com/investors/financial-performance/annual-reports).

---

## GAPS & UNCERTAINTIES (be explicit in the deck)
1. **2022–2023 "core-platform write-down" (Area 2):** Not found as a discrete, named impairment/euro figure. The defensible, citable facts are the **2016** €800m platform investment / €1.1bn restructuring charge and the **2019–2020** strategic refocus (Euromoney, paywalled). Verify FY2020/FY2021 disclosures if a specific number is required.
2. **Discrete IT/technology spend (Area 1):** Not publicly disclosed as a line item. Use adoption KPIs (IPC 67%, OnePipeline 85%, Touchpoint 75%) or the bundled Retail "€647m… technology" reference, with caveats.
3. **Chatbot brand "Marie" (Area 5):** GenAI contact-centre chatbot confirmed; the name "Marie"/"ING Assistant" is **unverified** in ING sources.
4. **"Forge" internal developer platform (Area 4):** No public repo; likely internal (maps to OnePipeline/IPC).
5. **Red Hat OpenShift / Kafka (Area 3):** Not confirmed in ING's own primary disclosures; Azure DevOps, Flink, Cassandra, Kubernetes are evidenced via ING's OSS.
6. **Sources read fully vs. by-title-only:** All ING PDFs (press releases, annual report, profile presentations, Investor Update), the McKinsey 2017 agile article (via Wayback), Wikipedia EPI, ING strategy page, EPI site, CNBC 2016, and the ing-bank GitHub org were **read directly**. Euromoney (2019/2020), the McKinsey GenAI/van Stiphout articles, Computer Weekly, FStech, Worldline, Temenos, Microsoft were **verified via Google News index (title/date/outlet)** but blocked from full fetch — recommend opening these directly before quoting specifics.

# Customer Copyright Commitment Required Mitigations - Microsoft Foundry | Microsoft Learn

Important

Non-English translations are provided for convenience only. Please consult the [`EN-US` version of this document](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/responsible-ai/openai/customer-copyright-commitment) for the definitive version.

Note

The requirements described below apply only to customers using Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry Models ("Azure OpenAI") and other Covered Products with configurable Metaprompts or other safety systems ("Configurable GAI Services"). They do not apply to customers using other Covered Products including Copilots with safety systems that are fixed. The only Configurable GAI Services are Microsoft Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot; the Universal Required Mitigations do not apply to these offerings, but service-specific mitigations apply instead.

The Customer Copyright Commitment ("CCC") is a provision in the Microsoft Product Terms that describes Microsoft's obligation to defend customers against certain third-party intellectual property claims relating to Output Content. For Azure OpenAI and any Configurable GAI Service, Customer also must have implemented all mitigations required by the Azure OpenAI documentation in the offering that delivered the Output Content that is the subject of the claim. The required mitigations to maintain CCC coverage are set forth below.

This page describes only the required mitigations necessary to maintain CCC coverage for Azure OpenAI and Configurable GAI Services. It is not an exhaustive list of requirements or mitigations required to use Azure OpenAI (or Configurable GAI Services) responsibly in compliance with the documentation. Azure OpenAI customers must comply with the [Code of Conduct](/en-us/legal/ai-code-of-conduct?context=%2Fazure%2Fcognitive-services%2Fopenai%2Fcontext%2Fcontext) at all times.

The mitigations below take effect on the dates indicated. For new Configurable GAI Services, features, models, or use cases, new CCC requirements will be posted and take effect at or following the launch of such Configurable GAI Service, feature, model, or use case. Otherwise, customers will have six months from the date of publication on this page to implement any new mitigations required to maintain coverage under the CCC. The Effective Date indicates when the mitigation must be deployed. If a customer tenders a claim for defense, the customer will be required to demonstrate compliance with all relevant requirements, both on this page and as listed in the Product Terms.

## Universal Required Mitigations

Universal required mitigations must be implemented to maintain CCC coverage for all offerings delivering Output Content from Azure OpenAI and Configurable GAI Services, with the exceptions of GitHub Offerings and Microsoft Copilot Studio. The requirements are set forth here:

**Azure OpenAI & Configurable GAI Services - Universal Required Mitigations:**

| **Category** | **Required Mitigation** | **Effective Date** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metaprompt | The customer offering must include a metaprompt directing the model to prevent copyright infringement in its output, for example, the sample system message component, "Protected Material – Text" at: [Safety system message templates](/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/concepts/safety-system-message-templates). | December 1, 2023 |
| Testing and Evaluation Report | The customer offering must have been subjected to evaluations (e.g., guided red teaming, systematic measurement, or other equivalent approach) by the customer using tests designed to detect the output of third-party content. Significant ongoing reproduction of third-party content determined through evaluation must be addressed. The report of results and mitigations must be retained by the customer and provided to Microsoft in the event of a claim. Customer is under no obligation to conduct direct testing of Microsoft services to maintain CCC coverage. More information on guided red teaming is at: [Red teaming large language models (LLMs)](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/red-teaming). More information on systematic measurement is at: [Overview of Responsible AI practices for Azure OpenAI models - Foundry Tools - Microsoft Learn.](overview) | December 1, 2023 |

## Additional Required Mitigations Per Azure OpenAI Use Case

Additional required mitigations are required to maintain CCC coverage for offerings delivering Output Content from Azure OpenAI, depending on what use cases the customer is using. As used below, “use case” refers to a major intended use of your application by your users. Use cases may have been indicated on a Limited Access Form. More information about use cases is available at: [Transparency Note for Azure OpenAI - Foundry Tools | Microsoft Learn](transparency-note). Requirements are cumulative, meaning that the customer offering must include the required mitigations for all use cases. These additional requirements do not apply to Configurable GAI Services, only Azure OpenAI.

Not all content types can be generated by every application. The following required mitigations must be enabled for any use case described below. Azure OpenAI Guardrails (previously content filters) include protected material detection and Prompt Shield. Protected material detection can analyze both text and code. Different filters must be on depending on content type.

The required mitigations are set forth here:

**Azure OpenAI Only - Additional Required Mitigations Per Use Case**

**Text and Code Use Cases:**

| **Content type** | **Use Case** | **Category** | **Required Mitigation** | **Effective Date** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Code generation | Code generation or transformation scenarios, or other open code generation scenarios | Guardrails (previously content filters) | The protected material code model must be configured on in either annotate or filter mode. If choosing to use annotate mode, customer must comply with any cited license provided for Output Content that is the subject of the claim.The jailbreak model (i.e., Prompt Shield for jailbreak attacks) must be configured on in filter mode. | December 1, 2023 |
|  |  |  | If using the asynchronous filter feature, Output Content retroactively flagged as protected material code is not covered by the CCC, unless customer complies with its cited license. | May 21, 2024 |
| Text generation | Journalistic content, writing assistance, or other open text generation scenarios | Guardrails | The protected material text model must be configured on in filter mode. The jailbreak model (i.e., Prompt Shield for jailbreak attacks) must be configured on in filter mode. | December 1, 2023 |
|  |  |  | If using the asynchronous filter feature, Output Content retroactively flagged as protected material text is not covered by the CCC. | May 21, 2024 |

**Image generation models, OpenAI transcription models, and all other use cases:**

No additional requirements.

## Required Mitigations for GitHub Offerings

The below are the only required mitigations that apply to GitHub Offerings, and as of April 3, 2026, there are no additional required mitigations. Use of the Duplicate Detection filter feature is no longer required for CCC coverage. This feature remains available for optional use. See [Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot](https://gh.io/cfb-dd).

**Required Mitigations for GitHub Offerings Only**

| **Category** | **Required Mitigation** | **Effective Date** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub Offerings | No additional required mitigations.

# Data, privacy, and security for Foundry Models sold by Azure in Microsoft Foundry - Microsoft Foundry | Microsoft Learn

Important

Non-English translations are provided for convenience only. Please consult the [`EN-US` version of this document](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/responsible-ai/openai/customer-copyright-commitment) for the definitive version.

This article provides details regarding how data provided by you to Foundry Models sold by Azure in Microsoft Foundry are processed, used, and stored. A 'model sold by Azure' is an AI model designated and deployed as such in Foundry, and includes Azure OpenAI models. Models sold by Azure store and process data to provide the service and to monitor for uses that violate the applicable product terms. Please also see [Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum](https://aka.ms/DPA), which governs data processing by Models sold by Azure. Foundry is an Azure service; [learn more](/en-us/compliance/regulatory/offering-home) about applicable Azure compliance offerings.

Important

Your prompts (inputs) and completions (outputs), your embeddings, and your training data:

- are NOT available to other customers.
- are NOT available to OpenAI or other providers of Models sold by Azure.
- are NOT used by providers of Models sold by Azure to improve their models or services.
- are NOT used to train any generative AI foundation models without your permission or instruction.
- Customer Data, Prompts, and Completions are NOT used to improve Microsoft or third-party products or services without your explicit permission or instruction.

Your fine-tuned Models sold by Azure are available exclusively for your use.

Foundry is an Azure service; Microsoft hosts the Models sold by Azure in Microsoft's Azure environment and Models sold by Azure do NOT interact with any services operated by providers of Models sold by Azure, for example, OpenAI (e.g. ChatGPT, or the OpenAI API).

## What data does Foundry process to provide Models sold by Azure?

Foundry processes the following types of data to provide Models sold by Azure:

- **Prompts and generated content**. When prompts are submitted by the user, content is generated by the service, via the completions, chat completions, images, and embeddings operations.
- **Uploaded data**. You can upload your own data for use with certain service features (e.g., [fine-tuning](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/fine-tuning?pivots=programming-language-studio), [assistants API](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/batch?tabs=standard-input&amp;pivots=programming-language-ai-studio), [batch processing](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/batch?tabs=standard-input&amp;pivots=programming-language-ai-studio)) using the Files API or vector store.
- **Data for stateful entities**. When you use certain optional features of Models sold by Azure and Agents, such as the [Responses API](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/responses), the Threads feature of the [Assistants API](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/assistant), and Stored completions, the service creates a data store to persist message history and other content, in accordance with how you configure the feature.
- **Augmented data included with or via prompts**. When you use data associated with stateful entities, the service retrieves relevant data from a configured data store and augments the prompt to produce generations that are grounded with your data. Prompts may also be augmented with data retrieved from a source included in the prompt itself, such as a URL.
- **Training & validation data**. You can provide your own training data consisting of prompt-completion pairs for the purposes of [fine-tuning a model](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/fine-tuning?pivots=programming-language-studio).

## How does Foundry process data to provide Models sold by Azure?

The diagram below illustrates how your data is processed. This diagram covers several types of processing:

1. How Foundry processes your prompts via inferencing with Models sold by Azure to generate content (including when additional data from a designated data source is added to a prompt using Azure OpenAI on your data, Assistants, or batch processing).
2. How the Assistants feature stores data in connection with Messages, Threads, and Runs.
3. How the Responses API feature stores data to persist message history.
4. How the Batch feature processes your uploaded data.
5. How Foundry creates a fine-tuned (custom) model with your uploaded data.
6. How Foundry and Microsoft personnel analyze prompts and completions (text and image) for harmful content and for patterns suggesting the use of the service in a manner that violates the Code of Conduct or other applicable product terms.

[![Data flow diagram for the service.](media/flow-3.png)](media/flow-3.png#lightbox)

As depicted in the diagram above, managed customers may [apply to modify abuse monitoring](https://customervoice.microsoft.com/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=v4j5cvGGr0GRqy180BHbR7en2Ais5pxKtso_Pz4b1_xUOE9MUTFMUlpBNk5IQlZWWkcyUEpWWEhGOCQlQCN0PWcu).

### Generating completions, images or embeddings through inferencing

Models sold by Azure (base or fine-tuned) deployed in your Foundry resource process your input prompts and generate responses with text, images, or embeddings. Prompts and completions are evaluated in real time for harmful content types and content generation is filtered based on configured thresholds. Learn more at [Guardrails (previously content filters) overview](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/content-filter).

Prompts and responses are processed within the customer-specified [geography](https://azure.microsoft.com/explore/global-infrastructure/geographies/) (unless you are using a Global or DataZone deployment type), but may be processed between regions within the geography for operational purposes (including performance and capacity management). See below for information about location of processing when using a Global or DataZone deployment type.

**The models are stateless: no prompts or completions are stored in the model. Additionally, prompts and completions are not used to train, retrain, or improve the base models.**

### Understanding location of processing for "Global" and "Data zone" deployment types

In addition to standard deployments, Foundry offers Models sold by Azure deployment options labeled as 'Global' and 'DataZone.' For any [deployment type](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/foundry-models/concepts/deployment-types) labeled 'Global,' prompts and responses may be processed in any geography where the relevant model sold by Azure is deployed (learn more about [region availability of models](/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/models#model-summary-table-and-region-availability)). For any deployment type labeled as 'DataZone,' prompts and responses may be processed in any geography within the specified data zone, as defined by Microsoft. If you create a DataZone deployment in a Foundry resource located in the United States, prompts and responses may be processed anywhere within the United States. If you create a DataZone deployment in a Foundry resource located in a European Union Member Nation, prompts and responses may be processed in that or any other European Union Member Nation. For both Global and DataZone deployment types, any data stored at rest, such as uploaded data, and including the abuse monitoring data store created for Global and DataZone deployments, is stored in the customer-designated geography. Contents of https://github.blog/news-insights/research/research-quantifying-github-copilots-impact-on-developer-productivity-and-happiness/:
Everyday, we use tools and form habits to achieve more with less. Software development produces such a high number of tools and technologies to make work efficient, to the point of inducing decision fatigue. When we first launched a technical preview of GitHub Copilot in 2021, our hypothesis was that it would improve developer productivity and, in fact, early users shared reports that it did. In the months following its release, we wanted to better understand and measure its effects with quantitative and qualitative research. To do that, we first had to grapple with the question: what does it mean to be productive?

## [Why is developer productivity so difficult to measure?](about:blank#why-is-developer-productivity-so-difficult-to-measure)

When it comes to measuring developer productivity, there is little consensus and there are far more questions than answers. For example:

*   What are the “right” productivity metrics? \[[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-020-09820-z), [2](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/8643844)\]
*   How valuable are self-reports of productivity? \[[3](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2635868.2635892?casa_token=j1_2RtHeHBoAAAAA:Ic_ycWwPvzW2a4SPzZ6vFrHQG4N7PzjoCP9cb1CaljCmGge4DNmYiSC2d_Lc7a5rz-9Otiph1nSm)\]
*   Is the traditional view of productivity—outputs over inputs—a good fit for the complex problem solving and creativity involved in development work? \[[4](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4842-4221-6)\].

In a 2021 study, we found that developers’ own view of productivity has a twist–it’s more akin to having [a good day](https://github.blog/2021-05-25-octoverse-spotlight-good-day-project/). The ability to stay focused on the task at hand, make meaningful progress, and feel good at the end of a day’s work make a real difference in developers’ satisfaction and productivity.

This isn’t a one-off finding, either. Other academic research shows that these outcomes are important for developers \[[5](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10090507/1/Barr_Today%20was%20a%20Good%20Day.%20The%20Daily%20Life%20of%20Software%20Developers_AAM2.pdf)\] and that satisfied developers perform better \[[6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.00922.pdf), [7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.4422.pdf)\]. Clearly, there’s more to developer productivity than inputs and outputs.

## [How do we think about developer productivity at GitHub?](about:blank#how-do-we-think-about-developer-productivity-at-github)

Because AI-assisted development is a relatively new field, as researchers we have little prior research to draw upon. We wanted to measure GitHub Copilot’s effects, but what are they? After early observations and interviews with users, we surveyed more than 2,000 developers to learn at scale about their experience using GitHub Copilot. We designed our research approach with three points in mind:

*   **Look at productivity holistically.** At GitHub we like to think [broadly and sustainably](https://github.swoogo.com/2021/session/692592/the-sustainable-future-of-developer-productivity) about developer productivity and the many factors that influence it. We used the [SPACE productivity framework](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3454124) to pick which aspects to investigate.
*   **Include developers’ first-hand perspective.** We conducted multiple rounds of research including qualitative (perceptual) and quantitative (observed) data to assemble the full picture. We wanted to verify: (a) Do users’ actual experiences confirm what we infer from telemetry? (b) Does our qualitative feedback generalize to our large user base?
*   **Assess GitHub Copilot’s effects in everyday development scenarios.** When setting up our studies, we took extra care to recruit professional developers, and to design tests around typical tasks a developer might work through in a given day.

[![](https://github.blog/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/1200x300-Blog_Ad-Master-1-1.png?w=1024&resize=1024%2C257)](https://github.com/features/copilot?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=blogB&utm_campaign=cta&utm_content=copilot)

Let’s dig in and see what we found!

### [Finding 1: Developer productivity goes beyond speed](about:blank#finding-1-developer-productivity-goes-beyond-speed)

Through a large-scale survey, we wanted to see if developers using GitHub Copilot see benefits in other areas beyond speeding up tasks. Here’s what stood out:

*   **Improving developer satisfaction.** Between 60–75% of users reported they feel more fulfilled with their job, feel less frustrated when coding, and are able to focus on more satisfying work when using GitHub Copilot. That’s a win for developers feeling good about what they do!
*   **Conserving mental energy.** Developers reported that GitHub Copilot helped them stay in the flow (73%) and preserve mental effort during repetitive tasks (87%). That’s developer happiness right there, since we know from previous research that context switches and interruptions can ruin a developer’s day, and that certain types of work are draining \[[8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/2635868.2635892?casa_token=QSunRfpWvOQAAAAA:2HVi9JV6N7A5KKMRXe23pT8j71mFXoxdzKwwMiBXd_UdqvAClkQ1H_w3DJx-AJbz9AD9PRHiSYau), [9](https://github.blog/2021-05-25-octoverse-spotlight-good-day-project/)\].

#### [Table: Survey responses measuring dimensions of developer productivity when using GitHub Copilot](about:blank#table-survey-responses-measuring-dimensions-of-developer-productivity-when-using-github-copilot)

![Survey responses measuring dimensions of developer productivity--perceived productivity, satisfaction and well-being, and efficiency and flow--when using GitHub Copilot](https://github.blog/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/copilot1.png?resize=1024%2C1024)  
_All questions were modeled off of [the SPACE framework](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3454124)._

Developers see GitHub Copilot as a productivity aid, but there’s more to it than that. One user described the overall experience:

> (With Copilot) I have to think less, and when I have to think it’s the fun stuff. It sets off a little spark that makes coding more fun **and** more efficient.

- Senior Software Engineer

The takeaway from our qualitative investigation was that **letting GitHub Copilot shoulder the boring and repetitive work of development reduced cognitive load**. This makes room for developers to enjoy the more meaningful work that requires complex, critical thinking and problem solving, leading to greater happiness and satisfaction.

### [Finding 2: … but speed is important, too](about:blank#finding-2-but-speed-is-important-too)

In the survey, we saw that developers reported they complete tasks faster when using GitHub Copilot, especially repetitive ones. That was an expected finding (GitHub Copilot writes faster than a human, after all), but >90% agreement was still a pleasant surprise. Developers overwhelmingly perceive that GitHub Copilot is helping them complete tasks faster—can we observe and measure that effect in practice? For that we conducted a controlled experiment.

#### [Figure: Summary of the experiment process and results](about:blank#figure-summary-of-the-experiment-process-and-results)

![Summary of the experiment process and results (described in following paragraph)](https://github.blog/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/copitlot2.png?resize=1024%2C870)  
 We recruited 95 professional developers, split them randomly into two groups, and timed how long it took them to write an HTTP server in JavaScript. One group used GitHub Copilot to complete the task, and the other one didn’t. We tried to control as many factors as we could–all developers were already familiar with JavaScript, we gave everyone the same instructions, and we leveraged GitHub Classroom to automatically score submissions for correctness and completeness with a test suite. We’re sharing a behind-the-scenes blog post soon about how we set up our experiment!

In the experiment, we measured—on average—how successful each group was in completing the task and how long each group took to finish.

*   The group that used GitHub Copilot had a **higher rate of completing the task** (78%, compared to 70% in the group without Copilot).
*   The striking difference was that **developers who used GitHub Copilot completed the task significantly faster–55% faster than the developers who didn’t use GitHub Copilot**. Specifically, the developers using GitHub Copilot took on average 1 hour and 11 minutes to complete the task, while the developers who didn’t use GitHub Copilot took on average 2 hours and 41 minutes. These results are statistically significant (_P=.0017_) and the 95% confidence interval for the percentage speed gain is \[21%, 89%\].

There’s more to uncover! We’re conducting more experiments and a more thorough analysis of the experiment data we already collected—looking into heterogeneous effects, or potential effects on the quality of code—and we are planning further academic publications to share our findings.

## [What do these findings mean for developers?](about:blank#what-do-these-findings-mean-for-developers)

We’re here to support developers while they build software—that includes working more efficiently and finding more satisfaction in their work. In our research, we saw that **GitHub Copilot supports faster completion times, conserves developers’ mental energy, helps them focus on more satisfying work, and ultimately find more fun in the coding they do.**

We’re also hearing that these benefits are becoming material to engineering leaders in companies that ran early trials with GitHub Copilot. When they consider how to keep their engineers healthy and productive, they are thinking through the same lens of holistic developer wellbeing and promoting the use of tools that bring delight.

> The engineers’ satisfaction with doing edgy things and us giving them edgy tools is a factor for me. Copilot makes things more exciting.

- CTO, Large Engineering Org

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_debt:
Cost of maintaining a low quality system

**Technical debt** (also known as **design debt**[\[1\]](about:blank#cite_note-Girish_2014-1) or **code debt**) is a qualitative description of the cost to maintain a [system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System "System") that is attributable to choosing an expedient solution for its development.[\[2\]](about:blank#cite_note-2) While an expedited solution can accelerate development in the short term, the resulting low quality may increase future costs if left unresolved.[\[3\]](about:blank#cite_note-Managing_Technical_Debt-3) The term is often used in the context of [information technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_technology "Information technology") and especially [software development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_development "Software development").

Technical debt is similar to yet differs significantly from [monetary debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt "Debt"). Incurring either generally makes future goals more challenging to attain. But unlike monetary debt, technical debt is often incurred without intention. The choice to minimize development time and cost, an ever-present aspect of [business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business "Business"), is the primary factor. Technical debt is generally only assessed retroactively (after a development effort).

Properly managing technical debt is essential for maintaining [software quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_quality "Software quality") and long-term sustainability. In some cases, taking on technical debt is a strategic choice to meet immediate goals, such as delivering a [proof of concept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_concept "Proof of concept") or a quick release. However, failure to prioritize and address the debt can result in reduced maintainability, increased development costs, and risk to production systems.[\[4\]](about:blank#cite_note-Jeffries_2015-4)[\[5\]](about:blank#cite_note-Knesek_2016-5)

Technical debt results from design and implementation decisions that may optimize for the short term, but at the expense of future adaptability and maintainability. System aspects that incur technical debt can be described as a collection of design or implementation constructs that make future changes more costly or impossible, primarily impacting internal system qualities such as maintainability and evolvability.[\[6\]](about:blank#cite_note-6)

[Ward Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward_Cunningham "Ward Cunningham") coined the term _technical debt_ in 1992.[\[7\]](about:blank#cite_note-7) After reading _[Metaphors We Live By](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphors_We_Live_By "Metaphors We Live By")_, Cunningham devised this debt metaphor to explain to his [boss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employer "Employer") the need to refactor the financial product they were working on:[\[8\]](about:blank#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](about:blank#cite_note-9)

> Shipping first time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with a rewrite.... The danger occurs when the debt is not repaid. Every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as [interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest "Interest") on that debt. Entire engineering organizations can be brought to a stand-still under the debt load of an unconsolidated implementation, [object-oriented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming "Object-oriented programming") or otherwise.[\[10\]](about:blank#cite_note-oopsla92-10)

Similar concepts had existed before this. In 1980, [Meir "Manny" Lehman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manny_Lehman_\(computer_scientist\) "Manny Lehman (computer scientist)") had published a similar [law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_law "Scientific law") using an ["architectural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture") metaphor" for the deteriorating nature of software. Manny's Law states: "As an evolving program is continually changed, its complexity, reflecting deteriorating structure, increases unless work is done to maintain or reduce it."[\[11\]](about:blank#cite_note-11)

Common causes of technical debt include:

Pressure to minimize development time

An ever-present aspect of business.

Unexpected and ill-defined features and changes

The implementation of last-minute [specification changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requirements_analysis "Requirements analysis") or changes that are insufficiently documented or tested,[\[12\]](about:blank#cite_note-SuryanarayanaSamarthyam2014-12):4[\[13\]](about:blank#cite_note-Sterling2010-13):22[\[14\]](about:blank#cite_note-RiosNicolliSp%C3%ADnolaMendon%C3%A7aSeaman2018-14)

Gaps in knowledge or skills

May manifest as a lack of [process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process "Process") understanding, insufficient knowledge, poor technological leadership, or inadequate mentoring or [knowledge sharing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_sharing "Knowledge sharing") practices.[\[13\]](about:blank#cite_note-Sterling2010-13)[\[13\]](about:blank#cite_note-Sterling2010-13):17

Issues in the development process

Such as sub-optimal solutions, insufficient [requirements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requirements_analysis "Requirements analysis") (from process inefficiencies), conflicting requirements on parallel branches, deferred [refactoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_refactoring "Code refactoring"), or delayed upstream contributions.[\[14\]](about:blank#cite_note-RiosNicolliSp%C3%ADnolaMendon%C3%A7aSeaman2018-14)[\[13\]](about:blank#cite_note-Sterling2010-13):29

Non-compliance with best practice

Such as insufficient [software documentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_documentation "Software documentation"), poor collaboration practices, lack of ownership, [rewrites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_rewriting "Code rewriting") for outsourced software, inadequate attention to code quality, [tightly coupled components](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupling_\(computer_programming\) "Coupling (computer programming)"), lack of a [test suite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_suite "Test suite"), or failure to align to standards (including ignoring industry standard [frameworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_framework "Software framework")).[\[12\]](about:blank#cite_note-SuryanarayanaSamarthyam2014-12)[\[12\]](about:blank#cite_note-SuryanarayanaSamarthyam2014-12):7[\[13\]](about:blank#cite_note-Sterling2010-13)

By increasing the cost of ongoing maintenance, technical debt makes it harder to predict release schedules. "Interest payments" result from incomplete work and escalating integration costs due to changes in the [upstream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upstream_\(software_development\) "Upstream (software development)") project. Increases in complexity and the amount of [uncompleted work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_backlog "Product backlog") make it increasingly difficult to accurately [estimate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimation_\(project_management\) "Estimation (project management)") effort, resulting in delays, missed deadlines, and stress on engineering teams, which can result in higher staff turnover, compounding the problem.[\[15\]](about:blank#cite_note-15) Carrying technical debt into production increases the risk of outages, financial losses, and potential legal issues due to breached [service-level agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service-level_agreements "Service-level agreements"). Future refactoring becomes riskier and costlier, with modifications to production code introducing greater chances of disruption.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

Failure to address technical debt can cause productivity to decline and slow down the delivery of features. The cumulative effects of technical debt result in increasingly fragile systems that can make bold improvements difficult. The domination of incremental changes, along with delays to critical refactoring, can result in stressed systems with inconsistent design, causing users to suffer from degraded performance and limited functionality while developers struggle to maintain quality.[\[1\]](about:blank#cite_note-Girish_2014-1)[\[16\]](about:blank#cite_note-rtp-16)

Kenny Rubin uses the following categories to help manage technical debt:[\[17\]](about:blank#cite_note-Essential_Scrum:_Velocity-17)

Happened-upon

The development team was unaware it existed until it was exposed during the normal course of performing work on the product. # Description

## Abstract
Point an AI coding agent at an unfamiliar codebase and ask it to explain the architecture, and for a few hundred files, it works beautifully. Point the same agent - with the same well-engineered prompt - at a ten-thousand-file enterprise Java monolith, and it quietly falls apart: the context window fills, compaction kicks in, the model starts forgetting details, and then it starts inventing them. This isn’t a prompt-quality problem. It’s a physics problem: a fixed-size processing container being asked to hold an unbounded amount of code.

This talk is a production report on solving it. Working on a real, ten-thousand-file legacy Java system, we built a five-layer, eleven-agent pipeline that reverse-engineers architecture, domain models, service boundaries, and workflows - without ever asking a single agent to read the whole codebase. Deterministic tools (build introspection, LSP, tree-sitter) handle structure; LLM agents are reserved exclusively for semantic reasoning; and a lightweight orchestrator (the Conductor) coordinates specialised agents tracking only the pipeline state, never code content. The result: 10,000+ classes indexed, 200+ living documents, 400+ database tables mapped, 140+ API endpoints catalogued, and documentation that regenerates incrementally as the code changes.

I’ll walk through the architecture layer by layer - Scout, Cartographers, Specialists, Surveyors, Chronicler, Conductor - and distill it into four transferable principles of context engineering: progressive disclosure, deterministic grounding, role isolation, and subagent isolation. I’ll also share what broke along the way: a symbol-indexing layer that had to be rebuilt for speed, the point where the full pipeline stopped being worth its cost, and why decoupled agent layers let us fix any one of them without touching the rest.

## Targe audience
Engineers and architects using AI agents on real codebases - especially anyone who has hit the wall where a coding agent starts hallucinating on a large, unfamiliar system - plus teams designing multi-agent pipelines for structural or high-volume analysis work.

## Key takeaways
A concrete architecture pattern for multi-agent pipelines that stay within context limits by design, not by luck
A working example of separating deterministic (tool) work from cognitive (LLM) work at scale
Four reusable principles of context engineering, and the production lessons that shaped them
How to tell when the full pipeline is worth building - and when a thinner approach is the better call

Youtube Video URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FCODql2UWM8
