# Workspace: HCLTech × ING — Core Banking BTA Knowledge Graph & Agent Architecture

## What this workspace is

This is a **research and pitch-authoring workspace**, not a software project. There is no
application to build, test, or deploy. The deliverable is a *business-level pitch deck*
backed by a *research-grade evidence dossier*.

**Audience of the deliverable:** ING Bank leadership (business + technology). The deck must
be understandable by non-technical executives, while the research behind it must be deep
enough that the presenter survives hostile technical questioning.

**Subject:** `PRIME.AI` — HCLTech's methodology for applying AI agents across the complete
SDLC on ING's Core Banking / BTA Payments programme, with a **knowledge graph / ontology
semantic layer** as the central technical thesis.

## Non-negotiable working rules

1. **Every factual claim carries a citation.** Inline URL to a primary source. If a claim
   cannot be sourced, it is labelled an assumption or removed. A bank's leadership will
   check numbers. An unsupportable number destroys the whole pitch.
2. **Separate verified fact from inference from aspiration.** Use the labels
   `[VERIFIED]`, `[INFERRED]`, `[ASSUMPTION — validate with client]`. Never present an
   inference about ING's internal estate as fact.
3. **Prefer primary sources**: arXiv papers, standards bodies (BIAN, ISO, EDM Council),
   regulator publications (EU, EBA, ECB, DNB), vendor *engineering* blogs, conference
   talks, annual reports. Deprioritise listicles, SEO content, and vendor marketing.
4. **Vendor marketing must be flagged as such.** Neo4j, Palantir, Microsoft and every SI
   publish self-serving numbers. Mark them. Prefer independent evidence.
5. **Steelman the counter-argument.** Every section that makes a claim must also record the
   strongest objection to it and the honest rebuttal. The METR RCT, DORA's stability
   findings, GitClear's code-quality data and Cognition's "Don't Build Multi-Agents" are
   deliberately kept in scope as counter-evidence.
6. **Do not overclaim.** The methodology must be credible and buildable with the client's
   real stack. Reject anything that reads as science fiction; reject anything that reads as
   a rebranding of what everyone already does.
7. **Everything stays inside this workspace.** No files, config, or state written outside
   this directory. No client material sent to third-party services.

## Client stack (as evidenced by the existing draft deck)

GitHub Copilot custom agents (GHCP) + Anthropic Claude · Azure DevOps (repos, boards,
pipelines) · OpenShift ("BIAB" region) · Red Panda (Kafka-compatible streaming) ·
"Orange Sharing" (SharePoint) · "Forge" (internal developer platform/documentation) ·
"INGenious" (test automation framework) · Teams meeting transcripts · FSA documents
(functional specification/architecture).

Anything about ING beyond this and public record is an assumption to validate.

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `My-prompt.md` | The originating brief from the user. Re-read before major decisions. |
| `HCLTech-ppt-screenshots/` | The existing draft deck (7 slides) being replaced. |
| `sahaj-software-ppt-and-desc/` | Competitor/peer talk being analysed and superseded. |
| `other-sources.md` | Source video list. |
| `research/raw/` | Source extracts: transcripts, PDF text, per-thread research dossiers. |
| `research/` | Synthesised dossier, methodology, and deck artefacts. |
| `.github/skills/` | Agent skills available in this workspace. |
| `.venv/` | Local Python venv for extraction tooling. Not a deliverable. |

## Skills available here

Vendored from [`mattpocock/skills`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills) (MIT, licence
retained at `.github/skills/LICENSE-mattpocock-skills.txt`), chosen because they encode the
same fundamentals this pitch argues for:

- `grilling/` — relentless interviewing to resolve every branch of a design tree. **Use
  this to stress-test the pitch narrative before it goes to the client.**
- `domain-modeling/` — build and sharpen a shared domain model / ubiquitous language.
  Directly relevant: the deck's thesis is that a ubiquitous language belongs in a graph.
- `codebase-design/` — deep modules, small interfaces. The "good code base" argument.
- `research/` — investigate against high-trust primary sources, capture as cited markdown.
- `writing-for-agents/` — how to write documents agents actually read.

Local additions live alongside them and are prefixed `prime-`.

## House style for the deliverables

- Business slides: one idea per slide, a number or a picture, no wall of text. Assume the
  reader is a director who will spend 20 seconds on it.
- Research dossier: dense, cited, sectioned, tables over prose where comparative.
- Never use "revolutionary", "game-changing", "seamlessly", "unlock", "supercharge".
- Prefer concrete nouns from the client's world (payment, FSA, sprint, defect, release)
  over abstract vendor language.

# Baseline Analysis — What We Have, What Sahaj Has, Where The Gaps Are

## Part 1 — Faithful transcription of the existing HCLTech draft deck

Seven slides, from `HCLTech-ppt-screenshots/`. Classification marking: *Internal*. Co-branded
HCLTech + ING.

### Slide 1 — Agenda
| Section | Stated purpose |
| --- | --- |
| AI Assisted Delivery Model | How the AI-assisted model reshaped the BTA delivery approach |
| PRIME.AI Methodology | The methodology underpinning the custom GHCP agent framework |
| Agent Overview & Architecture | The seven agents deployed across the SDLC and how they fit together |
| Agent Workflow | How the agents interact end-to-end across the engineering lifecycle |
| Demo | A live walkthrough of the agents in action |

### Slide 2 — "Acceleration Driven By AI-Assisted Delivery" (Transforming the BTA Payments Program)
- **Scope statement:** the Core Banking team adopted an AI-assisted methodology within the
  **BTA Payments stream** to meet an accelerated launch timeline; aim was to maximise
  development velocity "while strictly safeguarding software quality".
- **Challenge:** speed without sacrificing quality.
- **Approach:** "A PRIME.AI-based instructions, skills, agents, prompts — via custom agents
  build across SDLC phases."
- **Result:** *30% productivity improvement from the time of AI adoption*; freed ~2 sprints
  of capacity, used to absorb the additional **DG** requirements.
- **Impact at a glance:** 30% faster delivery velocity. **1 squad of 10 engineers assisted by
  7 agents.** Bar chart, "Timeline comparison (months)": Manual **3.5** → Agentic **2.5**.

### Slide 3 — "AI-Assisted BTA Project Delivery" (Deconstructing the 80/20 AI-Assisted Delivery Model)
Two streams, each split 80% AI-assisted / 20% non-AI:

| Stream | AI-assisted (80%) | Non-AI (20%) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coding & Unit Testing | Generating user stories; analysing dependencies; code development; unit test case generation; code coverage & fix defects | Pipeline creation; build application; deploy to ST & SIT; validation |
| Quality Engineering & Testing | Generating test cases; defect triage; analysing defects; defect reporting; test automation script generation | Test case execution; validation and approval |

- Illustrative squad: previously delivered endpoints in **API Factory**, now in BTA Payments.
- **Impact on endpoints delivery: 2 sprints → 1.4 sprints, ~30% faster.**

### Slide 4 — "Our Methodology & Approach"
- **PRIME.AI = Prompt driven, Reusable, Intent focused, Modular Engineering.**
- *Agent Configuration* — four markdown artefacts feeding "Agent Capability":
  - `instructions.md` — **who** the agent is
  - `skills.md` — **what** the agent can do
  - `agents.md` — **how** the agent executes
  - `prompts.md` — templates used
- Flanking concepts: **Dynamic Knowledge Graph** (left) and **Context Engineering** (right),
  funnelling into *"Engineered to be Token Efficient"*.
- Badge row: DevOps & SRE Enabled · Developer & Tester Friendly · Orchestration efficient ·
  Multi-Agentic Framework · LLM & token Friendly.

### Slide 5 — "Agents Overview" (seven agents, with a % badge each)

| # | Agent | Stated function | Declared inputs | Badge |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | User Story Generation | Analyses requirements docs, generates user stories with acceptance criteria and traceability links | FSA + transcript | ~30% |
| 2 | Test Case Generation | Reviews user stories and interaction models → functional and regression test cases | FSA + transcript + user stories | ~30% |
| 3 | Code Generation | Converts approved designs and specifications into production-ready code | FSA + user stories + dependent repos + transcript + query log + mapping doc | ~25% |
| 4 | Unit Test Case Generation | Creates and validates unit tests, improving coverage without manual scripting | FSA + user stories + repo | ~35% |
| 5 | INGenious Test Script Generator | Reviews FSA and test cases, generates automation scripts, validates coverage across key user workflows | FSA + test cases | ~20% |
| 6 | Defect Triage | Reviews test results, classifies root causes, routes defects to the right owners | test cases + defects | ~25% |
| 7 | Mechanic | Inspects functional requirements and specs, flags automation gaps, recommends fixes via automated scans | FSA + dependent repo + test cases + defects + user stories | ~25% |

### Slide 6 — "Agent Architecture & Integrations"
- **AI engine:** GHCP Custom Agent ("custom-built GitHub Copilot agent orchestrating BTA
  delivery workflows") **+** Claude LLM ("reasoning and code generation").
- **Integrations:** Azure DevOps pipeline logs *via Azure CLI* · BIAB Region (OpenShift logs)
  *via OpenShift CLI* · Red Panda logs *via CLI* · Orange Sharing *via PAT tokens* · Forge
  documentation *via Forge CLI* · Azure Repo *via Azure CLI* · Teams meeting transcripts
  (*footnoted: currently fed offline*).
- **Outcomes:** Knowledge Graph ("unified enterprise knowledge base built from all integrated
  sources") · Output Compression ("condenses agent outputs into concise, actionable
  artifacts") · Self Learning ("continuously improves agent accuracy from feedback loops").

### Slide 7 — "Multi Agent Automation: Automating SDLC"
Four lanes, with role owners and a `*` marking human-in-the-loop steps:

1. **Requirements Gathering** (Business Analyst) — Story Generator. Fetch feature page from
   Orange Sharing → fetch attached docs/files from SharePoint in the FSAs → generate EPIC-wise
   user stories → `*` once BAs confirm and verify, push directly to ADO or upload via CSV.
2. **Development** (Developers) — Developer Agent + Unit Test Generator. Refer Forge
   documentation for coding standards → connect to Azure DevOps for story → connect to
   dependent repo and clone a local copy → `*` analysis and share implementation plan for
   engineer to validate → generate code → feedback. Unit test lane: uses cached KG of FSAs,
   transcripts, user stories and the code generator agent → generates and validates unit tests
   with `mvn clean test` and install → `*` raise PR post verification → feedback.
3. **Test Preparation** (Testers) — Test Case Generator + Test Script Generator. Fetch US from
   ADO with related links, attachments, comments → `*` analyse gathered KG cache of the FSAs
   and the US → generate ADO-importable test cases → after verification push to task board.
   INGenious script generator: generates scripts from cached KG or ADO or Orange Sharing →
   builds reusable components for assertions → `*` post-verification PR raised and proceed.
4. **Testing & Resolution** (Testers & Developers) — Defect Triage + Mechanic. Fetch bug
   info/attachments/comments from ADO → generate daily triage report. Mechanic: uses cached KG
   for complete bug context → reproduces the error by getting response from the endpoint, OCP
   logs → thorough analysis, deep research RCA and resolution plan → does the fix and after
   engineer's verification pushes changes through build and release pipelines.

## Part 3 — Where the existing deck is weak (candid)

Ordered by how badly each would hurt in front of ING leadership.

### W1. The knowledge graph is asserted, never explained — and the words used undercut it
The KG appears three times and each time weaker than the last: as a flanking label on slide 4
("Dynamic Knowledge Graph"), as an *outcome* on slide 6 ("unified enterprise knowledge base
built from all integrated sources"), and on slide 7 as **"cached KG"**.

- Calling it an **outcome** is backwards. A knowledge graph that is a *by-product* of running
  agents is a log. The entire argument for a graph is that it is an *input* — the substrate
  agents read from *before* they act.
- Calling it a **cache** is worse. A cache is a disposable performance optimisation.
  If the KG is a cache, then the honest description of this architecture is
  "seven prompts with a shared scratch directory", and a sharp reviewer will say exactly that.
- There is no schema, no entity types, no relationships, no query, no persistence story, no
  refresh story, no ownership. Nothing that survives the question *"show me the graph."*

**This is the biggest gap, and it is also the biggest opportunity**, because the KG is
precisely where the strongest external evidence and the strongest differentiation live.

### W2. The percentage badges are indefensible as presented
Each agent carries a bare "~30%", "~25%", "~35%". Of what? Effort saved, cycle time, coverage,
adoption? Measured how, against what baseline, over what period, with what confidence? These
numbers are the first thing a CFO or a delivery lead will attack, and there is no methodology
slide to fall back on. Worse, they are *near-identical* (20–35%), which reads as estimation
rather than measurement.

### W3. "80% AI-assisted" is the single most attackable claim in the pack
Slide 3 says coding and unit testing are "80% AI-assisted". Taken literally this says 80% of
the bank's payments code is machine-written. In a regulated core banking payments context that
sentence is a risk-committee trigger, not a selling point. The intended meaning is almost
certainly "80% of *activities in this stream* had AI assistance available", which is a very
different and much weaker claim. As written it invites a supervisory question the team cannot
comfortably answer.

### W4. Quality and risk are asserted, not evidenced
Slide 2 says the goal was speed "while strictly safeguarding software quality" — and then the
deck presents no quality evidence at all. No defect escape rate, no change failure rate, no
coverage delta, no rework/churn measure, no security finding rate. The external evidence base
(DORA 2024/2025 on stability, GitClear on churn and duplication, METR on perceived vs actual
speed) says this is *exactly* where AI delivery claims break. Presenting velocity without
stability in front of a bank is presenting half of the DORA scorecard, and the missing half is
the one the CRO cares about.

### W5. There is no orchestration story
Seven agents are listed on slide 5 as a flat catalogue and sequenced on slide 7 as four swim
lanes. Nothing explains who schedules them, what happens when one fails, what runs in
parallel, what state passes between them, how conflicting outputs are reconciled, or how
context is prevented from leaking between them. Slide 4 claims "Orchestration efficient" as a
badge. Sahaj devotes an entire layer (the Conductor) to precisely this question and asks it
explicitly: *"Who watches the workers?"* We currently have no answer.

### W6. Nothing about governance, audit, or regulation
For a European systemically important bank this is a startling omission. Nothing on: who is
accountable for agent-authored code; how agent actions are logged and attributed; how
requirement→code→test→approval traceability is evidenced to an auditor; source-code
confidentiality and data residency; EU AI Act or DORA posture; agent identity and least
privilege. The deck is addressed to ING leadership but answers none of the questions ING
leadership is obliged to ask.

### W7. The agent roster is shaped like the org chart, not like the problem
The seven agents mirror job titles (BA, dev, tester, triage). That is intuitive but it means
every agent is a *generator* — story generator, code generator, test generator, script
generator. There is almost nothing that **understands** (comprehension of the existing
estate), nothing that **verifies** independently, nothing that **maintains the shared model**,
and nothing that **governs**. A fleet of seven generators pointed at a legacy core banking
estate will produce a large volume of plausible artefacts with no independent check —
which is the documented failure mode.

### W8. The reverse-engineering / legacy comprehension problem is entirely absent
Every input on slide 5 is a *document* (FSA, transcript, user story) or a raw repo. But the
hardest and most valuable problem in core banking transformation is understanding the existing
system — what it does, what depends on it, what breaks if it changes. Sahaj's entire talk is
about this problem. We do not mention it. In a *transformation* programme, that is the gap
that matters most commercially.

### W9. Weak framing: "AI-assisted delivery" is a commodity claim
Every SI in the world is currently saying this. Nothing on slides 1–3 could not be said by
Accenture, TCS, Infosys, Capgemini or Cognizant next week. The defensible asset — a
persistent, governed, queryable model of the bank's payments estate — is the one thing a
competitor cannot copy from a slide, and it is currently the least developed idea in the deck.

### W10. Presentation-level issues
Overlapping text on slide 5 (input lines collide with the card below), inconsistent styling
between slide 4 (different template, different footer, "Copyright © 2026 HCLTech |
Confidential") and the rest, and a demo slot with no stated success criteria.

## Part 4 — Sahaj Software: full reconstruction and assessment

Talk: *"The Practical Guide to Reverse Engineering XXL Codebases with Agentic AI"*,
Harshad Nawathe, Solution Consultant, Sahaj Software.

### Their argument, in order
1. **Constraints dictate architecture.** Opens on `std::sort`: in-memory algorithms assume
   unbounded resources; hardware limits shatter pure algorithmic theory; at sufficient scale
   you must pivot from *local computation* to *systemic coordination*. (This is the external
   merge-sort analogy, and it is a very good one.)
2. **APS**: **A**cknowledge the limits of the container · **P**artition into isolated,
   parallelisable workloads · **S**ynthesize distributed outputs into a cohesive state.
3. **The one-shot prompt fails.** They show a genuinely well-engineered ten-line "Principal
   Engineer" reverse-engineering prompt — and it still fails at scale.
4. **Compaction kills context.** The agent fills the window silently; compaction drops
   instructions; the model forgets, then invents. *"Larger context window? Same problem.
   Bigger bucket."*
5. **Four Perils of Context Overload**: context contamination · low signal-to-noise ratio ·
   lost in the middle · attention dilution.
6. **The pivot question: "What if the agents never read the code?"**
7. **Deterministic tools for deterministic work.** Cognitive tasks → LLM agents; parsing,
   indexing, dependency resolution → purpose-built tools. *"LLMs read for meaning — not for
   structure. Structure is already encoded in build files, LSP servers, symbol indexes. Don't
   burn context tokens on work a compiler does for free."*

### Their pipeline — five layers, eleven agents, one orchestrator

| Layer | Agent(s) | Reads | Code access | Produces |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | **Scout** | Build files only (`pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `package.json`) | **Never** | Project skeleton JSON + module summary |
| 1 | **Cartographers** | Scout's skeleton JSON | **Never** — only tool output (LSP, symbol indexers, dependency analysers) | Symbol index: classes, methods, interfaces, inter-file relationships |
| 2 | **Specialists** — Archaeologist, Taxonomist, BeanStalkJack | Symbol index | Surgical reads only — targeted, bounded, intentional | Entity models, Spring bean graphs, concept taxonomies |
| 3 | **Surveyors** — Port Mapper, Surveyor, Choreographer | All Layer-2 artefacts + symbol index | Surgical reads only | Service boundary maps, integration topology, workflow graphs |
| 4 | **Chronicler** | All artefacts from Layers 0–3 | **None** | Complete technical domain documentation |
| Orch. | **Conductor** | **Pipeline state only** — completed, failed, pending | None | Scheduling, scaling, retry/replan/escalate |

The Conductor is explicitly a **hub, agents are spokes**; *"state flows in, instructions flow
out"*; its context is *"the leanest in the entire system — state only, no content."* It is
introduced by three questions: who decides how many Cartographers to spin up, what happens
when a stage fails, and how the pipeline knows what runs in parallel versus what must wait.

### Their four principles of context engineering
- **Progressive Disclosure** — reveal information strictly as the role requires. *Structure
  before content. Boundaries before reads.*
- **Deterministic Grounding** — fast deterministic tooling for structural work; reserve LLM
  context exclusively for semantic reasoning.
- **Role Isolation** — one agent, one competency, one narrow context. *"Specialisation
  eliminates hallucination and instruction drifts."*
- **Subagent Isolation** — delegate cognitive tasks to disposable subagent contexts; keep the
  orchestration layer uncontaminated.

### Their claimed output
10,000+ classes/methods indexed and queryable · 200+ documents (~15MB) · 400+ database tables
mapped to entity classes · 80+ REST and 60+ SOAP endpoints catalogued · 15+ service boundaries
identified and "ready for decomposition" · 80+ workflow traces with sequence diagrams ·
C4 diagrams at three levels · incremental regeneration via input fingerprints.

### Their production lessons
Validate early (*"trust in generated documentation must be earned, not assumed"*) · evolve the
tools, the architecture holds · decoupled layers evolve independently, the inter-layer contract
is the only fixed thing · **respect the economics** — *"the full pipeline justifies its cost
only when a holistic view is needed."*

## Part 5 — Head-to-head: where each is stronger

| Dimension | HCLTech PRIME.AI (current draft) | Sahaj | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Lifecycle coverage** | Requirements → code → unit test → test case → script → triage → fix → release | Comprehension only; stops at documentation | **HCLTech far broader** |
| **Direction** | Forward engineering (spec → artefact) | Reverse engineering (code → understanding) | **Complementary — neither is complete** |
| **Legacy comprehension** | Absent | The entire thesis, done rigorously | **Sahaj decisively better** |
| **Context engineering** | One badge: "Engineered to be Token Efficient" | Four named principles, derived from stated failure modes | **Sahaj decisively better** |
| **Orchestration** | Not addressed; one badge | The Conductor — a designed component with scaling, scheduling, failure handling | **Sahaj decisively better** |
| **Deterministic vs cognitive split** | Not addressed; agents read repos directly | Central design rule; agents mostly never read code | **Sahaj decisively better** |
| **Role isolation / context hygiene** | Not addressed | Explicit principle | **Sahaj better** |
| **Knowledge representation** | "Knowledge graph" asserted, treated as cache/outcome | Symbol index + 200 markdown documents. Honest, but documents don't compose or answer arbitrary queries, and they go stale | **Both weak — this is the open ground** |
| **Ontology / business semantics** | Absent | Absent (a "Taxonomist" agent, but no formal ontology) | **Neither has it — biggest differentiator available** |
| **Business/requirements linkage** | Implicit via FSA and ADO | None at all | **HCLTech better, but not made explicit** |
| **Client-embeddedness** | Deep: real stream, real tools, real squad | Generic Java monolith | **HCLTech better** |
| **Measured outcomes** | 30%, unspecified methodology | Volumetric counts (classes, docs, endpoints) — countable but not value-linked | **Both weak; Sahaj's are at least verifiable** |
| **Governance / regulation** | Absent | Absent (not their audience) | **Neither — mandatory for us** |
| **Economics honesty** | Absent | Explicit: "respect the economics", says when *not* to build it | **Sahaj better, and it builds trust** |
| **Runtime / operations** | Touches OpenShift + Red Panda logs, Mechanic agent does RCA | None | **HCLTech better** |

### The single most important observation

**Sahaj's output is documents. Ours should be a model.**

Sahaj produces 200+ markdown files (~15MB) generated from current code. That is a real
achievement and it beats what we have today. But it has three structural weaknesses we can
name honestly and exploit:

1. **Documents don't compose.** You cannot ask 200 markdown files *"which services touch the
   SEPA instant payment flow and which of them have no regression coverage?"* You can ask a
   graph that.
2. **Documents are write-once per generation.** Their incremental fingerprinting regenerates
   *artefacts*; it does not maintain a *model* with identity and history. There is no way to
   ask what changed, when, and why.
3. **There is no business layer.** A symbol index and a taxonomy of code concepts is not a
   domain ontology. Nothing connects `PaymentProcessorImpl` to *"SEPA Instant Credit
   Transfer"*, to the regulation that mandates it, to the requirement that specified it, or to
   the test that proves it.

Meanwhile, this is *exactly* the gap the external primary sources point at:

- **Matt Pocock** independently arrives at the need for a shared "ubiquitous language" between

- **Matt Pocock** independently arrives at the need for a shared "ubiquitous language" between
  human and agent — and implements it as a markdown file.
- **Emil Eifrem (Neo4j)** answers that directly: *"markdown files… it is part of the solution,
  but it is not the solution"* — you need a **business ontology + technical ontology +
  execution traces**, i.e. thin agents on a smarter shared substrate.
- **Frank Coyle** supplies the third leg: the ontology is not just retrieval, it is a
  **validator** — a symbolic guardrail on probabilistic output (neuro-symbolic AI).
- **Sahaj** supplies the discipline for getting facts into that substrate cheaply and
  reliably (deterministic grounding, progressive disclosure, role isolation).

So the synthesis writes itself: **Sahaj's rigour, applied to build and maintain a
business-grounded ontology rather than a documentation set, spanning the whole lifecycle
rather than comprehension alone, and governed to banking standards.** That is a genuine
superset, and each of its four parts is externally supported rather than invented.

# Research Dossier: Static-Analysis / Code-Graph Tools for an Enterprise Java CODE Knowledge Graph

**Summary.** All 16 tools were verified against primary sources (official docs, GitHub READMEs, source code, academic papers). The standout for a Neo4j-backed code knowledge graph is **jQAssistant** — I extracted its full Java node/relationship model directly from its plugin's `scanner.adoc` and confirmed it against the descriptor source code (XO OGM → Neo4j). Three important corrections/caveats surfaced that matter for a "every-number-checked" deliverable: (1) **jarviz is ExpediaGroup's, not LinkedIn's** — I found no LinkedIn jarviz; (2) **NDepend is a .NET/C# tool, not Java** (its Java sibling is the separate product JArchitect); (3) **Structure101 was acquired by Sonar** (now hosted under sonarsource.com), and **LSIF is archived/superseded by SCIP**. Also note **Glean's Java indexer is NOT in its open-source release**, and **Joern's homepage is stale** (it does support Java via `javasrc2cpg`/`jimple2cpg`). Explicit published scale numbers exist for **CodeQL** (hardware table) but are largely **absent for jQAssistant** (flagged below).

Identity context: authenticated as `rounak-das2008` (Rounak, IIT Kharagpur); no private org repos were in scope, so all citations are public primary sources.

---

## 1. jQAssistant ⭐ (most detail)

**Canonical URLs**
- Homepage: https://jqassistant.org
- Manual (current): https://jqassistant.github.io/jqassistant/current/
- Core monorepo (framework + Java/Maven/JUnit plugins): https://github.com/jQAssistant/jqassistant — version **2.10.0-M3** (`jQAssistant/jqassistant:pom.xml`, `<version>2.10.0-M3</version>`)
- Plugin org (add-on plugins): https://github.com/jqassistant-plugin
- Tutorials: https://github.com/jqassistant-tutorials (per `jQAssistant/jqassistant:readme.adoc:6-15`)

**What it does (2–4 sentences).** jQAssistant scans a project's artifacts — primarily compiled Java **bytecode** (`.class` files), plus Maven POMs, JUnit results, XML/YAML/JSON, Git history (via community plugin), etc. — and imports the structure into an embedded **Neo4j** graph database. You then define **concepts** and **constraints** as **Cypher** queries (in XML/YAML rule files) that enrich the graph and validate architecture/design rules, failing the build on violations. It is explicitly a "software analysis and this-should-not-happen" tool built on a queryable graph.

**Does it produce a GRAPH? In what form.** Yes — a **Neo4j labeled property graph**. The object model is mapped with the XO OGM using Neo4j annotations (`@Label`, `@Relation`, `@Cypher`), confirmed in source: `jQAssistant/jqassistant:plugin/java/src/main/java/com/buschmais/jqassistant/plugin/java/api/model/TypeDescriptor.java:30-52` (`@Label(value="Type", …)` and an embedded Cypher `MERGE (type)-[:REQUIRES_TYPE_PARAMETER]->(variable:Java:ByteCode:Bound:TypeVariable{...})`). Labels **stack** on each node (e.g., a class node carries `:Java:ByteCode:Type:Class`).

**Java plugin node labels** (verified from `jQAssistant/jqassistant:plugin/java/src/main/asciidoc/scanner.adoc`, raw: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jQAssistant/jqassistant/master/plugin/java/src/main/asciidoc/scanner.adoc):
- `:Java:Artifact` (+ `:Directory`, + `:Jar:Archive`)
- `:Java:Package` (props `fqn`, `name`)
- `:Java:Type` — qualified by `:Class`, `:Interface`, `:Enum`, `:Record`, or `:Annotation`; also `:Type:Throwable`. Props: `fqn`, `name`, `sourceFileName`, `visibility`, `abstract`, `static`, `final`, `synthetic`, `byteCodeVersion`, `valid`.
- `:Java:Field` (props `name`, `signature`, `visibility`, `static`, `final`, `transient`, `volatile`, `synthetic`)
- `:Java:Method` (+ `:Method:Constructor`) — props incl. `name`, `signature`, `visibility`, `abstract/static/final/native/synthetic`, `firstLineNumber`, `lastLineNumber`, `effectiveLineCount`, **`cyclomaticComplexity`**
- `:Java:Parameter`, `:Java:Variable`
- `:Java:Value` (+ `:Primitive`, `:Annotation`, `:Class`, `:Enum`, `:Array`)
- `:Java:Bound` (+ `:TypeVariable`, `:ParameterizedType`, `:WildcardType`, `:GenericArrayType`) for generics
- `:Java:Module` (JPMS)

**Java plugin relationship types** (same source):
`DECLARES`, `DECLARES_TYPE_PARAMETER`, `REQUIRES_TYPE_PARAMETER`, `EXTENDS`, `EXTENDS_GENERIC`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `IMPLEMENTS_GENERIC`, `ANNOTATED_BY`, **`DEPENDS_ON`** (with `weight` property = count of references), `OF_TYPE`, `OF_GENERIC_TYPE`, `HAS`, **`READS`**, **`WRITES`**, **`INVOKES`** (all three carry `lineNumber`), `CATCHES`, `THROWS`/`THROWS_GENERIC`, `RETURNS`/`RETURNS_GENERIC`, `CONTAINS`, `REQUIRES`, `IS`, `HAS_UPPER_BOUND`/`HAS_LOWER_BOUND`, `HAS_ACTUAL_TYPE_ARGUMENT`, `OF_RAW_TYPE`, `HAS_COMPONENT_TYPE`, `DECLARES_MAIN_CLASS` (module). So the graph natively expresses `(:Type)-[:DECLARES]->(:Method)-[:INVOKES]->(:Method)`, `(:Method)-[:READS|WRITES]->(:Field)`, `(:Type)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(:Type)`, `(:Type)-[:EXTENDS|IMPLEMENTS]->(:Type)` — exactly the edges you want for a code KG.

**Important extraction nuances (scale-relevant):**
- It reads **bytecode**, so types referenced but not scanned (external libraries) appear as bare `:Type` nodes with only `fqn` and `DECLARES` to members with only a `signature` (per `scanner.adoc` NOTE). You must scan the compiled application to get full detail.
- **Local variables are OFF by default**: `(:Method)-[:DECLARES]->(:Variable)` is only created when `java.include.local-variables=true` (per `scanner.adoc` ClassFileScanner config) — a deliberate performance/size lever.

**Plugins that exist.** Core monorepo (`jQAssistant/jqassistant:plugin/`): `java`, `java-annotation`, `junit`, `maven`, `json`, `xml`, `yaml`, `common`. Add-on org (https://github.com/jqassistant-plugin) includes **spring** (`jqassistant-spring-plugin`), **jee**, **jmolecules**, **graphql**, **openapi**, **asyncapi**, **docker**, **github**, **plantuml-report**, **sarif-report**, **typescript**, **npm**, **rdbms**, **xmi**, **c4**, **context-mapper**, **cyclonedx**, **mapstruct**, etc. (verified via GitHub org repo listing). **Caveat:** there is **no official core "Git" plugin** — the Git scanner is community-maintained: https://github.com/kontext-e/jqassistant-git-plugin. (A GitHub-issues plugin exists at `jqassistant-plugin/jqassistant-github-plugin`.)

**Maven / Neo4j integration.**
- **Maven:** shipped as a Maven plugin (module `jQAssistant/jqassistant:maven/`), run via goals like `jqassistant:scan` / `jqassistant:analyze` bound to the build; also a standalone **CLI** (module `jQAssistant/jqassistant:cli/`).
- **Neo4j:** jQAssistant **embeds Neo4j** and can also connect to a server. The POM defines profiles for **Neo4j 4.4.48** (`neo4jv4`) and **Neo4j 5.26.30** (`neo4jv5`), Neo4j Java driver 4.4.27, Neo4j Browser 5.24.0, plus APOC (`jQAssistant/jqassistant:pom.xml` — `<neo4j_4x.version>4.4.48</neo4j_4x.version>`, `<neo4j_5x.version>5.26.30</neo4j_5x.version>`). This means you can open the resulting store in Neo4j Browser and run Cypher interactively.
- **Query language:** **Cypher**, embedded in rule files (`<concept>`, `<constraint>`, `<group>`) with `requiresConcept`/`providesConcept` ordering (verified on the manual page https://jqassistant.github.io/jqassistant/current/ "Rule Dependencies" section). Build JDKs: 11/17/21; Maven 3.8+ (`readme.adoc:34-44`).

**Scale / performance limits.** ⚠️ **Gap — could NOT verify official numbers.** I found **no published benchmark or documented hard limit** for large (e.g., 10k-file) codebases in the manual or repo. What is documented: local-variable scanning is opt-in for performance (above); the graph lives in Neo4j so memory/heap scales with graph size (external-lib types are stubbed to limit blow-up). The repo's "≥30 minutes" figure refers to *their own* integration-test suite (`readme.adoc:52-56`), **not** a user-codebase benchmark — do not cite it as a scan-time number. Suggested follow-up: jQAssistant Google Group / Stackoverflow tag for community datapoints, and Neo4j heap sizing guidance.

## 2. tree-sitter

**Canonical URLs:** https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/ · https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter · Java grammar: https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-java

**What it does.** "A parser generator tool and an incremental parsing library. It can build a concrete syntax tree for a source file and efficiently update the syntax tree as the source file is edited" (README). Goals: general (any language), fast (parse on every keystroke), robust (error-tolerant), dependency-free (pure-C runtime embeddable anywhere).

**Graph?** Produces a per-file **concrete syntax tree (CST/AST)** — **not** a semantic or cross-file graph. It performs **no type resolution, name binding, or cross-file linking**; you extract structure and build any graph yourself on top. Excellent for fast, resilient *structure extraction* across many languages.

**Scale/perf:** Incremental (re-parses only edited regions); designed for editor-speed per keystroke. **Language support:** grammar-driven (hundreds of community grammars, incl. Java, via separate `tree-sitter-*` repos); bindings for Rust, JS/WASM, Python, Go, C/C++, etc.

---

## 3. Eclipse JDT + Eclipse JDT Language Server (jdtls)

**Canonical URLs:** JDT: https://eclipse.dev/jdt/ · jdtls: https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls

**What it does.** Eclipse JDT is the Eclipse Java toolchain/compiler providing **AST + full type-binding resolution** (code completion, references, diagnostics). **jdtls** wraps JDT as a **Language Server Protocol** server (built on Eclipse LSP4J), usable by any LSP editor; adds Maven (M2Eclipse) and Gradle (Buildship) project import (README).

**Graph?** Not a persistent graph store — it answers **LSP queries**. Relevant graph-like capabilities: **Call Hierarchy**, **Type Hierarchy**, references/implementations (code lens), semantic highlighting, as-you-type diagnostics (README feature list). You'd drive it programmatically over LSP to harvest defs/refs/hierarchies.

**Scale/perf & versions.** Compiles projects **Java 1.8 → 25**; requires a **Java 21** runtime to run; sample launch uses `-Xmx1G` (README "Running from the command line"). Known clients: `redhat-developer/vscode-java`. It's the precise-resolution backbone many indexers reuse.

---

## 4. Spoon (INRIA)

**Canonical URLs:** https://github.com/INRIA/spoon · docs https://spoon.gforge.inria.fr/ · Paper (Software: Practice & Experience 2015, doi:10.1002/spe.2346): https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01078532/document

**What it does.** "Spoon is an open-source library to analyze, rewrite, transform, transpile Java **source** code. It parses source files to build a well-designed AST with powerful analysis and transformation API" (README). Supports modern Java **up to Java 25**; official Inria/OW2 project.

**Graph?** In-memory, well-typed **AST metamodel** (`CtClass`, `CtMethod`, `CtField`, …) with analysis/transformation APIs — **not** a persistent graph DB. Ideal if you need source-level rewriting or precise source AST (comments, generics) rather than a queryable store.

**Scale/versions/license.** Spoon 11.x needs JDK 17+, 10.x JDK 11+, 9.x Java 8 (README). Dual-licensed CeCILL-C / MIT. No official large-codebase throughput number published (flag).

---

## 5. JavaParser

**Canonical URLs:** https://javaparser.org · https://github.com/javaparser/javaparser · DOI 10.5281/zenodo.2667378

**What it does.** "A set of libraries implementing a Java 1.0 – Java 25 Parser with advanced analysis functionalities" (README). **JavaParser** builds the AST; **JavaSymbolSolver** (module `javaparser-symbol-solver-core`, bundled since v3.5.10) resolves an element to its declaration and type (e.g., a name → parameter/field with type + AST position).

**Graph?** In-memory **AST + symbol resolution** — **not** a graph DB. The AST can be **serialized to JSON** (`javaparser-core-serialization`, since 3.6.17), which you can load into your own graph. Current version **3.28.2**; license LGPL-3 **or** Apache-2 (user's choice).

**Scale:** No official benchmark published; widely used for source-level analysis of large Java projects (flag for exact numbers).

---

## 6. Soot / SootUp / WALA (call graphs, points-to, dataflow)

**Soot** — https://github.com/soot-oss/soot · docs https://soot-oss.github.io/soot
- Java optimization/analysis framework with four IRs: **Baf** (streamlined bytecode), **Jimple** (typed 3-address), **Shimple** (SSA), **Grimp** (aggregated) (README). Provides call-graph + points-to (**Spark**), interprocedural dataflow. Latest release **4.7.0** (`org.soot-oss:soot`). **Officially succeeded by SootUp (Dec 2022)**, but maintained for instrumentation and robust Android support (README banner).

**SootUp** — https://github.com/soot-oss/SootUp · docs https://soot-oss.github.io/SootUp/ · Paper (TACAS 2024, doi:10.1007/978-3-031-57246-3_13)
- Redesign of Soot: bytecode→**Jimple**, class-hierarchy generation, **call-graph generation with multiple algorithms/precisions**, **interprocedural IDE/IFDS dataflow** (via Heros), `BodyInterceptor` transforms, Jimple parse/serialize (README). Improvements: no global `Scene`/singletons, **fully parallelizable**, lazy class loading, immutable IR, **full Java 21 bytecode** support.

**WALA** — https://github.com/wala/WALA · javadoc https://wala.github.io/javadoc · quickstart https://github.com/wala/WALA-start
- IBM's static-analysis libraries for **Java bytecode** (and JavaScript): class-hierarchy analysis, **interprocedural dataflow (RHS solver)**, context-sensitive **slicer**, **pointer analysis + call-graph construction**, **SSA-based IR** (README). EPL-licensed; each release built for **Java 17+**.

**Graph?** All three produce **in-memory** call graphs / IRs / points-to graphs — **not** a persistent labeled-property store. **Scale:** designed for whole-program analysis; precision (context/flow sensitivity, points-to) trades off against time/memory. No single official "N-file" number — the honest statement for the deliverable is "scales to large Java but cost is configuration-dependent (call-graph algorithm, context sensitivity)." (Flag: get numbers from the SootUp TACAS'24 paper if you need citable benchmarks.)

---

## 7. Joern (Code Property Graph)

**Canonical URLs:** https://joern.io · https://github.com/joernio/joern (v**2.0.1**) · docs https://docs.joern.io · CPG spec https://cpg.joern.io · CPG paper (IEEE S&P 2014): https://fabianyamaguchi.com/files/2014-ieeesp.pdf

**What it does.** "Joern is a platform for analyzing source code, bytecode, and binary executables. It generates **code property graphs (CPGs)**… stored in a custom graph database… mined using search queries formulated in a **Scala-based domain-specific query language**" (README). Built for vulnerability discovery.

**What the CPG is.** A single intermediate representation merging **syntax (AST) + control-flow + data-flow** into one **"directed, edge-labeled, attributed multigraph"**; nodes have a type (e.g., `METHOD`, `LOCAL`) and key-value properties; edges are labeled (e.g., `CONTAINS`) and directed (docs https://docs.joern.io/code-property-graph/). Historically stored in **OverflowDB**; CPG implementation/spec open-sourced by Qwiet/ShiftLeft (github.com/ShiftLeftSecurity/codepropertygraph).

**Query language.** **CPGQL** — a Scala-based traversal DSL run in the Joern shell (`joern>`).

**Java support & scale.** ✅ Java IS supported (homepage text "coming soon" is **stale**): frontends `javasrc2cpg` (**Java source**, `--language JAVASRC`) and `jimple2cpg` (**Java bytecode** via Soot, `--language JAVA`) per https://docs.joern.io/frontends/. Also C/C++, Ghidra binaries, C#, Go, JS, Kotlin, PHP, Python, Ruby, Swift. Requires **JDK 21**; has a `--server` mode. No official max-LOC published (flag).

---

## 8. CodeQL

**Canonical URLs:** https://codeql.github.com · docs https://codeql.github.com/docs/ · CLI docs https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/codeql-cli · License terms https://securitylab.github.com/tools/codeql/license

**What it does & how it models code.** CodeQL "extracts a single **relational** representation of each source file" — AST + name-binding + type info — into a **CodeQL database** that also bundles the copied source and a language-specific **database schema (dbscheme)** "which specifies the mutual relations in the data" (https://codeql.github.com/docs/codeql-overview/about-codeql/). You then run **QL** — "a specially-designed object-oriented query language" (Datalog-like logic language) — producing **SARIF** results. **Compiled languages** (incl. Java) require build monitoring: `codeql database create --command=<build>`.

**Graph?** The store is **relational tables**, not a labeled-property graph; graph/relationship semantics are expressed via QL predicates over those relations. (So it's "graph-queryable," not a graph DB.)

**Languages.** C/C++, C#, Go, **Java/Kotlin**, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Swift, Rust, GitHub Actions (https://codeql.github.com/docs/codeql-overview/supported-languages-and-frameworks/ and CLI page). Rich built-in Java framework models: Spring MVC, Spring JDBC, Hibernate, JPA, JAX-RS, MyBatis, Jackson, Guava, Struts, etc.

**Scale (published!) & cost.** Recommended hardware (https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/code-scanning/codeql/hardware-resources-for-codeql): **Small <100K LOC → 8 GB / 2 cores; Medium 100K–1M LOC → 16 GB / 4–8 cores; Large >1M LOC → 64 GB / 8 cores; SSD 14 GB+**. A 10k-file Java monolith is likely Medium–Large → plan **16–64 GB RAM, 8 cores**. **Cost/licensing:** "The CodeQL CLI is free to use on public repositories… also available in private repositories owned by organizations that use GitHub Team or GitHub Enterprise Cloud and have a license for **GitHub Code Security**" (CLI docs NOTE) — i.e., **private bank code requires a paid GitHub Code Security / Advanced Security license**. Not compatible with musl/Alpine Linux.

---

## 9. Sourcegraph SCIP, LSIF, and src-cli

**SCIP** — https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip (redirects to https://github.com/scip-code/scip) · site https://scip-code.org · announcement https://about.sourcegraph.com/blog/announcing-scip
- "SCIP (…'skip') is a **language-agnostic protocol for indexing source code**, which can be used to power code navigation functionality such as Go to definition, Find references, and Find implementations" (README). Defined by a **Protobuf schema** (`scip.proto`); ships Go/Rust bindings (+ generated TS/Haskell) and a `scip` CLI. It is an **index format of symbols/occurrences/relationships**, not a full semantic graph DB. Java indexer: **scip-java** (https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java) — *known to exist; not separately fetched here — flag as needs-confirmation for feature specifics.*

**LSIF** — https://lsif.dev
- ⚠️ **"This project is now archived. LSIF … has been superseded by SCIP"** (site banner). LSIF = Language Server Index Format: "a standard format for language servers or other programming tools to emit their knowledge about a code workspace," precomputed in CI so browsers/editors answer LSP requests (defs/refs/hover) without a live server. Use SCIP for new work; LSIF only for legacy compatibility.

**src-cli** — https://github.com/sourcegraph/src-cli
- The Sourcegraph CLI (`src`): search, GraphQL API, batch changes, admin — and **uploads code-intel indexes** to a Sourcegraph instance (`src code-intel upload`, formerly `src lsif upload`). Install via curl/Homebrew/npm/Docker; auth via `SRC_ENDPOINT` + OAuth or `SRC_ACCESS_TOKEN` (README).

**Incremental/precise.** SCIP/LSIF are **precise** (emitted from a compiler-grade indexer) and designed for **CI-time, per-commit** production; SCIP was explicitly built to be more efficient/incremental than LSIF (announcement blog).

---

## 10. Kythe (Google)

**Canonical URLs:** https://kythe.io · https://github.com/kythe/kythe · schema https://kythe.io/docs/schema/ · overview https://kythe.io/docs/kythe-overview.html

**What it does.** Kythe "grew out of… a large-scale **semantic index of cross-references** for the enormous, multi-lingual internal codebase at Google" (overview). Its premise: language tools should interoperate via a shared schema. The repo provides "**Indexer implementations for C++, Go, and Java**," "**Compilation extractors for javac, Maven, cmake, Go, and Bazel**," a generic verifier, and a sample cross-reference service (README).

**Graph?** Yes — a **language-agnostic semantic graph**: **nodes** (identified by `VName`s) carrying facts, connected by **labeled edges** (e.g., `defines/binding`, `ref`, `childof`, `extends`, `instantiates`, `typed`), emitted as "entries" (schema docs). This is the classic cross-reference graph model (defs/refs/hierarchy).

**Scale/languages.** Built for Google-scale monorepos; **Java is a first-class indexer** with javac/Maven/Bazel extractors. ⚠️ **Partial gap:** I could not cleanly enumerate the full node/edge-kind catalog — the schema page (single-page doc) repeatedly returned only the C++ `instantiates`/`specializes` section via fetch. The kinds above are verified as *examples*; treat the exhaustive list as **needs direct read** of https://kythe.io/docs/schema/. No published throughput number.

---

## 11. Glean (Meta)

**Canonical URLs:** https://glean.software · docs https://glean.software/docs/introduction/ · https://github.com/facebookincubator/Glean · Angle https://glean.software/docs/angle/intro/

**What it does & scale design.** "Glean is a system for working with **facts about source code**" — per-symbol location/type/relationships, cross-references (calls), call/type hierarchies (README). Storage is an **efficient RocksDB backend**; "Facts are immutable terms described by user-defined schemas, and form a **DAG**… automatically de-duplicated" — "designed around an efficient storage model that enables storing information about code **at scale**" (intro). Components: **Angle** query engine, a **Thrift server** "designed to be deployed at scale, serving replicated databases," an interactive shell, a CLI, **Glass** (language-agnostic symbol server), and a **generic LSP server**.

**Query language.** **Angle** — "a declarative query language based on **logic programming and Datalog**," Glean's schema *and* query language; can derive new facts via rules (https://glean.software/docs/angle/intro/).

**Graph?** Effectively a queryable fact graph (DAG of typed facts); language-neutral abstractions built by deriving facts (e.g., `codemarkup.angle`).

**⚠️ Critical caveat for a Java shop.** The README lists **Java** (with Python, Kotlin, Erlang, Thrift, C#, Swift) under **"Custom indexers for these languages exist but aren't in the open source release yet"**. So out-of-the-box OSS Glean does **not** index Java; you'd rely on SCIP/LSIF import (supported) or an unreleased indexer. This makes Glean high-effort for your use case.

---

## 12. Semgrep

**Canonical URLs:** https://semgrep.dev · https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep · languages https://semgrep.dev/docs/supported-languages/

**What it does.** "A fast, open-source, static analysis tool that searches code, finds bugs, and enforces… coding standards" — **pattern-based** "semantic grep": patterns "look like the code you already write" and match the **AST**, not regex (README). Runs in IDE/pre-commit/CI; **local by default, code is not uploaded**.

**Graph?** **No** — AST pattern matching plus dataflow. **Community Edition** analyzes only "within the boundaries of a **single function or file**"; the paid **AppSec Platform / Pro engine** adds **cross-file, cross-function, data-flow reachability (taint)** (README). ⚠️ **Vendor-marketing flag:** README's "reduce false positives by 25% / increase true positives by 250% / noise −20%" are Semgrep's own numbers — treat as marketing.

**Languages.** 30+ incl. **Java** (Semgrep Code); Supply Chain (SCA) covers Java Gradle/Maven.

## 13. jdeps (JDK) and jarviz

**jdeps** — https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/jdeps.html
- Bundled **JDK tool**: "shows the **package-level or class-level dependencies** of Java class files"; input = `.class`/dir/JAR/classname (man page). **Graph output:** `--dot-output` emits one `*.dot` per archive **plus a `summary.dot`** of inter-archive deps (GraphViz DOT) — so it *does* produce a dependency graph, but as static DOT, not a queryable store. Rich module analysis: `--check`, `--list-deps`, `--list-reduced-deps`, `--print-module-deps`, `-apionly`, `-verbose:class`, filters. Java-only. Free (JDK).

**jarviz** — ⚠️ **CORRECTION: it is ExpediaGroup's, not LinkedIn's.** https://github.com/ExpediaGroup/jarviz (163★). I found **no LinkedIn "jarviz."** (A different, unrelated `kordamp/jarviz` JAR analyzer also exists.)
- "A **dependency analysis tool for Java applications**… deeply analyzes Java **bytecode**" using a custom classloader + **ASM**, "generates a complete **graph** of dependency couplings **between methods** across multiple artifacts" (README). Output = **method-level coupling records** as JSON Lines (`sourceClass/sourceMethod → targetClass/targetMethod`), plus a Node.js **HTML graph** and a CLI. Notable for **field/method-level** (not just class/library) coupling, including inside lambdas. JAR/WAR only.

---

## 14. ArchUnit

**Canonical URLs:** https://archunit.org · https://github.com/TNG/ArchUnit (v**1.5.0**, `com.tngtech.archunit:archunit`)

**What it does.** "A free, simple and extensible library for checking the **architecture** of your Java code… dependencies between packages and classes, layers and slices, cyclic dependencies and more. It does so by analyzing given Java **bytecode**, importing all classes into a Java code structure" and expressing rules as **plain JUnit tests** (README).

**Graph?** No persistent graph — an **in-memory `JavaClasses` model** (`new ClassFileImporter().importPackages(...)`) queried through a fluent `ArchRule` API (`classes()...`). Perfect for *enforcing* KG-derived rules in CI. Apache-2.0.

---

## 15. Depends (multilang-depends)

**Canonical URL:** https://github.com/multilang-depends/depends

**What it does.** "A source code **dependency extraction** tool… infers syntactical relations among source code entities, such as **files and methods**," language-independent, intended as a reusable foundation for visualization/architecture/DSM tools (README). Explicitly created to replace per-vendor extractors (it name-checks Understand, Structure101, Lattix).

**Graph/output.** Emits dependency data (a matrix/graph), **not** a DB: formats **json, xml, excel, dot, plantuml** (Excel limited to <256 elements; DOT→GraphViz; json/xml→**DV8** DSM). Granularity: **file / method / folder-level** (`-g`). **Dependency types:** Call, Cast, Contain, Create, Extend, Implement, Import/Include, Mixin, Parameter, Return, Throw (README). Languages: **cpp, java, ruby, python, pom**. Java needs no include paths (uses `import`s). OOM → raise `-Xmx`. CLI-only, JRE-portable.

**Structure101** — ⚠️ now hosted at **https://www.sonarsource.com/structure101/** (structure101.com **redirects** → **Structure101 was acquired by Sonar/SonarSource**). Historically: architecture/dependency management via **DSM** and Levelized Structure Maps, complexity/tangle metrics. **Commercial.** Product roadmap under Sonar is uncertain — **flag** before recommending.

**Lattix** — https://www.lattix.com (product **Lattix Architect**). **DSM-based** architecture & dependency analysis, cycle/tangle detection, refactoring, and **CI/DevOps automation** (site case studies: Teradyne, Siemens Healthineers, Our Next Energy). Supports Java among multiple languages/systems. **Commercial.** (Site content is marketing/case-studies — flag; get language/scale specifics from their docs, not the homepage.)

**NDepend** — https://www.ndepend.com · features https://www.ndepend.com/features/
- ⚠️ **Important: NDepend is a .NET / C# tool, not Java.** Its features are .NET-centric — **CQLinq** queries, **Visual Studio / Azure DevOps** integration, `NDepend.API`, dependency **graph + Dependency Structure Matrix**, technical-debt estimation via "C# formulas" (features page). For a **Java** codebase, NDepend itself does **not** apply; its **Java-equivalent sibling is JArchitect** (https://www.jarchitect.com, same vendor/engine lineage) — *I did not fetch JArchitect in this pass; verify independently before citing its specifics.* **Commercial.**

## Cross-references / how these fit a Java code KG
- **Direct Neo4j KG:** jQAssistant (native `:Type/:Method/:Field` + `DECLARES/INVOKES/READS/WRITES/DEPENDS_ON`) is the closest turnkey match; feed Cypher directly.
- **Rich CPG (AST+CFG+DFG) for security/dataflow:** Joern (`javasrc2cpg`/`jimple2cpg`) or CodeQL (relational + QL, published hardware guidance).
- **Precise defs/refs indexes to hydrate a KG:** SCIP (via scip-java) / Kythe (Java indexer) / JDT-LS over LSP; Glean if you can supply an (unreleased) Java indexer.
- **Fast structure extraction primitives:** tree-sitter (CST), JavaParser+SymbolSolver, Spoon (source AST).
- **Whole-program call/points-to graphs:** Soot/SootUp/WALA (in-memory, feed edges into the KG).
- **Dependency edges / DSM / rule enforcement:** jdeps + jarviz (couplings), Depends (DSM export), ArchUnit (CI rules), Lattix/Structure101 (commercial DSM).

1. **jQAssistant scale/perf numbers — NOT found** in official docs; the only time figure in-repo ("≥30 min") is *their* test suite, not a user benchmark. Do not cite it as scan time.
2. **Kythe node/edge kind catalog — partially verified**; the single-page schema doc kept returning only the C++ `instantiates` section via fetch. Read https://kythe.io/docs/schema/ directly for the exhaustive list.
3. **scip-java** and **JArchitect** were referenced but **not directly fetched** this pass — verify feature/version specifics before citing.
4. **jarviz attribution:** the prompt's "LinkedIn" is unconfirmed; the real project is **ExpediaGroup/jarviz** (no LinkedIn jarviz found via GitHub repo search).

# Research Dossier: Fusing Code KG with Runtime, Work-Management & Data-Lineage

**Summary:** All 10 items verified against primary sources (official docs, ASF/LF project docs, GitHub source, an arXiv paper, and vendor technical docs). The strongest "fusion" primitives are: OpenTelemetry's service-graph connector (spans → service dependency edges), OpenLineage's Job/Run/Dataset object model (the de-facto lineage standard), and Glean's ownership-set incrementality model (the most detailed public design for incremental code-graph maintenance). Vendor/commercial sources are flagged inline. Items I could not fully verify are listed in the final **Gaps** section (notably the exact URL of Tornhill's 2018 TechDebt paper, and Bazel's Merkle-tree input representation which lives in the Remote Execution API spec I did not fetch).

---

## CLUSTER 1 — Runtime → dependency graph

### Item 1 — OpenTelemetry: traces/spans → SERVICE DEPENDENCY graph

**Canonical primary URLs:**
- Service Graph connector: `https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/tree/main/connector/servicegraphconnector` (README verified: `open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:connector/servicegraphconnector/README.md`)
- Span Metrics connector: `https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/tree/main/connector/spanmetricsconnector` (README verified: `open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:connector/spanmetricsconnector/README.md`)

**What it does / data model:** The service graph connector "builds a map representing the interrelationships between various services," consuming a **traces** pipeline and producing a **metrics** pipeline (stability: **alpha**). It pairs spans belonging to the same request and emits one metric series per graph **edge**, labelled `client`, `server`, `connection_type`. It is explicitly "based on Grafana Tempo's service graph processor," and the component was **renamed `servicegraph` → `service_graph`** (old name deprecated).

**What edges are derived from spans (hard facts):** The connector inspects parent-child spans and forms an edge for three request types (`servicegraphconnector/README.md`, "How it works"):
1. **Direct (RPC) edge** — outgoing span `span.kind=client` paired with incoming `span.kind=server`.
2. **Messaging edge** — outgoing `span.kind=producer` paired with incoming `span.kind=consumer` (→ `connection_type=messaging_system`).
3. **Database edge** — a `span.kind=client` span that also carries a `db.name` attribute (→ `connection_type=database`).

Unpaired spans are held in an in-memory store (`store.ttl` default **2s**, `store.max_items` default **1000**) until the matching side arrives or TTL expires. Uninstrumented peers become **virtual nodes** via `virtual_node_peer_attributes` (default `[peer.service, db.name, db.system]`).

**Emitted metrics (the graph as metrics):**
| Metric | Type | Labels |
|---|---|---|
| `traces_service_graph_request_total` | Counter | client, server, connection_type |
| `traces_service_graph_request_failed_total` | Counter | client, server, connection_type |
| `traces_service_graph_request_server` | Histogram | client, server, connection_type |
| `traces_service_graph_request_client` | Histogram | client, server, connection_type |
| `traces_service_graph_unpaired_spans_total` | Counter | … |
| `traces_service_graph_dropped_spans_total` | Counter | … |

Example edge series: `traces_service_graph_request_total{client="app", server="db", connection_type="database"} 20`. Grafana renders these natively **since v9.0.4**. Because both edge sides must be processed together, spans of a trace must land on the same collector instance (recommended fix: the load-balancing exporter).

**spanmetrics connector (complementary):** Aggregates **R.E.D. (Request, Error, Duration)** metrics from spans. Every series carries at least `service.name`, `span.name`, `span.kind`, `status.code`, `collector.instance.id` (`spanmetricsconnector/README.md`, "Overview"). This gives per-node/per-operation health to annotate the service-graph edges. Also renamed `spanmetrics` → `span_metrics`.

**Vendor note:** Both are OpenTelemetry (CNCF) open-source components — not vendor marketing. Visualization examples reference Grafana/Tempo (Grafana Labs) but the connector is vendor-neutral.

---

### Item 2 — Kafka topic topology → producer/consumer ⇄ topic graph

**Canonical primary URLs:**
- Kafka Streams topology meta-model: `https://kafka.apache.org/40/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/streams/TopologyDescription.html`
- Kafka Admin API: `https://kafka.apache.org/40/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/admin/Admin.html`
- Confluent Schema Registry SerDes / subject-name strategies: `https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/serdes-develop/index.html`

**What each exposes / data model:**

1. **Kafka Streams `TopologyDescription`** (`Topology.describe()`) — the cleanest explicit graph: "nodes of a topology are grouped into **sub-topologies** if they are connected… two sub-topologies… can be linked to each other via topics, i.e., if one sub-topology **writes** into a topic and another sub-topology **reads** from the same topic" (`addSink`/`addSource`). So for Streams apps you get **source topics (consumer edges)** and **sink topics (producer edges)** directly, per sub-topology. *Hard limitation:* "Message forwards using custom Processors are not considered in the topology graph."

2. **Admin API (broker-side, consumer side only)** — relevant methods on `org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin`: `listConsumerGroups`, `describeConsumerGroups`, `listConsumerGroupOffsets` (committed offsets per topic-partition per group), `describeTopics`, `listTopics`. Together these reconstruct the **consumer-group → topic/partition** edges of the graph from broker metadata (no code access needed).

3. **Producer side is NOT tracked by brokers (hard fact / gap in the platform):** the only producer method is `describeProducers`, documented as "**Describe active producer state on a set of topic partitions**" — it returns transactional/producer **PIDs** per partition, not logical application identity, and only for currently-active producers. There is **no producer-group concept**. Consequently a producer→topic graph must be derived from (a) client instrumentation — OpenTelemetry messaging semantic conventions attach `messaging.destination.name`, which is exactly what the service-graph connector's producer/consumer pairing (Item 1) consumes — or (b) static config/code analysis.

4. **Schema Registry as a topic-mapping oracle:** Confluent Schema Registry's default **`TopicNameStrategy`** names subjects `<topic>-key` and `<topic>-value`; alternatives are `RecordNameStrategy` and `TopicRecordNameStrategy`. So enumerating subjects and applying the strategy yields a **schema-subject → topic** mapping, and (via which apps register/consume a subject) an approximate producer/consumer inventory.

**Vendor flag:** Apache Kafka javadocs = ASF, authoritative. **Confluent** Schema Registry is Confluent's product (Community License); the *subject-name strategy* is a real, documented standard, but Confluent **Stream Lineage** (a fuller producer/consumer→topic lineage UI) is a **Confluent Cloud commercial feature** — treat marketing claims there with caution.

## CLUSTER 2 — Git history / behavioural code analysis

### Item 3 — Adam Tornhill: hotspots, change coupling, CodeScene, research

**Canonical primary URLs:**
- Author hub: `https://www.adamtornhill.com/`
- *Your Code as a Crime Scene*, 2nd ed. (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2024): `https://pragprog.com/titles/atcrime2/your-code-as-a-crime-scene-second-edition/`
- *Software Design X-Rays* (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018): `https://pragprog.com/titles/atevol/software-design-x-rays/`
- CodeScene hotspots/technical-debt docs: `https://codescene.io/docs/guides/technical/hotspots.html`
- CodeScene change-coupling docs: `https://codescene.io/docs/guides/technical/change-coupling.html`
- Peer-reviewed paper "Code Red" (arXiv): `https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04374`

**Books / bio:** Tornhill "combines degrees in engineering and psychology… founder of CodeScene" (`adamtornhill.com`). The 2nd-edition *Crime Scene* explicitly frames the method: "Visualize codebases via a geographic profile from commit data to find development **hotspots**, prioritize technical debt, and uncover hidden dependencies" (pragprog `atcrime2`). *Software Design X-Rays* subtitle is "Fix Technical Debt with **Behavioral Code Analysis**," built on "behavioral data that you already have: your version-control system," and states hotspots + change-coupling "lay the foundation" (chapters 2–3) (pragprog `atevol`).

**HOTSPOTS (definition, hard facts):** "Most development activity tends to be located in relatively few modules. A Hotspot analysis helps you identify those modules where you spend most of your development time" (`codescene.io/docs/…/hotspots.html`). CodeScene ranks by combining **Code Health × development activity (change frequency)**: "Low code health in a development hotspot is expensive. Prioritize improvements here. Low code health in stable parts… has lower priority."

**CHANGE COUPLING / logical / temporal coupling — how it's computed from the Git log (hard facts):** "Change Coupling means that two (or more) modules change together over time." CodeScene considers two modules coupled in time if (`codescene.io/docs/…/change-coupling.html`, "Understand Change Coupling"):
- they are **modified in the same commit**, **or**
- they are **modified by the same programmer within a specific period of time**, **or**
- they **refer to the same Ticket ID** in their commit messages.

Trend colouring shows whether coupling strengthens (red)/weakens (blue)/stable (yellow). The **"Sum of Couplings"** metric = "summing how many times a module has been coupled to another one in a commit," used to find architecturally central modules. (Note: this is *logical/temporal* coupling — co-change over VCS history — distinct from static/compile-time dependencies.)

**Research (verified, with metrics):** *"Code Red: The Business Impact of Code Quality — A Quantitative Study of 39 Proprietary Production Codebases,"* Adam Tornhill & Markus Borg, **arXiv:2203.04374**, "Accepted for International Conference on **Technical Debt 2022**." Method: analyse 39 proprietary codebases "using the CodeScene tool based on a combination of **source code analysis, version-control mining, and issue information from Jira**," across **30,737 files**. Findings (abstract): **low-quality code has 15× more defects**; issue resolution takes **124% more time**; and shows **9× longer maximum cycle times** (uncertainty); framed against the claim that technical debt "waste[s] up to **42%** of developers' time." This is the paper predicting defects/throughput from behavioural + code-quality data.

**Vendor flag:** **CodeScene is a commercial product and Tornhill is its CTO/founder** — the docs are technical but promote the product; the arXiv paper, however, is peer-reviewed (TechDebt 2022) and is the citable primary evidence.
