## CLUSTER 3 — Data lineage / metadata

### Item 4 — OpenLineage (the lineage standard/spec)

**Canonical primary URL:** `https://openlineage.io/docs/spec/object-model/`

**Object model (hard facts):** OpenLineage is an open spec for emitting lineage as events. Three core entities + facets:
- **Job** — "a process that consumes or produces Datasets"; identified by unique **name within a `namespace`**; abstract (a task, model, query, or checkpoint).
- **Run** — "an instance of a Job… one of its occurrences in time"; **`runId` is a client-generated UUID** (spec **recommends UUIDv7**); the client keeps `runId` stable across state updates.
- **Dataset** — "an abstract representation of data" (a table / object / directory); unique **name within a namespace derived from physical location** (`db.host.database.schema.table`).

**Event types:** `RunEvent` (runtime; run states typically **START … COMPLETE**, additive updates); `JobEvent` (design-time/**static lineage**, not tied to a Run); `DatasetEvent` (static dataset metadata). The lineage graph is "created by weaving together observations of many Jobs across multiple platforms."

**Facets (extensibility):** Job facets — `sourceCodeLocation`, `sourceCode`. Run facets — `nominalTime`, `parent` (parent Job/Run, e.g. Airflow DAG→task, Spark), `errorMessage`, `sql`. Dataset facets — `schema`, `dataSource`, `lifecycleStateChange` (alter/create/drop/overwrite/rename/truncate), `version`; **input** facets — `dataQualityMetrics`, `dataQualityAssertions`; **output** facets — `outputStatistics`. Facet detail pages: `/docs/spec/facets/job-facets`, `/run-facets`, `/dataset-facets`.

**Vendor flag:** LF AI & Data project (originated at Astronomer/Datakin); vendor-neutral standard.

---

### Item 5 — dbt lineage (manifest.json, DAG)

**Canonical primary URL:** `https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/artifacts/manifest-json`

**How lineage is exposed (hard facts):** `manifest.json` is "a full representation of your dbt project's resources," produced by **any dbt command that parses the project** (all except `deps`, `clean`, `debug`, `init`), written to `target/manifest.json`. **Top-level keys that form the DAG:**
- `nodes` (models, seeds, snapshots, tests, analyses), `sources`, `metrics`, `exposures`, `groups`, `macros`, `docs`;
- **`parent_map`** — "the first-order parents of each resource" and **`child_map`** — "the first-order children of each resource" → these two maps **are the lineage edge lists**;
- `group_map`, `disabled`.

Each node's `unique_id` = `<resource_type>.<package>.<resource_name>` (the node key / graph node id). The manifest is **schema-versioned** (e.g. **v12** for dbt Core 1.8–1.11 and Fusion v2.0; v11 for 1.7; v10 for 1.6), with JSON Schemas published at `https://schemas.getdbt.com/`. dbt uses it internally to populate the docs site and to do state comparison.

**Vendor flag:** dbt Labs product; `manifest.json` schema and the parent/child maps are documented, stable, and openly consumable.

---

### Item 6 — Apache Atlas (metadata + lineage graph; type system)

**Canonical primary URL:** `https://atlas.apache.org/2.0.0/TypeSystem.html`

**Type system (hard facts):** Atlas lets users define **types**; instances are **entities**. A type has a **metatype**: primitives (boolean…date), **enum**, **collection** (`array`, `map`), or **composite** (**Entity, Struct, Classification, Relationship**). Entity/Classification types support **multiple supertypes** ("extend"). Every **entity has a server-assigned GUID** constant for its lifetime, plus a `status` and typed attribute values. Attributes carry `isOptional`, `isIndexable`, `isUnique`, `cardinality`; unique/indexable attributes are backed by **JanusGraph** indexes (Atlas's graph store). Struct = embedded, no identity; Entity = has GUID identity and is referenceable.

**Lineage model (the key fact):** Pre-defined system types establish lineage:
- **Referenceable** (unique `qualifiedName`), **Asset** (name/description/owner), **Infrastructure**;
- **DataSet** extends Referenceable — "types that extend DataSet… have a Schema" (e.g. `hive_table.columns`);
- **Process** extends Asset and has two special attributes **`inputs` and `outputs`, both arrays of DataSet entities**. "An instance of a Process type can use these inputs and outputs to capture how the **lineage of a DataSet** evolves." → **lineage/provenance graph = Process nodes linking input/output DataSet nodes.**

**Vendor flag:** Apache TLP (open source); not marketing.

---

### Item 7 — DataHub (metadata graph, entity model)

**Canonical primary URL:** `https://docs.datahub.com/docs/metadata-modeling/metadata-model/` (redirected from `datahubproject.io/docs/metadata-modeling/metadata-model/`)

**Entity/edge model (hard facts):** "schema-first," modelled in **PDL (Pegasus schema language)** with custom annotations. Four abstractions:
- **Entities** — "the primary node in the metadata graph"; an entity = **type** (e.g. `dataset`) + **unique identifier (urn)** + groups of **aspects**.
- **Aspects** — "the smallest atomic unit of write"; independently updatable; sharable across entities. Common aspects (with source links): `ownership`, `globalTags`, `glossaryTerms`, `institutionalMemory`, `status`, `subTypes` (all under `datahub-project/datahub:metadata-models/src/main/pegasus/com/linkedin/common/…`).
- **Relationships** — "a named edge between 2 entities… declared via foreign key attributes within Aspects along with a custom annotation (`@Relationship`)"; **bi-directionally traversable** (e.g. `OwnedBy` walkable from Chart or CorpUser).
- **Identifiers (Keys & Urns)** — a **Key aspect** holds primary-key fields, serialisable to/from an **Urn** (stringified key for primary-key lookup).

Core entity types include **DataPlatform**, **Dataset** (Tables/Views/Streams/Files), plus CorpUser, Chart, Dashboard, etc. The storage/serving/indexing/ingestion layers operate directly on this typed model.

**Vendor flag:** Open source (originated at LinkedIn); commercially backed by **Acryl Data / "DataHub"** (docs now on `docs.datahub.com`). Model docs are technical, not marketing.

---

### Item 8 — Egeria (open metadata standard)

**Canonical primary URL:** `https://egeria-project.org/types/`

**Open metadata type system (hard facts):** Egeria defines a shared metadata standard so repositories can interoperate. Types are organised into **subject "Areas" 0–7**:
- **Area 0** — base types & infrastructure: root type **`OpenMetadataRoot`**, plus **`Asset`, `DataSet`, `Infrastructure`, `Process`, `Referenceable`, `SoftwareServer`, `Host`**.
- **Area 1** — collaboration/feedback from people using assets.
- **Area 2** — data assets (sources, APIs, models) + connectivity (Open Connector Framework).
- **Area 3** — glossary (terms/concepts, linked to assets to define meaning).
- **Area 4** — governance (classifications, policies, rules).
- **Area 5** — standards (data models, schema fragments, reference data).
- **Area 6** — discovery results (profiles, quality scores, suggested classifications).
- **Area 7** — **lineage and traceability to the business** (this is the lineage area).

Types are expressed as entities, relationships, and classifications; per-area type detail pages are at `/types/0` … `/types/7`.

**Vendor flag:** LF AI & Data (ODPi/Egeria) open project; not marketing.

---

### Item 9 — OpenMetadata (entity model)

**Canonical primary URL:** `https://docs.open-metadata.org/latest/main-concepts/high-level-design` (served as `…/v2.0.x/main-concepts/high-level-design`)

**Entity/edge model (hard facts):** OpenMetadata is "based on a **standard definition** for metadata," with the vocabulary defined as **JSON Schemas** as the single source of truth; codegen then produces **Java (API), Python (ingestion), TypeScript (UI)** classes from the same schemas. Runtime components: **API** (central; all interaction), **UI**, **Ingestion Framework** (connectors), **Entity Store = MySQL** holding "real-time information on the state of all the Entities **and their Relationships**," and **Search Engine = ElasticSearch** for discovery. Entities are addressed by **id or fully-qualified name (FQN)**: `GET /api/v1/<collectionName>/<id>` or `…/name/<FQN>`. The API validates "the Entities data and all the **relationships**." So the graph = typed **Entities** + explicit **Relationships**, decoupled behind a REST serving layer.

**Vendor flag:** Open source; commercially backed by **Collate**. Design doc is technical.

---

## CLUSTER 4 — Incremental graph maintenance

### Item 10 — Keeping a code index/graph fresh (per-commit / hashing / CI)

**A) Sourcegraph — precise index in CI (per-commit).**
Canonical URL: `https://sourcegraph.com/docs/code-navigation/how-to/adding-scip-to-workflows` (source verified: `sourcegraph/docs:docs/code-navigation/how-to/adding-scip-to-workflows.mdx`).
- Mechanism: run a **SCIP indexer** (e.g. `scip-go`, `scip-typescript`) in CI and **upload the index with the `src` CLI** (`src code-intel upload`). "Setting up a source code indexing job in your CI build… ensures accuracy… by keeping in sync with changes in your repository."
- **Recommended frequency: "a CI job that runs on every commit (including branches)."**
- **Incrementality fact:** on non-indexed commits you still get precise nav "on lines that are unchanged since the nearest indexed commit," **provided the indexed commit is a direct ancestor/descendant no more than 100 commits away** (constant linked in `sourcegraph-public-snapshot/…/lsif/src/shared/constants.ts#L25`). SCIP is Sourcegraph's index format (successor to LSIF).
- Vendor flag: Sourcegraph is commercial; the CI/SCIP how-to is technical/open.

**B) Glean — incrementality via ownership (the most detailed public design).**
Canonical URLs: `https://glean.software/docs/introduction` and source docs `facebookincubator/Glean:glean/website/docs/implementation/incrementality.md` and `…/databases.md`.
- Glean stores immutable **facts** (a DAG) in RocksDB, auto-deduplicated; queried via the Datalog-like **Angle** language; new facts can be **derived**.
- **Incrementality model (hard facts, `implementation/incrementality.md`):**
  - **Units** — arbitrary strings owning facts (recommended granularity **one unit per file/module**); each gets a `UnitId`.
  - **Ownership sets** — a fact's owner is a `unit`, a **disjunction** (`set_1 || … || set_n`), or a **conjunction** (`set_1 && … && set_n`); each unique set → `UsetId`. Assumption: "**10–100× more facts than sets**," so ownership storage is small.
  - **Slices** — an incremental DB **excludes** some units from a base DB by building a **slice** (a **bitmap** of visible `UsetId`s); a fact is visible iff its `UsetId` is in the slice.
  - **Propagation invariant** — "every fact referenced by a visible fact is also visible"; achieved by making a fact F (owner A) referencing a fact (owner B) get owner **`A || B`**; runs in *O(facts)* time (`computeOwnership` in `glean/rts/ownership.cpp`). Derived facts get owner **`O1 && … && On`**.
  - **Stacked DBs** — an incremental DB layered on a base DB can induce new ownership on base facts; Glean uses "first owner in the stack" (`A || B`) and does incremental derivation.
  - DB identity = **`<name>/<hash>`** where the **hash is "the revision of the repository that was indexed"** (`databases.md`) — i.e. content/revision-addressed database versions.
- Vendor flag: Meta open source (`facebookincubator/Glean`); design doc, not marketing.

**C) Bazel — content-addressing / remote caching.**
Canonical URL: `https://bazel.build/remote/caching`.
- A build is split into **actions** (declared inputs, output names, command line, env). The remote cache stores **two** things: (1) the **action cache** — "a map of **action hashes** to action result metadata," and (2) a **content-addressable store (CAS)** — "of output files" keyed by content hash. Outputs are "a list of output file names and the **hashes of their contents**."
- Reuse rule: if the build is **reproducible**, outputs from one machine are safely reused on another (cache hit lookup by action hash before executing locally). This is the content-addressing / fingerprinting primitive for incremental, cross-machine graph/artifact reuse.
- Vendor flag: Google open source.

**Content-hashing / Merkle-tree synthesis:** Bazel CAS = content addressing by hash; Glean identifies DB versions by **revision hash** and de-duplicates facts by content; both are fingerprinting strategies for "only recompute what changed." (See Gaps re: Merkle trees.)

---

## Cross-references — how these fuse into one KG

- **Runtime → CODE graph:** OTel `service_graph` edges (`client→server`, `producer→consumer`, `client+db.name→db`) map service nodes to code-owned services; join on `service.name` (shared dimension in both service-graph and spanmetrics). Messaging edges reuse `messaging.destination.name`, which is the same Kafka **topic** identity used in Cluster 1/Item 2 — so OTel is the bridge that supplies the **producer→topic** edges Kafka brokers don't track.
- **Kafka ⇄ lineage:** Schema Registry `TopicNameStrategy` (`<topic>-value`) links **schemas → topics → Datasets**; OpenLineage `Dataset` namespace (`kafka://host`) and Atlas/DataHub Dataset entities can represent the same topic, letting runtime topology and static lineage share node identity.
- **Lineage standards interop:** OpenLineage (event stream) is the emission standard; **Atlas** (Process.inputs/outputs), **DataHub** (`@Relationship` edges), **OpenMetadata** (Entity+Relationship in MySQL), and **Egeria Area 7** are the storage/graph models that ingest it. All share a **DataSet/Job(Process)** duality — the natural join key to a code KG (dbt `unique_id`, OpenLineage Job `namespace/name`).
- **Work-management:** Tornhill/CodeScene's change-coupling explicitly keys on **Ticket ID in commit messages** — the same Jira issue keys used in the *Code Red* study — giving a concrete edge type from **commits ↔ work items ↔ files/hotspots**.
- **Freshness:** Sourcegraph (per-commit SCIP upload), Glean (unit-scoped ownership slices), and Bazel (action-hash CAS) are three published strategies to update only the changed subgraph on each commit.

# Research Dossier: Business/Ontology Layer for a Payments SDLC Knowledge Graph

**Summary.** All 13 items are verified against primary sources (standards-body specs, official GitHub repos, OASIS/OMG documents, DOIs via Crossref, arXiv). The highest-accuracy-risk facts — ISO 20022 `pacs`/`pain`/`camt` message codes and BIAN payment Service Domains — were verified against the issuers' **own** artefacts (ISO 20022's archived message catalogue; the `bian-official/public` GitHub repo). Note one access limitation: the live `iso20022.org` host was unreachable through my fetcher (repeated DNS/timeout failures), so ISO 20022 codes were verified via ISO 20022's own catalogue captured in the Internet Archive (Oct 2016 snapshot) — message stems and names are correct; only the trailing `.001.NN` version digits have since incremented. `coest.org` is now a defunct/parked domain. Details, exact URLs, and per-item verification flags below.

## CLUSTER 1 — Requirements/tests/defects as graph entities + traceability

### 1. Software Requirements Traceability research (CoEST / Cleland-Huang et al. / TLR)
**Canonical references (verified via Crossref DOIs):**
- **"The Grand Challenge of Traceability (v1.0)"** — Gotel, Cleland-Huang, Hayes, Zisman, Egyed, Grünbacher, Dekhtyar, Antoniol, Maletic. Chapter in *Software and Systems Traceability*, Springer, 2012. **DOI: [10.1007/978-1-4471-2239-5_16](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4471-2239-5_16)** (book DOI [10.1007/978-1-4471-2239-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4471-2239-5)). This is the field's agenda-setting document; it defines traceability terminology and the "purposed traceability" vision. Companion chapter "Traceability Fundamentals" is DOI [10.1007/978-1-4471-2239-5_1](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4471-2239-5_1).
- **"Software traceability: trends and future directions"** — Cleland-Huang, Gotel, Hayes, Mäder, Zisman. *FOSE 2014* (Future of Software Engineering). **DOI: [10.1145/2593882.2593891](https://doi.org/10.1145/2593882.2593891)**.
- **"Grand challenges, benchmarks, and TraceLab"** — Cleland-Huang et al. **DOI: [10.1145/1987856.1987861](https://doi.org/10.1145/1987856.1987861)** (introduces TraceLab, the experimental workbench for traceability benchmarking).

**Traceability Link Recovery (TLR), IR-based seminal work (verified):**
- **Antoniol, Canfora, Casazza, De Lucia, Merlo — "Recovering traceability links between code and documentation"**, *IEEE TSE*, 2002. **DOI: [10.1109/tse.2002.1041053](https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2002.1041053)**. The foundational IR/vector-space + probabilistic model paper for recovering links between artefacts. Earlier: ICSM 2000, **DOI [10.1109/icsm.2000.883003](https://doi.org/10.1109/icsm.2000.883003)**. A 2025 retrospective by the same authors: *IEEE TSE*, **DOI [10.1109/tse.2025.3534027](https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2025.3534027)**.

**LLM-based TLR (recent, verified via arXiv API):** the arXiv title-"traceability" + abstract-"large language model" query returns **49 results**. Representative: *"An Empirical Study on the Impact of Normalized Use-Case Specifications on Traceability"* — uses controlled natural language + LLM prompt engineering to normalize requirements and improve requirement↔code link recovery on four public datasets (**arXiv: [2608.15726](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15726)**).

⚠️ **Verification flag:** **`coest.org` is defunct** (now a parked/ad domain; archived at [web.archive.org/…/coest.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20190101032931/http://coest.org/)). CoEST was founded by Cleland-Huang (now at University of Notre Dame) and Gotel; cite the DOIs above as the authoritative CoEST corpus rather than the dead domain.

### 2. OSLC (Open Services for Lifecycle Collaboration) — **key item**
**Canonical URLs:** [open-services.net](https://open-services.net/) and the OASIS OSLC Open Project docs at [docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/).

**What it is:** A set of REST/Linked-Data standards to integrate lifecycle tools by exposing artefacts as RDF resources with stable URLs, built on **W3C Linked Data Platform (LDP)**. Servers expose **RDF vocabularies** + **OSLC Resource Shapes** (constraints: value-types, allowed values, cardinality) — the RDF equivalent of schemas (open-services.net Core overview). OSLC Core 3.0 is an **OASIS Standard**: [Core 3.0 OS](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/core/v3.0/os/oslc-core.html).

**OSLC domains (verified, with exact spec URLs):**
| Domain | Spec (OASIS) |
|---|---|
| **RM** — Requirements Management 2.1 | [requirements-management-spec.html](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/rm/v2.1/os/requirements-management-spec.html) — namespace `oslc_rm` = `http://open-services.net/ns/rm#` |
| **CM** — Change Management 3.0 (Errata 01) | [change-mgt-spec.html](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/cm/v3.0/errata01/os/change-mgt-spec.html) |
| **QM** — Quality Management 2.1 | [quality-management-spec.html](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/qm/v2.1/os/quality-management-spec.html) |
| **AM** — Architecture Management 3.0 | [architecture-management-spec.html](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/am/v3.0/os/architecture-management-spec.html) |
| Config Mgmt / Query 3.0 / TRS 3.0 | [Query 3.0](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/query/v3.0/os/oslc-query.html), [TRS 3.0](https://docs.oasis-open-projects.org/oslc-op/trs/v3.0/os/tracked-resource-set.html) |

**How it models links between artefacts (verified, directly quoted mechanism):** A link *is* an RDF triple — subject URI (source artefact), predicate (the relationship property), object URI (target artefact). From the RM spec §2.9: a Requirement in one tool links to a Requirement in another tool via `oslc_rm:elaboratedBy`, cross-tool by URL. Verified Turtle example:
```turtle
@prefix oslc_rm: <http://open-services.net/ns/rm#> .
<http://example.com/requ/4321> a oslc_rm:Requirement ;
    oslc_rm:elaboratedBy <http://anotherexample.com/requ/123> .
```
Links can be **reified** (`rdf:Statement` with `rdf:subject/predicate/object` + `dcterms:title`) to give the link itself a human label. This is exactly the mechanism to connect a requirement (RM) ↔ change request/defect (CM) ↔ test case (QM) ↔ architecture element (AM) across tools in a knowledge graph. TRS 3.0 lets a server publish a "tracked resource set" so a KG can incrementally harvest changes. (Source: OSLC RM 2.1 §2.3, §2.9; full predicate list in RM Part 2 Vocabulary: `requirements-management-vocab.html`.)

⚠️ **Vendor flag:** OSLC the *standard* is vendor-neutral (OASIS). The dominant *implementations* are vendor products — **IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management (ELM)/Jazz**, PTC, Dassault (ENOVIA), Siemens — treat their marketing as secondary to the OASIS specs above.

### 3. ReqIF (Requirements Interchange Format) — OMG
**Canonical URL:** [omg.org/spec/ReqIF](https://www.omg.org/spec/ReqIF/) — current version page **[omg.org/spec/ReqIF/1.2](https://www.omg.org/spec/ReqIF/1.2/)** (verified to exist). An **OMG formal standard**, XML-based interchange format for exchanging requirements (plus attributes, links/`SpecRelation`, and hierarchy/`SpecHierarchy`) between different requirements tools/organisations that cannot share a repository. It originated in the German automotive HIS group's "RIF" and was standardized by OMG. Core objects: `SpecObject` (a requirement), `SpecType`/`AttributeDefinition` (typing), `SpecRelation` (typed links between requirements), `Specification` (document tree). ⚠️ *Flag:* I confirmed the 1.2 spec page loads but did not extract the exact `formal/` document date this session.

### 4. SysML v2 — OMG systems modelling language
**Canonical URLs:** [github.com/Systems-Modeling/SysML-v2-Release](https://github.com/Systems-Modeling/SysML-v2-Release) (release repo) and the [OMG Systems Modeling Community](https://www.omg.org/communities/systems-modeling-community.htm). **Verified facts from the release repo:** three specifications form the stack — **KerML (Kernel Modeling Language) v1.0**, **SysML v2.0** (Part 1: Language Specification; Part 2: v1→v2 transformation), and **Systems Modeling API & Services v1.0**. Beta specs adopted by OMG **June 2023**; **formally adopted 30 June 2025**; editorially updated March 2026 for ISO submission. The language has a **textual notation** (plus graphical) and a normative **model library** distributed as `.kerml`/`.sysml` files and XMI. The **API & Services** (REST/PSM) basis is what makes SysML v2 KG-friendly — models are queryable via a standard API rather than only file interchange.

### 5. SPDX and CycloneDX — SBOM standards
**SPDX** — Canonical: [spdx.dev](https://spdx.dev/about/overview/). Verified: SPDX is "the international open standard … recognized as **ISO/IEC 5962:2021**" for SBOM/provenance/license/security data; governed under the **Linux Foundation**. It models components, files, packages, license expressions, and **relationships** between elements (e.g., `DEPENDS_ON`, `CONTAINS`, `GENERATED_FROM`). (⚠️ *Flag:* ISO/IEC 5962:2021 corresponds to SPDX 2.2.1; SPDX 3.0.x is current — 3.0 version number not re-verified this session; spec repo: `spdx.github.io/spdx-spec`.)

**CycloneDX** — Canonical: [cyclonedx.org](https://cyclonedx.org/) and [spec overview](https://cyclonedx.org/specification/overview/). Verified: **"CycloneDX: The International Standard for Bill of Materials (ECMA-424)"**, driven by the **OWASP Foundation** and **Ecma International TC54** (Software & System Transparency). Object model (verified from spec): **BOM Metadata, Components** (software/hardware/ML-models/data), **Services** (external APIs, trust boundaries), **Dependencies** (direct + transitive dependency graph), **Compositions, Vulnerabilities** (incl. VEX), **Formulation, Annotations, Definitions, Declarations** ("compliance-as-code"), **Citations**. IANA media types registered (`application/vnd.cyclonedx+xml`, `…+json`; version param e.g. `version=1.7`); file conventions `bom.json`/`bom.xml`, `*.cdx.json`. For a KG, CycloneDX's explicit component→component and component→service dependency edges map cleanly to graph relationships linking code artefacts to third-party components/CVEs.

### 6. Gherkin / BDD (Cucumber)
**Canonical URL:** [cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference](https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/). Verified: Gherkin is a line-oriented, keyword-driven language for **executable specifications**. Primary keywords: **`Feature`**, **`Rule`** (a business rule, since v6), **`Example`/`Scenario`**, and steps **`Given` / `When` / `Then` / `And` / `But`**; plus `Background`, `Scenario Outline`, `Examples`, and secondary tokens (`"""` doc-strings, `|` data tables, `@` tags, `#` comments). Each step's trailing text is matched to a **step definition** (code), making the same Given/When/Then text simultaneously (a) business-readable acceptance criteria and (b) an executable test — the semantic bridge you want. A `Rule` groups scenarios that illustrate one business rule. ⚠️ *Vendor flag:* Cucumber/`cucumber.io` is stewarded by **SmartBear** (vendor), but the Gherkin language reference itself is open; BDD's conceptual origin is Dan North ("Introducing BDD," 2006, `dannorth.net`).

## CLUSTER 2 — Domain-Driven Design as ontology bridge

### 7. Eric Evans DDD & Vaughn Vernon
- **Eric Evans — *Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software* (2004)** — the "Big Blue Book." Canonical hub: **[domainlanguage.com/ddd](https://www.domainlanguage.com/ddd/)** (ISBN 0321125215). Free, authoritative **DDD Reference (2015)** PDF: [domainlanguage.com/…/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf](https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf) — concise pattern catalog: **Bounded Context, Ubiquitous Language, Context Map, Aggregate, Entity, Value Object, Domain Event, Anticorruption Layer**, etc.
- **Vaughn Vernon — *Implementing Domain-Driven Design* (IDDD, 2013) and *Domain-Driven Design Distilled* (2016)** — Canonical: **[kalele.io/books](https://kalele.io/books/)** (verified). Vernon frames Bounded Contexts + a Ubiquitous Language *within an explicitly bounded context*, Subdomains for legacy integration, and Context Map relationship patterns.

### 8. EventStorming (Alberto Brandolini)
**Canonical URL:** **[eventstorming.com](https://www.eventstorming.com/)** (verified). A collaborative, workshop-based modelling technique using colour-coded sticky notes (Domain Events → Commands → Aggregates → Policies → Read Models → external systems) to design services with business + IT + design stakeholders and surface bounded contexts. The reference text is Brandolini's ***Introducing EventStorming*** (Leanpub: `leanpub.com/introducing_eventstorming` — cited but not fetched this session).

### 9. Formalising DDD as an ontology (academic/practitioner)
Strongest **peer-reviewed formalization** (verified via Crossref):
- **Kapferer & Zimmermann — "Domain-specific Language and Tools for Strategic Domain-driven Design, Context Mapping and Bounded Context Modeling"**, *MODELSWARD 2020*. **DOI: [10.5220/0008910502990306](https://doi.org/10.5220/0008910502990306)**. This is the academic basis of **Context Mapper** ([contextmapper.org](https://contextmapper.org/)): a formal **metamodel + DSL** where Bounded Contexts, Aggregates, Entities and the strategic Context Map relationship types (Partnership, Shared Kernel, Customer/Supplier, Conformist, **Anticorruption Layer**, Open Host Service, Published Language) are first-class, machine-processable constructs — the closest rigorous "ubiquitous-language-as-controlled-vocabulary / bounded-context-as-module" formalization.
- **Directly on-target for your project:** "**Domain-Driven Design and BIAN Service Models for Financial Microservices**", *J. Computational Analysis & Applications*, 2025 — **DOI: [10.48047/jocaaa.2025.34.12.32](https://doi.org/10.48047/jocaaa.2025.34.12.32)** (maps DDD bounded contexts onto BIAN Service Domains for banking microservices).
- Supporting: "**Domain-Driven Design for Microservices: An Evidence-based Investigation**", *IEEE TSE* 2024 — **DOI: [10.1109/tse.2024.3385835](https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2024.3385835)**.

⚠️ **Gap/uncertainty:** Explicit peer-reviewed work that literally casts *bounded context = OWL ontology module* and *ubiquitous language = SKOS/controlled vocabulary* is **sparse**. Context Mapper (DSL/metamodel, not OWL) is the most defensible formalization; the OWL/ontology framing is more common in practitioner/grey literature. (Semantic Scholar API was rate-limited — HTTP 429 — during this session, so I could not exhaustively sweep that corpus; recommend a follow-up Semantic Scholar/DBLP search on "bounded context ontology module".)

## CLUSTER 3 — Banking domain models for PAYMENTS (reuse, don't invent)

### 10. BIAN (Banking Industry Architecture Network)
**Canonical URLs:** [bian.org](https://bian.org/), Service Landscape v12.0 → [bian.org/servicelandscape-12-0-0](https://bian.org/servicelandscape-12-0-0/); official artefacts on GitHub → [github.com/bian-official/public](https://github.com/bian-official/public). BIAN publishes a **Service Landscape** (reference architecture) decomposing a bank into **Service Domains** — elementary, non-overlapping business capabilities — plus **semantic APIs** (OAS3) and a **Business Object Model (BOM)**.

**Payment-relevant Service Domains (VERIFIED verbatim from `bian-official/public`, release 12.0.0 — `release12.0.0/semantic-apis/oas3/yamls/Readme.md`):**
- **Payment Order**
- **Payment Instruction**
- **Payment Execution**
- **Payment Rail Operations**
- **Direct Debit Mandate**
- **Standing Order**
- (adjacent: Correspondent Bank Relationship Management, Cash Concentration, Notional Pooling, Account Reconciliation, Current/Corporate Current Account, Virtual Account)

**How banks map internal services to BIAN:** banks treat Service Domains as a reference taxonomy and map internal microservices/APIs onto them; BIAN ships **Service Domain semantic APIs (OpenAPI 3)** and BOM-extended API definitions (verified: the repo's `semantic-apis/oas3` tree) so an internal "payment initiation" service maps to *Payment Order*, an interbank-settlement service to *Payment Execution*, and rail connectivity to *Payment Rail Operations*. ⚠️ *Flag:* BIAN is a non-profit association whose members include vendors (Temenos, SAP, IBM); the Service Landscape itself is vendor-neutral.

### 11. ISO 20022 — payments message types
**Canonical URL:** iso20022.org (⚠️ **live host was unreachable via my fetcher** — repeated DNS/timeout errors). All codes/names below were **verified against ISO 20022's own message catalogue captured in the Internet Archive** ([web.archive.org snapshot of iso20022.org/full_catalogue.page, 2016-10-20](https://web.archive.org/web/20161020212300/https://www.iso20022.org/full_catalogue.page)). **Message identifier structure:** `businessarea.msgnumber.variant.version` (defined by ISO 20022 / ISO 20022-1).

**Business areas (verified present in catalogue):** `pain` = **Payments Initiation**; `pacs` = **Payments Clearing and Settlement**; `camt` = **Cash Management**; plus `acmt` (Account Management), `remt` (Payments Remittance Advice), `reda` (Reference Data).

**`pacs` — FI-to-FI (verified name ↔ code):**
| Code | Message name |
|---|---|
| **pacs.008** | FIToFICustomerCreditTransfer |
| **pacs.009** | FinancialInstitutionCreditTransfer |
| **pacs.002** | FIToFIPaymentStatusReport |
| **pacs.004** | PaymentReturn |
| **pacs.003** | FIToFICustomerDirectDebit |
| **pacs.007** | FIToFIPaymentReversal |
| **pacs.010** | FinancialInstitutionDirectDebit |

**`pain` — customer-initiated (verified):**
| Code | Message name |
|---|---|
| **pain.001** | CustomerCreditTransferInitiation |
| **pain.002** | CustomerPaymentStatusReport |
| **pain.008** | CustomerDirectDebitInitiation |
| **pain.007** | CustomerPaymentReversal |
| **pain.013 / pain.014** | CreditorPaymentActivationRequest / …StatusReport |

**`camt` — cash management (verified):**
| Code | Message name |
|---|---|
| **camt.052** | BankToCustomerAccountReport |
| **camt.053** | BankToCustomerStatement |
| **camt.054** | BankToCustomerDebitCreditNotification |
| **camt.056** | FIToFIPaymentCancellationRequest |
| **camt.055** | CustomerPaymentCancellationRequest |
| **camt.029** | ResolutionOfInvestigation |

**"What business area covers a payment stream end to end?"** — **No single one does.** A payment flows across business areas: **`pain` (initiation)** → **`pacs` (interbank clearing & settlement)** → **`camt` (reporting / statements / exceptions & investigations)**, supported by `acmt`/`reda`/`remt`. Design the KG so a "payment" entity threads pain.001 → pacs.008 → pacs.002 → camt.054/camt.053, with camt.056/camt.029 for cancellations/investigations.

⚠️ **Version caveat (important for the bank's reviewers):** the archived snapshot shows 2016-era version digits (e.g., `pacs.008.001.06`, `pain.001.001.07`, `camt.053.001.06`). The **stems and names are current and correct**, but the trailing `.001.NN` increments over time — e.g., CBPR+/SEPA-2023 profiles use higher versions such as `pacs.008.001.08/.09/.10`, `pain.001.001.09`, `camt.053.001.08`. Confirm the exact `.NN` for your rulebook (SWIFT CBPR+, EPC SEPA, or your market infrastructure) on the live iso20022.org catalogue.

### 12. FIBO (Financial Industry Business Ontology)
**Canonical URLs:** [spec.edmcouncil.org/fibo](https://spec.edmcouncil.org/fibo/) (FIBO Viewer/spec), [edmcouncil.org](https://edmcouncil.org), source of truth on GitHub [github.com/edmcouncil/fibo](https://github.com/edmcouncil/fibo), OMG spec **[omg.org/spec/EDMC-FIBO](https://www.omg.org/spec/EDMC-FIBO/)**. **Verified (repo README):** FIBO is a **formal ontology in W3C OWL** (Description-Logic based), sponsored by the **EDM Council**, **standardized by OMG**, originating from post-2008-crisis data-governance needs, first published **2014**, updated quarterly via an open community process. Structure: **domains → modules → ontologies**, each tagged **Release / Provisional / Informative** maturity.

**FIBO domains (verified from repo directory + README):** **FND** (Foundations), **BE** (Business Entities), **FBC** (Financial Business & Commerce), **SEC** (Securities), **DER** (Derivatives), **LOAN** (Loans), **IND** (Indices & Indicators), **MD** (Market Data), **CAE** (Corporate Actions & Events), **BP** (Business Process). Reuse angle: FIBO gives you consensus OWL classes for parties, accounts, financial instruments and **contracts** (in FND) so you don't invent a finance ontology — anchor your payments KG's party/account/instrument concepts to FIBO IRIs (browsable at `spec.edmcouncil.org/fibo/ontology/<DOMAIN>/…`).

### 13. ACTUS (Algorithmic Contract Types Unified Standards)
**Canonical URLs:** [actusfrf.org](https://www.actusfrf.org/) (ACTUS Financial Research Foundation), dictionary/spec on GitHub [github.com/actusfrf/actus-dictionary](https://github.com/actusfrf/actus-dictionary) (CC BY-SA 4.0). **What it standardises (verified):** a machine-readable, algorithmic representation of the **cash-flow logic of financial contracts** — each contract type is an algorithm producing deterministic cash flows from a common set of **contract terms**, **contract events**, and **state variables**.

**Contract Type taxonomy (verified from `actus-dictionary-taxonomy.json`, v1.4, 2023-12-08 — 32 types).** Families **Basic / Combined / Credit Enhancement**; classes include Fixed Income, Ownership, Symmetric, Asymmetric, Securitization, Credit Enhancement. Key acronyms:
- **PAM** — Principal At Maturity (bonds, term deposits, bullet loans/mortgages); **ANN** — Annuity (level-payment mortgages/leases); **LAM** — Linear Amortizer; **NAM** — Negative Amortizer; **LAX/ANX/NAX** — exotic variants; **CLM** — Call Money; **UMP** — Undefined Maturity Profile (**savings/current accounts**); **CSH** — Cash; **STK** — Stock; **COM** — Commodity.
- Combined: **FXOUT, SWAPS, SWPPV** (plain-vanilla swap), **FUTUR, OPTNS, CAPFL, CDSWP, FUTUR**. Credit enhancement: **CEC** (Collateral), **CEG** (Guarantee), **MAR** (Margining), **REP** (Repo).

**Contract Events (verified from `actus-dictionary-event.json`, 24 event types):** **IED** (Initial Exchange), **FP** (Fee Payment), **PR** (Principal Redemption), **PD** (Principal Drawing), **IP** (Interest Payment), **IPCI** (Interest Capitalization), **RR/RRF** (Rate Reset variable/fixed), **DV** (Dividend), **PP** (Prepayment), **MD** (Maturity), **MR** (Margin Call), **TD** (Termination), **XD** (Exercise), **STD** (Settlement), **CE** (Credit Event). Each event carries `payoff (PYO)`, `eventTime (TEV)`, `currency (CUR)` and a post-event `state (EVS)`. For a payments/core-banking KG, ACTUS is the standard for representing the *product/contract* behind a payment stream (e.g., a loan instalment or direct-debit schedule) as deterministic, simulatable events. ⚠️ *Flag:* ACTUS is a non-profit standard, not a vendor product.

# Research Dossier: Agent Fleet on an Enterprise SDLC Knowledge Graph — Verified Primary Sources

**Verification method:** Each URL below was fetched live. Classic papers were cross-checked against Crossref/Semantic Scholar/arXiv metadata APIs for authoritative bibliographic data. **Vendor/self-serving sources are explicitly flagged 🟠. Peer-reviewed/classic sources are flagged 🟢. Open-source-foundation project sites are flagged 🔵** (not marketing per se, but first-party). Anything I could not fully verify is called out in-line and consolidated at the end.

## CLUSTER 1 — Multi-agent architecture patterns

### 1. BLACKBOARD architecture (classic AI pattern) 🟢

**Primary ref A — Hearsay-II.** Erman, L. D., Hayes-Roth, F., Lesser, V. R., & Reddy, D. R. (1980). "The Hearsay-II Speech-Understanding System: Integrating Knowledge to Resolve Uncertainty." *ACM Computing Surveys*, Vol. 12, No. 2, pp. 213–253.
- Canonical URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/356810.356816 — DOI `10.1145/356810.356816`
- Verified via Crossref: exact title, all four authors + affiliations (USC/ISI; RAND; UMass Amherst; CMU), CACM Surveys vol. 12 issue 2, pp. 213–253, June 1980, **854 citations** recorded by Crossref.
- Substance: Hearsay-II is the canonical origin of the *blackboard* model — multiple independent "knowledge sources" (specialists) cooperatively read/write a shared, hierarchically-structured global data structure (the blackboard) to incrementally resolve uncertainty in speech understanding. This is the direct historical antecedent of your "many specialist agents read/write a shared knowledge graph" design.

**Primary ref B — Nii's survey.** Nii, H. Penny (1986). "Blackboard Systems, Part One: The Blackboard Model of Problem Solving and the Evolution of Blackboard Architectures." *AI Magazine*, Vol. 7, No. 2, pp. 38–53. (Part Two appeared in *AI Magazine* Vol. 7, No. 3.)
- Canonical URL: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/aimagazine/article/view/537 — DOI `10.1609/aimag.v7i2.537`
- Verified via Semantic Scholar API (paperId `0807973a…`, DBLP key `journals/aim/Nii86`) — confirmed exact title, author (H. Penny Nii), venue (*The AI Magazine*), year 1986.
- Substance: The definitive retrospective defining the blackboard model's three components — the **blackboard** (shared solution-state, partitioned into levels of abstraction), the **knowledge sources** (independent specialists), and a **control component** that opportunistically decides which KS acts next. Directly maps to a governance/scheduler layer over a shared graph.
- ⚠️ *Caveat:* My fetch tool could not open `ojs.aaai.org` directly (repeated DNS/TLS transport failures on my side — the URL itself is valid and canonical). Bibliographic details confirmed via Semantic Scholar + DBLP; the page range 38–53 comes from those secondary bibliographic records, not from the fetched PDF.

### 2. CONTRACT NET protocol 🟢

Smith, Reid G. (1980). "The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Control in a Distributed Problem Solver." *IEEE Transactions on Computers*, Vol. C-29, No. 12, pp. 1104–1113.
- Canonical URL: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1675516 — DOI `10.1109/TC.1980.1675516`
- Verified via Crossref: exact title, author Reid G. Smith (affiliation "Defence Research Establishment Atlantic"), IEEE Trans. Computers vol. C-29 issue 12, pp. 1104–1113, Dec 1980, **2,394 citations** recorded.
- Substance: Defines negotiation-based task allocation via **announce → bid → award** (a market/auction mechanism): a "manager" node broadcasts a task announcement, idle "contractor" nodes submit bids, the manager awards the contract to the best bidder. This is the canonical primary reference for **market/auction-style agent coordination** and directly underpins modern "bid for subtask" agent routing.
- ⚠️ *Caveat:* IEEE Xplore body is behind a login wall (fetch returned no article text); all metadata above is from Crossref, which is authoritative.

### 3. Orchestrator-worker / hub-and-spoke 🟠 **(VENDOR — Anthropic, self-serving)**

**Ref A — "Building Effective Agents"** (Anthropic, Dec 2024). https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
- Substance: Draws the key distinction between **workflows** (LLMs/tools orchestrated through predefined code paths) and **agents** (LLMs dynamically directing their own process). Catalogs five composable patterns: **prompt chaining** (pipeline), **routing**, **parallelization** (sectioning/voting), **orchestrator-workers** (a central LLM dynamically decomposes tasks, delegates to worker LLMs, synthesizes results), and **evaluator-optimizer**. Explicitly advises "find the simplest solution possible; agents trade latency and cost for better task performance." (Note: page now carries a banner redirecting to newer "Managed Agents" content, but the patterns section is intact.)

**Ref B — "How we built our multi-agent research system"** (Anthropic, ~June 2025). https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
- Substance: Production write-up of an explicit **orchestrator-worker (lead agent + parallel subagents)** architecture. Hard facts (all vendor-reported internal evals):
  - A multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 lead + Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) **outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%** on Anthropic's internal research eval.
  - On BrowseComp, **token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance**; token usage + number of tool calls + model choice explained **95%**.
  - Explicit effort-scaling heuristics baked into prompts: simple fact-finding = **1 agent, 3–10 tool calls**; comparisons = **2–4 subagents, 10–15 calls each**; complex research = **>10 subagents**.
  - Failure modes cited: early agents "spawning 50 subagents for simple queries" (agent sprawl); subagents duplicating work absent detailed task boundaries.
- 🟠 Flag: Anthropic sells the models these systems consume; the 90.2% figure is an unaudited internal benchmark. (Token-economics numbers from this post are re-used in Cluster 4/5 below.)

### 4. Cognition AI — "Don't Build Multi-Agents" (counter-argument) 🟠 **(VENDOR — Cognition/Devin, self-serving)**

Walden Yan (Cognition). "Don't Build Multi-Agents." https://cognition.ai/blog/dont-build-multi-agents (redirects to https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents)
- Substance: Argues against parallel multi-agent architectures on reliability grounds, via two principles: **(1) Share context — share full agent traces, not just individual messages;** **(2) Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results.** Concludes you should **default to a single-threaded linear agent**, and for very long tasks introduce a dedicated **context-compression model** (Cognition says it has fine-tuned a small model for this) rather than parallel subagents. Explicitly criticizes OpenAI **Swarm** and Microsoft **AutoGen** as "the wrong way to build agents." Notes Claude Code (as of June 2025) deliberately spawns subagents that *only answer questions and never write code in parallel*, precisely to avoid conflicting decisions.
- Directly relevant to your "error compounding across hops" concern — the Flappy Bird example illustrates subagent miscommunication compounding into an unusable merge.

### 5. Pipeline/assembly-line and market/auction patterns

- **Pipeline / prompt-chaining:** Best primary references are (a) Anthropic's "prompt chaining" workflow (URL in item 3A above) and (b) **MetaGPT** 🟢 — Hong, S., Zhuge, M., … Schmidhuber, J. (2023/2024). "MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework." arXiv:2308.00352 (accepted **ICLR 2024**). https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00352 — verified via arXiv API (14 authors, cs.AI/cs.MA). MetaGPT explicitly **"utilizes an assembly line paradigm to assign diverse roles to various agents,"** encoding Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) into prompt sequences so agents verify each other's intermediate results — the canonical "assembly-line" multi-agent reference. Repo: https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT
- **Market/auction:** Contract Net (item 2) is *the* primary reference; there is no better classic source for auction-based agent coordination.
- ⚠️ *Gap:* There is no single canonical peer-reviewed "assembly-line agents" paper beyond MetaGPT; the pipeline pattern is otherwise documented only in vendor engineering blogs (Anthropic prompt chaining).

## CLUSTER 2 — Agents querying a graph (not files)

### 6. text2cypher (NL→Cypher) and GraphRAG

**Neo4j Text2Cypher paper** 🟠 **(VENDOR-affiliated — Neo4j authors; arXiv preprint, not formally peer-reviewed)**
- Ozsoy, M. G., Messallem, L., Besga, J., Minneci, G. (2024). "Text2Cypher: Bridging Natural Language and Graph Databases." arXiv:2412.10064. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10064 — verified via arXiv API.
- Hard facts: Combined/cleaned 16 (selected from 25 identified) public datasets into **44,387 instances (39,554 train / 4,833 test)**. Benchmarking result (from paper body via ar5iv): *"large-foundational models performed the best, however… **all the fine-tuned models achieve better results than their baseline models**,"* with improvements measured in **Google-BLEU and Exact Match**.
- Dataset (HuggingFace) 🟠: https://huggingface.co/datasets/neo4j/text2cypher-2024v1 — verified: Apache-2.0, 44,387 rows; 22,093 train rows (55.85%) have live DB access.
- Blog overview 🟠: https://medium.com/neo4j/introducing-the-neo4j-text2cypher-2024-dataset-995496936172

**Token-savings evidence for structured retrieval** 🟠: Ozsoy, M. G. (2025). "Enhancing Text2Cypher with Schema Filtering." arXiv:2505.05118. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05118 — verified. Key finding: injecting only *relevant* schema elements (vs. the full schema) **"improves query generation while reducing token costs,"** especially for smaller models; larger models benefit less on accuracy but still gain on cost. This is your cleanest primary evidence that *structured/schema-scoped* retrieval cuts tokens.

**Microsoft GraphRAG** 🟠 **(VENDOR-affiliated — Microsoft Research; arXiv preprint)**
- Edge, D., Trinh, H., Cheng, N., … Larson, J. (2024). "From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization." arXiv:2404.16130. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130 — verified via arXiv API (10 authors, cs.CL/cs.AI/cs.IR).
- Substance: Builds an LLM-derived **entity knowledge graph + pre-generated community summaries**; for **global "sensemaking" questions over ~1M-token corpora, GraphRAG substantially beats conventional vector RAG on answer comprehensiveness and diversity.**
- Repo 🟠: https://github.com/microsoft/graphrag — **now in maintenance mode**; carries an explicit cost warning: *"GraphRAG indexing can be an expensive operation… understand the process and costs involved, and start small."* (Important counter-weight to any "graph retrieval is always cheaper" claim.) MS Research blog: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/graphrag-unlocking-llm-discovery-on-narrative-private-data/
- ⚠️ *Gap:* I did **not** find a rigorous, independent (non-vendor) study giving a clean "X% token savings, structured graph retrieval vs. vector/raw-file retrieval" headline number. The strongest defensible claims are: schema-filtering reduces Text2Cypher token cost (2505.05118), GraphRAG improves answer quality on global queries but is expensive to index (2404.16130 + repo), and Anthropic's "token usage explains 80% of variance" (item 3B). Treat any single "graph saves N× tokens" figure as vendor marketing unless independently benchmarked.

### 7. MCP (Model Context Protocol) + graph MCP servers

**MCP standard** 🔵/🟠 (open standard, originally created by Anthropic): https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction
- Substance: Open-source standard for connecting AI apps to external systems (data, tools, workflows); described as "a USB-C port for AI applications." Verified live (docs now versioned, e.g. 2026-07-28 spec).

**Neo4j MCP server (exposes a graph)** 🟠 **(VENDOR — Neo4j Labs)**: https://github.com/neo4j-contrib/mcp-neo4j
- Substance: `mcp-neo4j-cypher` = **"natural language to Cypher"** server — gets DB schema and executes generated read/write Cypher (requires the APOC plugin for schema inspection). Sibling servers: `mcp-neo4j-memory` (knowledge-graph memory), `mcp-neo4j-cloud-aura-api`, `mcp-neo4j-data-modeling`. MIT-licensed; transports STDIO/SSE/HTTP; deployable on AWS ECS Fargate / Azure Container Apps. Note it explicitly points to an **official** product server at https://github.com/neo4j/mcp (Labs repo carries no SLA).
- This is the concrete "agent queries the graph via MCP instead of files" integration pattern.

## CLUSTER 3 — Governance / guardrails for regulated SDLC

### 8. OPA / Rego (policy-as-code) 🔵 (CNCF project site)

- Homepage: https://www.openpolicyagent.org/ — "a general-purpose policy engine that unifies policy enforcement across the stack," using the high-level declarative **Rego** language; enforces policy in "applications, proxies, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, API gateways, and more." Live examples cover API authz, Envoy ext-authz, Kubernetes admission control, and AI tool-calling.
- CNCF project page: https://www.cncf.io/projects/open-policy-agent-opa/ — confirms OPA is a CNCF-hosted project. (OPA reached CNCF **Graduated** status in 2021 — widely documented; the CNCF page confirms hosting, though I did not fetch the specific graduation-date announcement.)
- SDLC relevance: Rego is the standard mechanism for gating agent/CI actions ("this commit/deploy is allowed only if…") as code.

### 9. SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) 🔵 (OpenSSF/Linux Foundation project site)

- Homepage: https://slsa.dev/ — Levels of assurance for build/source/dependency integrity.
- Levels spec (v1.0): https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/levels — verified. v1.0 focuses on the **Build track**: **L0** none; **L1** provenance exists (how the package was built; trivial to forge); **L2** signed provenance from a hosted build platform (deters tampering after build); **L3** hardened build platform (protects against tampering *during* the build). (Older v0.1 used unnamed SLSA 1–4; Source track deferred to future versions.)
- SDLC relevance: SLSA is the canonical framework for "prove this artifact was built by our pipeline from our source" — essential when agents can trigger builds.

### 10. Sigstore + signed commits (gitsign) 🔵 (OpenSSF project)

- Sigstore overview: https://docs.sigstore.dev/about/overview/ — verified. Open-source supply-chain signing using **ephemeral ("keyless") keys**; three components: **Cosign** (signing client), **Fulcio** (CA that issues short-lived certs bound to an OIDC identity), **Rekor** (immutable, append-only public **transparency log**). Backed by OpenSSF/Linux Foundation with Google, Red Hat, Chainguard, GitHub, Purdue.
- **gitsign** (keyless Git commit signing): https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign — verified. *"Keyless Git signing with Sigstore… uses keyless Sigstore to sign Git commits with your own GitHub/OIDC identity."* Configured via `git config gpg.x509.program gitsign` + `gpg.format x509` + `commit.gpgsign true`; default Fulcio at `https://fulcio.sigstore.dev`.
- SDLC relevance: gives every commit (including agent-authored commits) a verifiable, non-repudiable, publicly-logged identity — no long-lived keys to leak.

### 11. Agent identity / least privilege — SPIFFE/SPIRE 🔵 (CNCF project)

- SPIFFE overview: https://spiffe.io/ and https://spiffe.io/docs/latest/spiffe-about/overview/ — verified. **SPIFFE = Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone**; open-source specs for issuing identity to workloads across heterogeneous environments. Core artifact = **SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document)** — a *short-lived* cryptographic identity (X.509 cert or JWT) delivered via the **Workload API** for automatic rotation. **SPIRE** is the reference runtime (supports X.509+JWT SVIDs, node/workload attestation, federation).
- SDLC/agent relevance: This is the standard way to give each agent a **scoped, attested, auto-rotating workload identity** (rather than a static API key), enabling least-privilege mTLS/JWT authentication between agents and the graph/tools.

### 12. EU AI Act + DORA 🟢 (official EUR-Lex legislation)

- **EU AI Act:** Regulation (EU) **2024/1689** of 13 June 2024, "laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)." Official OJ text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj — verified (title, date, EEA relevance, risk-based framework confirmed in recitals). Note: financial-sector recitals reference the ECB opinion; the Act uses a risk-tiered model (unacceptable/high-risk/limited/minimal).
- **DORA:** Regulation (EU) **2022/2554** of 14 December 2022, "on digital operational resilience for the financial sector." Official OJ text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2554/oj — verified. Substance: harmonizes ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, and third-party (incl. cloud/ICT provider) oversight across ~**22,000 EU financial entities** (figure stated in Recital 3).

## CLUSTER 4 — Cost / token economics 🟠 **(all VENDOR — Anthropic docs)**

### 13. Prompt caching, Message Batches, model routing, real token figures

**Prompt caching:** https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching (redirected from docs.anthropic.com) — verified. Mechanics: `cache_control: {type: "ephemeral"}` on prompt prefixes; **5-minute or 1-hour TTLs**; automatic caching or explicit breakpoints. **Pricing multipliers (verified from the pricing table):**
- 5-minute cache **write = 1.25× base input**; 1-hour cache **write = 2× base input**; cache **read = 0.1× base input** (i.e., ~90% cheaper on cache hits). "These multipliers stack with… the Batch API discount."

**Message Batches API (50% discount):** https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing — verified. **"reducing costs by 50% and increasing throughput"**; asynchronous; most batches finish **< 1 hour**; hard limits **100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch**; results retrievable when done or after 24h (whichever first), available for **29 days**.

**Model routing (small vs. large):** From "Building Effective Agents" (item 3A) — the **Routing** workflow explicitly recommends *"Routing easy/common questions to smaller, cost-efficient models like Claude Haiku 4.5 and hard/unusual questions to more capable models like Claude Sonnet 4.5."* Reinforced by the price gap in the caching-page table (e.g., **Haiku 4.5 = $1/MTok input** vs **Sonnet 5 = $2/MTok** vs **Opus 5 = $5/MTok**).

**Real-deployment token figures (the headline you referenced):** From the multi-agent research post (item 3B): *"agents typically use about **4× more tokens** than chat interactions, and **multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens** than chats,"* so multi-agent economics only work "where the value of the task is high enough." Also: token usage explained **80%** of BrowseComp performance variance.

## CLUSTER 5 — Production failure modes

### 14. Context poisoning / rot / "lost in the middle"

**"Lost in the Middle"** 🟢 (peer-reviewed): Liu, N. F., Lin, K., Hewitt, J., Paranjape, A., Bevilacqua, M., Petroni, F., Liang, P. (2023). "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts." arXiv:2307.03172; **published in TACL 2024**. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172 — verified via arXiv API. Finding: performance is **highest when relevant info is at the beginning or end of the context and degrades significantly in the middle** (U-shaped curve), even for explicitly long-context models — tested on multi-document QA and key-value retrieval.

**Drew Breunig — "How Long Contexts Fail"** 🟢-ish (independent engineer, well-sourced): https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html — verified. Defines four failure modes with primary citations:
- **Context Poisoning** — a hallucination/error enters context and is repeatedly referenced; cites Google DeepMind's **Gemini 2.5 technical report** (Pokémon agent fixating on impossible goals). https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_v2_5_report.pdf
- **Context Distraction** — context grows so long the model over-focuses on history and repeats past actions instead of reasoning; cites a **Databricks** study finding Llama 3.1 405B correctness begins falling around **32k tokens**. https://www.databricks.com/blog/long-context-rag-performance-llms
- **Context Confusion** — too many/irrelevant tools degrade output; cites the **Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard** (every model does worse with >1 tool) and a GeoEngine case where a quantized Llama 3.1 8B failed with 46 tools but succeeded with 19.
- **Context Clash** — accrued context self-contradicts; cites a **Microsoft/Salesforce** paper (arXiv:2505.06120): "sharded" multi-turn prompts caused an **average 39% performance drop**, with **OpenAI o3 falling from 98.1 → 64.1** — "when LLMs take a wrong turn… they get lost and do not recover."
- Follow-up (mitigations): "How to Fix Your Context," https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/26/how-to-fix-your-context.html

**Chroma — "Context Rot"** 🟠 (VENDOR — Chroma, but a controlled research report): https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot (redirects to https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot) — verified. Evaluated **18 LLMs**, holding task complexity constant while varying only input length; shows **non-uniform performance degradation as input grows**, even on simple tasks. Argues Needle-in-a-Haystack (lexical) overstates real long-context ability; uses NoLiMa (non-lexical: 72.4% of pairs need external knowledge), LongMemEval, and distractor experiments. Replication code: https://github.com/chroma-core/context-rot

### 15. Error compounding, non-determinism, agent sprawl, eval gaps 🟠 **(VENDOR post-mortems, but concrete)**

**Anthropic multi-agent post** (item 3B URL) — production-reliability section, verified quotes:
- **Error compounding:** *"Agents are stateful and errors compound… minor system failures can be catastrophic."* Mitigations: resume-from-checkpoint execution, retry logic, regular checkpoints, letting the model adapt to failing tools.
- **Non-determinism:** *"Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts,"* which breaks conventional debugging → they added full production tracing + decision-pattern monitoring.
- **Emergent behavior / coordination:** *"small changes to the lead agent can unpredictably change how subagents behave."*
- **Agent sprawl:** early agents "spawning 50 subagents for simple queries," "scouring the web endlessly for nonexistent sources."
- **Eval gaps:** LLM-as-judge scaled evaluation, but **"human evaluation catches what automation misses"** (e.g., agents preferring SEO content farms over authoritative academic PDFs). Also notes synchronous subagent execution creates bottlenecks; uses **rainbow deployments** to avoid breaking in-flight agents.
- Self-improvement figure: a tool-testing agent that rewrote tool descriptions **"resulted in a 40% decrease in task completion time"** (⚠️ the sentence was truncated at my capture point at "40% decrease in…"; the "task completion time" completion is the widely-cited reading of this passage — verify against the live page if quoting exactly).

**Cognition post** (item 4 URL) — the compounding-error argument from the builder's side: parallel subagents make "implicit decisions" that conflict and cannot be reconciled at merge time; reliability requires continuous shared context, hence single-threaded-by-default.

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11532v3</id>
    <title>CKGFuzzer: LLM-Based Fuzz Driver Generation Enhanced By Code Knowledge Graph</title>
    <updated>2024-12-20T11:25:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11532v3" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.11532v3" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In recent years, the programming capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have garnered significant attention. Fuzz testing, a highly effective technique, plays a key role in enhancing software reliability and detecting vulnerabilities. However, traditional fuzz testing tools rely on manually crafted fuzz drivers, which can limit both testing efficiency and effectiveness. To address this challenge, we propose an automated fuzz testing method driven by a code knowledge graph and powered by an LLM-based intelligent agent system, referred to as CKGFuzzer. We approach fuzz driver creation as a code generation task, leveraging the knowledge graph of the code repository to automate the generation process within the fuzzing loop, while continuously refining both the fuzz driver and input seeds. The code knowledge graph is constructed through interprocedural program analysis, where each node in the graph represents a code entity, such as a function or a file. The knowledge graph-enhanced CKGFuzzer not only effectively resolves compilation errors in fuzz drivers and generates input seeds tailored to specific API usage scenarios, but also analyzes fuzz driver crash reports, assisting developers in improving code quality. By querying the knowledge graph of the code repository and learning from API usage scenarios, we can better identify testing targets and understand the specific purpose of each fuzz driver. We evaluated our approach using eight open-source software projects. The experimental results indicate that CKGFuzzer achieved an average improvement of 8.73% in code coverage compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, CKGFuzzer reduced the manual review workload in crash case analysis by 84.4% and successfully detected 11 real bugs (including nine previously unreported bugs) across the tested libraries.</summary>

    <summary>Knowledge graphs have been proven extremely useful in powering diverse applications in semantic search and natural language understanding. In this paper, we present GraphGen4Code, a toolkit to build code knowledge graphs that can similarly power various applications such as program search, code understanding, bug detection, and code automation. GraphGen4Code uses generic techniques to capture code semantics with the key nodes in the graph representing classes, functions, and methods. Edges indicate function usage (e.g., how data flows through function calls, as derived from program analysis of real code), and documentation about functions (e.g., code documentation, usage documentation, or forum discussions such as StackOverflow). Our toolkit uses named graphs in RDF to model graphs per program, or can output graphs as JSON. We show the scalability of the toolkit by applying it to 1.3 million Python file

// An index contains one or more pieces of information about a given piece of
// source code or software artifact. Complementary information can be merged
// together from multiple sources to provide a unified code intelligence
// experience.
//
// Programs producing a file of this format is an "indexer" and may operate
// somewhere on the spectrum between precision, such as indexes produced by
// compiler-backed indexers, and heurstics, such as indexes produced by local
// syntax-directed analysis for scope rules.

syntax = "proto3";

package scip;

option go_package = "github.com/scip-code/scip/bindings/go/scip/";
option java_multiple_files = true;
option java_outer_classname = "ScipProto";
option java_package = "org.scip_code.scip";

// Index represents a complete SCIP index for a workspace this is rooted at a
// single directory. An Index message payload can have a large memory footprint
// and it's therefore recommended to emit and consume an Index payload one field
// value at a time. To permit streaming consumption of an Index payload, the
// `metadata` field must appear at the start of the stream and must only appear
// once in the stream. Other field values may appear in any order.
message Index {
  // Metadata about this index.
  Metadata metadata = 1;
  // Documents that belong to this index.
  repeated Document documents = 2;
  // (optional) Symbols that are referenced from this index but are defined in
  // an external package (a separate `Index` message). Leave this field empty
  // if you assume the external package will get indexed separately. If the
  // external package won't get indexed for some reason then you can use this
  // field to provide hover documentation for those external symbols.
  repeated SymbolInformation external_symbols = 3;
  // IMPORTANT: When adding a new field to `Index` here, add a matching
  // function in `IndexVisitor` and update `ParseStreaming`.
}

message Metadata {
  // Which version of this protocol was used to generate this index?
  ProtocolVersion version = 1;
  // Information about the tool that produced this index.
  ToolInfo tool_info = 2;
  // URI-encoded absolute path to the root directory of this index. All
  // documents in this index must appear in a subdirectory of this root
  // directory.
  string project_root = 3;
  // Text encoding of the source files on disk that are referenced from
  // `Document.relative_path`. This value is unrelated to the `Document.text`
  // field, which is a Protobuf string and hence must be UTF-8 encoded.
  TextEncoding text_document_encoding = 4;
}

enum ProtocolVersion {
  UnspecifiedProtocolVersion = 0;
}

enum TextEncoding {
  UnspecifiedTextEncoding = 0;
  UTF8 = 1;
  UTF16 = 2;
}

message ToolInfo {
  // Name of the indexer that produced this index.
  string name = 1;
  // Version of the indexer that produced this index.
  string version = 2;
  // Command-line arguments that were used to invoke this indexer.
  repeated string arguments = 3;
}

// Document defines the metadata about a source file on disk.
message Document {
  // The string ID for the programming language this file is written in.
  // The `Language` enum contains the names of most common programming languages.
  // This field is typed as a string to permit any programming language, including
  // ones that are not specified by the `Language` enum.
  string language = 4;
  // (Required) Unique path to the text document.
  //
  // 1. The path must be relative to the directory supplied in the associated

  // 2. The path must not begin with a leading '/'.
  // 3. The path must point to a regular file, not a symbolic link.
  // 4. The path must use '/' as the separator, including on Windows.
  // 5. The path must be canonical; it cannot include empty components ('//'),

  string relative_path = 1;
  // Occurrences that appear in this file.

  // Symbols that are "defined" within this document.
  //
  // This should include symbols which technically do not have any definition,

[music] >> All right. At Neo4j, we work with some of the largest companies in the world to help make their data ready for AI agents. And today I want to talk to you 
about a problem that we saw emerging over the last, call it, 6 to 9 months and propose a solution blueprint for that. So, let's say that we work at a big organization, a 
big bank, and we want to write an agent. Let's say that agent is helping automate the opening of a bank account. Right? You can imagine that's very ripe for automation. 
You want to be able to orchestrate that process. And I'm going to use the powers bestowed upon me by a short keynote slot to grossly simplify what that agent looks like. 
I'm going to say there's two pieces. The first one is, let's call it, the business logic. Some version of interpreting intent and plan, act, and we loop around that. 
It's what your agent does. And we know that when an agent act, it doesn't always operate on data, but we equally know that in order for agents to be successful, a huge 
part of that is giving it access to the right data at the right time. So, the second big bucket is, let's call it, the data sources. Need to identify, figure out, okay, 
in order to solve my problem, I need access to these few things, and wire them up and make them available to the agent. In the example of our account opening agent, 
maybe we can imagine that we need to be able to validate identity. And so, we might look at two data sources for that, the Department of Motor Vehicles, the DMV 
registry, and maybe some kind of passport verification service. So, we wire that up into our agent, and it works. It's great. It's fantastic. And at the same time, you 
and other teams in your organization are building other agents, and conceptually, they look very similar. That's great. It's fantastic. It works. But, it has a few 
problems. So, first of all, every single time a team has to build an agent, they have to figure out from scratch where the data that they require for that agent to 
operate, where it sits, which if you work at a startup and you have one application, it sits on top of one Postgres database, that's not hard. The data is in that 
Postgres database. But, in an enterprise ecosystem, you don't have one database, you have a hundred databases, and you have Snowflake and Databricks, probably, and you 
have S3 buckets, and so on and so forth. You have to do that work manually from scratch every single time. And then, when you found the data sources, you know, in an 
enterprise, there's lots of duplication of data. So, then you need to figure out like, is this the right data? Is it the right version? Can I trust it? Am I allowed to 
access it? So on and so forth. It also violates one of the core principles of software engineering, the DRY principle, don't repeat yourself. So, when something change, 
that cascades across all of your agents. You have to kind of manually rewire all of them all the time, which works, but it's just a a lot of work. And then, finally, 
there's no learning around the data sources and how your agents operate on them. So, when your agent wake up wakes up tomorrow, it's not smarter than it was today, and 
there certainly isn't any cross-agent learning because all of that wiring between business intent and the data sources is encoded in a combination of code and prompts. 
So, I know what you're all thinking. Markdown files, skills to the rescue. And yes and no. Um you can come talk to me afterwards for kind of the full version of this, 
but we've seen a ton of team that tried to solve this problem using just Markdown files. And the summary is it is part of the solution, but it is not the solution. Uh 
but, don't take it from me, take it from Swyx. A week ago on the Latent Space Spot podcast, I said, "Hey guys, you got to learn your databases. You cannot vibe code with 
just markdown files." So, we've been solving this problem at scale for some really massive organizations recently, including a Fortune 20 global bank, a massive tech 
platform company based here in the Bay Area, and a leading fintech company. And the pattern that is emerging is that in order to do things at scale, we need thin agents 
on a smarter shared substrate. Thin agents on a smarter shared substrate. And what does that look like in practice? There are three pillars to that. The first pillar is 
a business-facing ontology. And the word ontology, like I grew up in this world, people talked about ontologies forever. More recently, it's become very hype, probably 
thanks to Palantir, but also the rise of AI. And there's a lot of people who want to make ontologies really complex. But the core concepts are actually super simple. 
What are the key concepts in your organization? In our banking example, customers, accounts, um debit cards, checks, transactions, and how do they all relate? But very 
importantly, they are expressed in a way that makes sense to all the human beings working in your universe, right? All the people working in your company, it's expressed 
in that name, in that way. In other words, you don't say if underscore name. No, you have a customer and they have a first name. So, that's the first, a business-facing 
ontology. The second pillar is a technical ontology. This is all the metadata of all the data sources and data assets in your enterprise ecosystem. I have 14 Oracle 
databases, I have 15 Neo4j databases, I have Snowflake and Databricks and I have S3 buckets and all all that kind of stuff. Where do they sit? What are the schemas? All 
of that kind of good stuff. You can You construct that technical ontology in three key ways that we can talk about later, though not in this in this talk. And then you 
have a mapping between the two. So that customer that has a first name, that first name has a system of record and over there there's an Oracle database with a column 
called F_name. The mapping between the two. And then the third pillar is the run time signals out of your agents. When they walk this graph and they execute, they leave 
the traces around. What have I tried? Was I successful? What was the outcome? The execution traces. Those three pillars. Okay, so let's look at that in the context of 
our bank account opening agent. This is a simplified view, but you can see this graph here. It has a combination of business concepts like checks and accounts and credit 
history and stuff like that. This is a process following agent or a process guided agent. We want this type of agent to actually follow a process. We've also encoded 
that in the ontology, a business process. And then if you look at the node that is surrounded by green, the check compliance one, we flip to the technical ontology and 
we've put in the graph here. We've discovered and encoded that in order to do a compliance check, you might imagine that you need to resolve a government issued ID. And 
then we say that in this particular organization, there are two data sources that can help us with that. It's the motor vehicle records and the passport verification 
one. Which is that's really great. So then when our agents come in here and they realize I'm going to check compliance, I need a government issued ID. Here are the two 
ways that I can resolve that. When they execute and they try that, they leave the third pillar, the execution traces for that. And they're more sophisticated than what's 
on this simplified slide, but involves things like, okay, where was I? What did I do? What is my context? And was I successful? And ultimately it leads out to some kind 
of a score. And you use that as input. It's like, okay, I've been very successful using the DMV lookup, for example, then I'm more likely to choose one if I'm in the 
right context in my next invocation. Three pillars of the ontology-based semantic layer, a business ontology, a technical ontology, the execution traces taken together, 
they solve all four of the problems. We now have a very easy way to discover the data sources. We know if they're trustworthy or not. We know that top-down by some kind 
of human curated knowledge, right? An administrator of some sort saying it. We also know it bottom-up through the execution traces. This is what actually worked in 
reality, in practice. We have a single governed place that maps business intent and the concepts to those data sources. So, we don't repeat ourselves. If something 
changes, that cascades across all my agents, right? And we have self-learning. So, my agent that wakes up tomorrow is slightly smarter than it was today. And not just 
self-learning on an individual agent, but across agents as well. So, we're moving from this world, a world of thick agents with manually wired data sources, into this 
world where we have thin agents on a smarter shared ontology-based semantic layer. And this allows us to do a ton more agents without having to re-engineer them every 
time. Thin agents on top of a smarter shared substrate. If you think this is interesting, there's a documentation webpage that outlines more information about this. If 
you see the QR code here, you can also come and talk to us at the booth. We have a big booth here at the Expo, P3. We love talking about this this kind of stuff. But not

                            Inspiring Brilliance




The Practical Guide to
